Latest Update: What to Do About These High Interest Rates

📅 04 Sep 2023 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2555 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Whoa, have you seen what just happened to interest rates!?
  • Suddenly, after at least fourteen years of our financial world being mostly the same, somebody flipped over the table and now things are quite different.
  • Interest rates, which have been gliding along at close to zero since before the Dawn of Mustachianism in 2011, have suddenly shot back up to 20-year highs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Whoa, have you seen what just happened to interest rates!?

Suddenly, after at least fourteen years of our financial world being mostly the same, somebody flipped over the table and now things are quite different.

Interest rates, which have been gliding along at close to zero since before the Dawn of Mustachianism in 2011, have suddenly shot back up to 20-year highs.

Which brings up a few questions about whether we need to worry, or do anything about this fresh development.

These questions are on everybody’s mind these days, and I’ve been ruminating on them myself. But while I’ve seen a lot of play-by-play stories about each little interest rate increase in the financial newspapers, none of them seem to get into the crucial part, which is,.

“Yeah, interest rates are way up, but what should I do about it?”.

Why Is This Happening, and What Got Us Here?

Interest rates are like a giant gas pedal that revs the engine of our economy, with the polished black dress shoe of Federal Reserve Chairman Jerome Powell pressed upon it.

For most of the past two decades, Jerome’s team and their predecessors have kept the pedal to the metal, firing a highly combustible stream of easy money into the system in the form of near-zero rates. This made mortgages more affordable, so everyone stretched to buy houses, which drove demand for existing homes and latest construction alike.

According to recent reports, it also had a similar effect on business investment: borrowed money and venture capital was cheap, so lots of entrepreneurs borrowed lots of money and started new companies. These companies then rented offices and built factories and hired employees – who circled back to buy more houses, cars, fridges, iPhones, and all the other luxurious amenities of modern life.

This was a great party and it led to lots of good things, because we had two decades of prosperity, growth, raising our children, inventing latest things and all the other good stuff that happens in a successful rich country economy.

Until it went too far and we ended up with too much money chasing too few goods – especially houses. That led to a trend of unacceptably fast Inflation, which we already covered in a recent article.

According to recent reports, so eventually, Jay-P noticed this and eased his foot back off of the Easy Money Gas Pedal. And of course when interest rates get jacked up, almost everything else in the economy slows down.

In a recent development, and that’s what is happening right now: mortgages are suddenly way more expensive, so people are putting off their looks to buy houses. Companies find that borrowing money is costly, so they are scaling back their plans to build new factories, and cutting back on their hiring. Facebook laid off 10,000 people and Amazon shed 27,000.

We even had a miniature banking crisis where some significant mid-sized banks folded and gave the financial world fears that a much bigger set of dominoes would fall.

All of these things sound kinda bad, and if you make the mistake of checking the news, you’ll see there is a big dumb battle raging as usual on every media outlet. Leftists, Right-wingers, and anarchists all have a different take on it:.

The one thing all sides seem to agree on is that we are “experiencing hard economic times” and that “the country is headed in the wrong way”.

Which, ironically, is completely wrong as well – our unemployment rate has dropped to 50-year lows and the economy is at the absolute best it has ever been, a surprise to even the most grounded economists.

Recent findings suggest that the reality? We’re just putting the lid back onto the ice cream carton until the economy can digest all the sugar it just wolfed down. This is normal, it happens every decade or two and it’s no massive deal.

Okay, but should I take my money out of the stock market because it’s going to crash?

This answer never changes, so you’ll see it every time we talk about stock investing: Holy Shit NO!!!

Sources indicate that the stock market always goes up in the long run, although with plenty of unpredictable bumps along the way. Since you can’t predict those bumps until after they happen, there is no point in trying to dance in and out of it.

In a recent development, but since we do have the benefit of hindsight, there are a few things that have changed slightly: From its peak at the beginning of 2022 until right now (August 2023 as I write this), the overall US market is down about 10%. Or to view it another way, it is roughly flat since June 2021, so we’ve seen two years with no gains aside from total dividends of about 3%.

Since the future is always the same, unknowable thing, this means I am about 10% more excited about buying my monthly slice of index funds today than I was at those peak prices.

Should I start putting money into savings accounts instead because they are paying 4.5%?

This is a slightly trickier question, because in theory we should invest in a logical, unbiased way into the thing with the highest expected return over time.

When interest rates were under 1%, this was an easy decision: stocks will always return far more than 1% over time – consider the fact that the annual dividend payments alone are 1.5%!

But there has to be some interest rate at which you’d be willing to stop buying stocks and prefer to just stash it into the stable, rewarding environment of a money market fund or long-term bonds or something else similar. Right now, if a reputable bank offered me, say, 12% I would probably just start loading up.

It has been revealed that but remember that the stock market is also currently running a 10% off sale. When the market eventually reawakens and starts setting newly introduced highs (which it will someday), any shares I buy right now will be worth 10% more. And then will continue going up from there. Which quickly becomes an even bigger number than 12%.

In other words, the cheaper the stocks get, the more excited we should be about buying them rather than chasing high interest rates.

As you can see, there is no easy answer here, but I have taken a middle ground:.

It has been revealed that for most of us, the biggest thing that interest rates affect is our decisions around buying and selling houses. Financing a home with a mortgage is suddenly way more expensive, any potential rental house investments are suddenly far less profitable, and keeping our old house with a locked-in 3% mortgage is suddenly far more tempting.

Consider these shocking changes just over the past two years as typical rates have gone from about 3% to 7.5%.

Assuming a buyer comes up with the average 10% down payment:.

This all sounds kind of bleak, but unfortunately it’s the way things are supposed to work – the tough medicine of higher interest rates is supposed to make the following things happen:.

The net effect of all this is that prices should stop going up, and ideally fall back down in many areas.

When Will House Prices Go Back Down?

This is a tricky one because the real “value” of a house depends entirely on supply and demand. The right price is whatever somebody is willing to pay for it. However, there are a few fundamentals which influence this price over the long run because they determine the supply of housing.

The first item (construction cost) is pretty interesting because it is subject to the magic of technological progress. Just as TVs and computers get cheaper over time, house components get cheaper too as things like computerized manufacturing and global trade make us more efficient.

I remember paying $600 for a fancy-at-the-time undermount sink and $400 for a faucet for my first kitchen remodel in the year 2001. Today, you can get a nicer sink on Amazon for about $250 and the faucet is a flat hundred. Similarly, nailguns and cordless tools and easy-to-install PEX plumbing make the process of building faster and easier than ever.

On the other hand, the last item (bullshit restrictions) has been very inflationary in recent times. I’ve noticed that every year another layer of red tape and complicated codes and onerous zoning and approval processes gets layered into the local book of rules, and as a result I just gave up on building new houses because it wasn’t worth the hassle. Other builders with more patience will continue to plow through the murk, but they will have less competition, fewer permits will be granted, and thus the shortage of housing will continue to grow, which raises prices on average.

Recent findings suggest that thankfully, every city is different and some have chosen to make it easier to build upcoming houses rather than more difficult. Even better, places like Tempe Arizona are allowing good housing to be built around people rather than cars, which is even more affordable to construct.

But overall, since overall US house prices adjusted for inflation are just about at an all-time high, I think there’s a chance that they might ease back down another 25% (to 2020 levels). But who knows: my guess could prove totally wrong, or the “fall” could just come in the form of flat prices for a decade that don’t keep up with inflation, meaning that they just feel 25% cheaper relative to our higher future salaries.

When Will Interest Rates Go Back Down?

The funny part about our current “high” interest rates is that they are not actually high at all. They’re right around average.So they might not go down at all for a long time.

Industry observers note that remember that graph at the beginning of this article? I deliberately cropped it to show only the years since 2009 – the long recent period of low interest rates. But if you zoom out to cover the last seventy years instead, you can see that we’re still in a very normal range.

Recent findings suggest that but a better answer is this one: Interest rates will go down whenever Jerome Powell or one of his successors determines that our economy is slowing down too much and needs another hit from the gas pedal. In other words, whenever we start to slip into a genuine recession.

In order to do that however, we need to see low inflation, growing unemployment, and other signs of an economy that is finally cooling down. And right now, those things keep not showing up in the weekly economic data.

You can get one reasonable prediction of the future of interest rates by looking at something called the US Treasury Yield Curve. It typically looks like this:.

In a recent development, what the graph is telling you is that as a lender you get a bigger reward in exchange for locking up your money for a longer time period. And way back in 2018, the people who make these loans expected that interest rates would average about 3.0 percent over the next 30 years.

Today, we have a very strange opposite yield curve:.

It has been revealed that if you want to lend money for a year or less, you’ll be rewarded with a juicy 5.4 percent interest rate. But for two years, the rate drops to 4.92%. And then ten-year bond pays only 4.05 percent.

This situation is weird, and it’s called an inverted yield curve. And what it means is that the buyers of bonds at the moment believe that interest rates will almost certainly drop in the future – starting a little over a year from now.

Sources indicate that and if you recall our earlier discussion about why interest rates drop, this means that investors are forecasting an economic slowdown in the fairly near future. And their intuition in this department has been pretty good: an inverted yield curve like this has only happened 11 times in the past 75 years, and in ten of those cases it accurately predicted a recession.

So the short answer is: nobody really knows, but just for fun I’ll make a guess. Then if I’m wrong in public, you can come back and make fun of this in the comments.

I think we’ll probably see interest rates start to drop within 18-24 months, and the event may be accompanied by some sort of recession as well.

The Ultimate Interest Rate Strategy Hack.

In a recent development, I like to read and write about all this stuff because I’m still a finance nerd at heart. But when it comes down to it, interest rates don’t really affect long-retired people like many of us MMM readers, because we are mostly done with borrowing. I like the simplicity of owning just one house and one car, mortgage-free.

Industry observers note that with the current overheated housing market here in Colorado, I’m not tempted to even look at other properties, but someday that may change. And the great thing about having actual savings rather than just a high income that lets you qualify for a loan, is that you can be ready to pounce on a good deal on short notice.

Industry observers note that maybe the entire housing market will go on sale as we saw in the early 2010s, or perhaps just one perfect property in the mountains will come up at the right time. The point is that when you have enough cash to buy the thing you want, the interest rates that other people are charging don’t matter. It’s a nice position of strength instead of stress. And you can still decide to take out a mortgage if you do find the rates are worthwhile for your own goals.

Recent findings suggest that so to tie a bow on this whole lesson: keep your lifestyle lean and happy and don’t lose too much sweat over today’s interest rates or house prices. They will probably both come down over time, but those things aren’t in your control. Much more important are your own choices about earning, saving, healthy living and where you choose to live.

With these big sails of your life properly in place and pulling you ahead, the smaller concerns of interest rates and whatever else they write about in the financial news will gradually shrink down to become just ripples on the surface of the lake.

Sources indicate that in the comments: what have you been thinking about interest rates recently? Have they changed your decisions, increased, or perhaps even decreased your stress levels around money and housing?

Wahoo’s Elemnt Bolt 3 is a favorite of our editors and test riders for its small size, accuracy, and ease of use. The Bolt features a 2.3-inch full-color display, 20-hour battery life, and an 85-gram weight. For simple operation and a lower price, the Bolt uses buttons instead of a touchscreen.

Keep your hot drinks warm on cold winter rides. CamelBak’s Podium bottles are popular among gravel and off-road riders due to their open/closed twist-lock cap. The Podium Steel is a vacuum-sealed insulated stainless steel version of the brand’s classic plastic Podium model. It’s a classy-looking bottle and available in several colors. Plus, CamelBak offers custom printing on these bottles through its site.

Industry observers note that last winter, I tested 8 of the top insulated bottles in winter conditions. Read about the testing and results: “Some Insulated Bike Bottles Promise 12 Hours of Hot Drinks. Which Ones Survived Our Experts’ Sub‑Freezing Tests?”.

In a recent development, cycling radars are a new technology that gets a lot of attention for keeping riders safe on the road. Mirrors have been around for generations and do a great job, never require charging, and don’t chirp endlessly in traffic. I added a Spurcycle mirror to my custom bike this summer. I love its simplicity and clean looks—it doesn’t look out of place, even on high-end race bikes.

Recent findings suggest that “Flat pedals win medals” is an age-old bike saying. While many riders have switched to clipless pedals for road and gravel, many prefer flats for mountain biking and commuting. They’re intuitive, compatible with almost any shoes, and you never have to worry about unclipping too late. OneUp’s Composite Pedals are lightweight and durable—plus they’re available in two sizes and six colors.

According to recent reports, lazer’s Tonic Kineticore helmet performs much better than its $80 MSRP suggests—and at $60 (25% off), it’s a steal. At 240 grams, the Tonic is relatively light for its price. It features a modern road aesthetic and has comfortable, easy-to-adjust straps. Lazer offers the Tonic in four sizes, and four color options are on sale. It’s a solid pick for any road or gravel rider.

In a recent development, wahoo reinvented indoor training when it released its original Kickr in 2012. Now on its sixth generation, the Kickr remains our top pick for high-performance indoor smart trainers. The Kickr is super accurate, folds easily for storage, and is stable during workouts. The latest version adds WiFi connectivity, which enhances connection speeds during Zwift rides and races.

Garmin’s Tacx Neo 2 sits at the top of the performance-trainer pyramid. However, most indoor cyclists don’t need its pricey features. The Tacx Flux 2 has a large 7.6 kg flywheel with up to 2,000 watts of resistance (more than enough for almost any rider). It also simulates gradients up to 16%, to replicate the toughest climbs in virtual cycling worlds such as Zwift and Rouvy.

Tights are a must-have for riding in temps below 45 degrees. Pearl Izumi’s Quest tights feature a soft ThermaFleece lining, thigh pockets to hold your phone or snacks, and a single-density chamois pad. Men’s and women’s sizing is available.

WOMEN’S QUEST TIGHTS - $110 $82.

Stay warm on winter rides and commutes with Pearl Izumi’s AmFib gloves. These gloves feature Primaloft insulation, AmFib material to block wind and rain, and synthetic leather palms for grip. Unlike many winter gloves, they’re touchscreen compatible. The AmFibs also have an extended cuff, so cold air doesn’t get into your gloves or jacket.

Recent findings suggest that rapha makes excellent, high-performance cycling apparel. However, it tends to be too pricey for many riders. The Core line is Rapha’s base-level kit, but it has much of the fit and comfort of the brand’s premium clothing. These bibs use the same chamois found in the more expensive Classic bibs. With proper care and washing, the bibs will last you several seasons.

We love these shorts because they’re great for hot summer rides and sweaty indoor workouts in the dead of winter. Plus, they have thigh pockets to hold your cell phone or snacks while you ride.

Recent findings suggest that if you log a lot of time on the trainer, it’s worth refreshing your shorts regularly; worn-out shorts are a recipe for discomfort. The extra sweat from indoor rides breaks down the chamois faster than outdoor miles and leads to saddle sores. At this price, you should grab a pair (or two!) before they sell out.

It’s notable to have a warm, thermal jersey in your closet when the temperature drops. On its own or paired with a light vest, this fleece grid jersey breathes well and keeps you from becoming sweaty and cold. On colder days, wear the Attack Thermal under a windproof jacket to keep your core insulated and cozy.

In a recent development, A test editor favorite for years, Smartwool’s socks are light—but not too light—and have the right amount of compression to keep your feet snug without feeling squeezed. When I find socks I love, I buy a pair every time they go on sale— you can never have too many cycling socks!

Industry observers note that for riders who only go full coverage when absolutely necessary, this waterproof cycling cap will be right in their wheelhouse. It offers extra protection from rain, sleet, and wind without added bulk. It’s thin and fits comfortably under a cycling helmet.

If you’re fresh to winter cycling, you need a thin hat like this one for cold days. It goes under your helmet while keeping your ears and forehead covered. And if you’ve been riding through winters for years, you probably need a new one anyway—that crusty old hat you bought a decade ago has definitely seen better days.

It has been revealed that the CTY 1.1, by REI’s Co-op Cycles house brand, is perfect for commuting, getting around town or campus, or leisurely weekend rides. REI equips the CTY with 40mm-wide, flat-resistant tires, a dependable Shimano 24-speed drivetrain, and disc brakes. The bike is available in five sizes (to fit riders from 5-foot to 6-foot-3) and two colors.

The Topstone 3 is a perfect entry point into gravel riding. It’s also a great upgrade for riders who need a dependable all-arounder for fitness, commuting, or even bikepacking. The Topstone features a high-quality aluminum frame and a carbon fork, equipped with plenty of mounts for racks, fenders, and bags. For climbing hills, the bike has a Shimano Cues 2x10-speed wide-range drivetrain and easy-to-maintain cable disc brakes for descents. At under $1,400, it’s a great deal for anyone looking for a versatile gravel or all-road bike.

Scott’s Speedster Gravel 30 notes exactly what it is upfront: a speedy gravel bike ideal for racing, group rides, or fast rides on unpaved roads. Sharing design elements with Scott’s more expensive gravel race bikes, the 30 features an aluminum frame, carbon fork, 45mm-wide tires, and a Shimano Cues 1x10 drivetrain with sure-stopping hydraulic disc brakes. The frame uses a UDH hanger, so it’s future-proof if you want to upgrade to a lighterweight groupset once you get addicted to the spirit of gravel.

#149707. Tech Report: Research Indicates Cold Muscles Produce Less Power. Here’s How to Protect Your Performance on Frigid Runs.

Tech Report: Research Indicates Cold Muscles Produce Less Power. Here’s How to Protect Your Performance on Frigid Runs.

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1558 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that when temperatures rise, running performance tends to drop.
  • But what about when the mercury moves in the opposite direction?
  • A recent review published in Temperature suggests it does.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that when temperatures rise, running performance tends to drop. Both the research and anyone who’s put in miles on a hot summer afternoon can confidently tell you that much.

But what about when the mercury moves in the opposite direction? Does colder weather in the winter—ranging from just a bit chilly to downright frigid—take a toll on your running too?

A recent review published in Temperature suggests it does. According to the study’s authors, when our muscles get too cold, neuromuscular function becomes impaired. On the run, this can contribute to stiffness, less power output, and decreased endurance, all of which may cause your winter workouts to feel harder than usual.

According to recent reports, the good news? You can still run strong when the temps drop—as long as you make a few key training adjustments before, during, and after you log your miles in the colder months of the year. Here’s how to do just that.

There’s no exact number on the thermometer at which runners can universally expect their power, speed, or endurance to decline, Stephen Cheung, PhD, the lead author of the aforementioned review, tells Runner’s World.

It has been revealed that temperature is just one of the many factors that contribute to how well we perform in the cold, Cheung explains. “It’s a function of the environment, as well as how much heat you’re generating, the speed that you’re moving at, and of course, the amount of clothing that you’re wearing,” he states.

Each of these factors varies significantly from runner to runner and affects how quickly their bodies lose heat. You only need to consider those in your run group who run shirtless when it’s freezing versus those who bundle up when it’s 50 degrees Fahrenheit to understand that we all thermoregulate (maintain our internal body temperature) differently. And the equation only becomes more complex when you account for wind and moisture—both in the environment and what you create yourself from air resistance and sweat.

In a recent development, heather Milton, CSCS, lead exercise physiologist at Primary MD and cofounder of Master My Run, agrees. “It would be great to be able to say, when the temperature outside reaches [a certain point], your pace slows down by this many seconds per mile—but that’s not how it works,” she notes.

Keeping this in mind, Milton says the cleanest reference point for runners to begin paying more attention to how they prepare for runs in the cold is when the temperature drops below freezing. Generally speaking, the colder it gets from there, the more noticeable the negative effects on performance will be, she explains.

Cold weather leads to vasoconstriction, Milton explains, which means our blood vessels constrict more, so the muscles farther away from the core don’t receive as much blood flow. If your fingers or toes have ever gone numb in the cold, for example, you’ve experienced the joy of vasoconstriction. Our bodies prioritize heating our core over our extremities because it helps our vital organs maintain a consistent temperature, which is essential for survival in dangerous conditions.

This physiological response, however, doesn’t bode especially well for running performance.

Sources indicate that “The cold slows nerve conduction so you have to work harder for the same power output,” Milton says. “And as temperatures drop further below freezing, that slower nerve conduction and the effects of vasoconstriction are going to be even more noticeable.” As a result, your overall exercise capacity decreases, meaning you may not be able to run for as long or at the same pace you normally would.

What else might you notice when temperatures drop? “Physically, if your muscles and tendons are cold, they’re going to be tighter, less elastic, and you won’t be able to contract them as strongly,” indicates Cheung. “Stiff muscles can also put you at greater risk for tears or strain injuries.”.

Milton claims this analogy, used by an old coach of hers, provides an easy way to understand what’s happening: When your muscles and tendons get too cold, they’re like a cold rubber band that can snap when pulled.

Industry observers note that if you’re a runner who dislikes the cold, you might wonder if the smarter choice is to just run on the treadmill this winter. Don’t worry: As long as you prepare appropriately and use caution, you can absolutely continue logging regular miles outdoors.

Sources indicate that running well outside in the cold starts with warming up indoors first, claims Milton. “An indoor warmup increases your internal metabolism and enhances blood flow, which helps prepare your muscles for contraction,” she explains. This also produces heat so your internal body temperature is more resilient to the cold outdoor environment.

Your winter warmup does not have to be any different or longer than your usual routine, Milton states. But you do want to make sure that you’re getting in a solid five minutes of prerun drills to adequately raise your body temperature and activate your muscles.

Industry observers note that she recommends starting with slower, more controlled movements that help activate the core and the glutes, such as planks with leg raises, lunges with rotation, and hip CARs (controlled articular rotations). Finish with quicker drills that require your nerves to fire more rapidly, such as leg swings and butt kicks.

Equally important to warming up is layering up—with an important caveat.

Sources indicate that when dressing for winter runs, keep in mind how you personally respond to cold temperatures, says Cheung, because everyone has different tolerances and susceptibilities. “I get very cold in my hands, so I’ll wear really thick gloves, even when I may be wearing relatively little on my torso,” he adds. “Pay attention to what’s an problem for you and adapt your clothing to both the conditions and your own peculiarities.” Cheung emphasizes this because you don’t want to end up sweating too heavily, which can then leave you chilled and clammy.

It has been revealed that if you need a starting point for your winter running wardrobe, aim for two to three layers of breathable, moisture-wicking fabrics. If possible, choose a wind- and water-resistant shell for your outermost layer, suggests Milton. For your lower body, wear shorts over your tights to help keep your glutes warm. Finally, cover any exposed skin on your head, ears, and hands, and opt for a pair of wool socks—all of which can help ensure adequate blood distribution to the extremities, Milton adds.

When you head out for runs in the cold, slowly build up to your usual pace.

In a recent development, gradually easing into your workout gives your muscles more time to adjust, and it can also help your airways get used to the colder temperatures, Milton says. You don’t necessarily need to go slower for your entire run, but you should try to match your rate of perceived exertion (RPE) with your typical effort, rather than aiming for your usual pace or heart-rate zone.

According to recent reports, “Think about it the same way as if you were running on an extremely hot day,” Milton indicates. “Let’s say your RPE for an easy run is about 3 out of 10. Keep that 3 out of 10, even if your pace is a little slower.”.

In a recent development, if you find that your run feels more difficult than usual, slow down if you need to, but don’t stop completely, Cheung advises. “Don’t take long breaks, because that’s when you aren’t generating as much heat. Just keep moving so you have that constant heat generation,” he says.

Recent findings suggest that if you start to get cold on a run, try speeding up a little bit to stoke that metabolic heat production, Cheung states. But make sure you do it safely: Don’t force the effort in icy conditions or when your muscles feel especially stiff. Scouting out run routes with more tree coverage to block wind on blustery days can also help you stay warmer, he adds.

As soon as you finish your workout, change out of your sweaty running gear and into warm, dry clothes, Milton states.

Recent findings suggest that even if you’ve only sweated a small amount—for example, maybe you just have some dampness under your armpits—you still want to remove any wet fabrics against your skin. “Even that small amount of wetness can start to drop your core temperature,” Milton explains. If you wait until you’re near shivering, you’ll face an uphill battle to get yourself warm again.

You can also opt for a relaxing shower and hot chocolate—extra marshmallows.

Morgan is a gear editor who has been with Runner’s World since 2017. She started as an intern ghostwriting The Warmup, a bygone version of the daily RW newsletter. Now, she tests and reviews anything you might find on runners’ feet-from crew socks and compression boots to carbon-plated super shoes.

According to recent reports, A lifelong runner and shoe geek, Morgan has been chasing the perfect pair of kicks since she joined her grade school cross-country team. Since then, she ran as a Division I walk-on for the cross-country and track & field teams at the University of Delaware, where she studied English and Biology. She has one full marathon under her belt, and has raced more halfs and 5Ks than she can count.

#149704. Zwift’s Dedicated Indoor Bike Makes Your Winter Riding Better—and Protects Your Road Bike

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1321 w)

Zwift’s Dedicated Indoor Bike Makes Your Winter Riding Better—and Protects Your Road Bike

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1321 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Recent findings suggest that I’ve used a handful of indoor trainers over the years, but a few years ago I picked up a Wahoo Kickr Core and I thought that would be my trainer for the foreseeable future.
  • Sources indicate that when I ran a shop, we would sell through the Wahoo Kickr Core because it has always been a product I personally love—it is easier to sell products that I genuinely believe in and use.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve used a handful of indoor trainers over the years, but a few years ago I picked up a Wahoo Kickr Core and I thought that would be my trainer for the foreseeable future. It’s easy to use and reliable. It did exactly what I needed it to do—turn my bike into a trainer for offseason training.

Sources indicate that when I ran a shop, we would sell through the Wahoo Kickr Core because it has always been a product I personally love—it is easier to sell products that I genuinely believe in and use. More than that, every shop team I’ve worked with would use the Wahoo Kickr Core as their trainer of choice. Then I was introduced to the Zwift Ride and realized I was not done buying trainers just yet.

As the shop’s service manager, I got firsthand experience assessing bikes after a season of sitting on the trainer; let alone season after season, year after year. The level of maintenance needed for those bikes was initially shocking to me as well as to the customer. Most of us are aware we need to do maintenance on our bikes that we ride outside, but it’s easy to forget about our unsung hero—our trainer bike sitting in the basement constantly covered in sweat, spilled drink mix, and getting the watts cranked into it day in and day out.

There’s a better way than just throwing your bike on the trainer for your offseason. The Zwift Ride V2 with the Wahoo Kickr Core is now my top recommended way to use a bike trainer. It’s easy to see why.

Sources indicate that for those who have multiple riders in one house, this may be one of the biggest benefits. When I had my bike set up on the Kickr Core it was harder for my wife to just hop on the trainer. Since my old trainer bike was carbon, even a simple saddle adjustment required a torque wrench. I’ve even gone so far as to change out stems to change the reach too—not the hardest thing to do, but by no means convenient. On the Zwift Ride, most fit adjustments are super easy and take just seconds.

The Zwift Ride 2 I’ve been on even has multiple crank length options set up in the cranks, so you just swap the pedals to a different hole in the crank to change the effective crank length. Taking out one more friction point between me and being able to start my trainer ride means I’m even more likely to get my winter trainer miles in.

In a recent development, the other day I was a few minutes into my warmup and I needed to adjust my reach a bit. I pulled the integrated 6mm Allen key out from its place under the top tube, easily adjusted the reach at the handlebars, tightened everything down, and reinstalled the tool all without interrupting my cadence. Having the tool I need to adjust just about anything on the bike is a fresh level of convenience I was not used to.

It has been revealed that as Matt Phillips pointed out in his Zwift Ride 2 review, “Mechanically, the Ride is almost primitive.” For clarity, this is by no means a negative—when it comes to a trainer bike, mechanically primitive but extremely functional is a best-case scenario. This bike has a chain that goes from the chainring, through a chain tensioner, around the Zwift Cog attached to the Wahoo Kickr, and back up to the chainring. There’s no derailleur, no front tire that needs air, no brakes to knock out of alignment. The handlebars don’t even turn, so there’s no headset to replace in the spring because it was sitting in a pool with sweat all winter.

On the other side, you’re saving your daily driver from a lot of unseen mechanical damage. As the snow thaws out on the roads, road riders are ready to get back in the saddle under the sun, but if you use your bike on the trainer all winter, it may need A LOT of love before it’s road-worthy.

Industry observers note that A bike that sits on the trainer all winter collects significant corrosion in headset and bottom bracket bearings. The sweat that comes off your head drops straight onto your headset and sweat from your body (and any of those sticky drink mixes) drop straight down toward the bottom bracket. Then we get to the drivetrain. I’ve had bikes come in around March that need full drivetrain replacement: chainrings, cassette, and chain after a good season of indoor miles. Finally, we get to the handlebar—at a minimum you should replace that bar tape after a season riding on the trainer. This also gives you a chance to get the handlebar looked at to make sure all that corrosion (sweat) hasn’t eaten into the them.

It has been revealed that I’ve seen service tickets range anywhere from $100 to almost a thousand dollars just to get a bike off the trainer and ready to ride outside. For some people one season of trainer riding on the Zwift Ride 2 could be more cost-effective than using your road bike on a trainer.

Recent findings suggest that before an activity becomes a habit people are good at finding reasons not to do something. It doesn’t take long to setup a bike on the Wahoo Kickr Core, but even that little bit of set up time to pop your bike on the trainer is one more hurdle for you not to ride today. If you have to swap your cassette over from your bike to the trainer—you can almost forget about it.

Recent findings suggest that it doesn’t just go for getting your bike on the trainer. This week in Pennsylvania we’re having a stretch of perfect riding weather—relatively low humidity, sunny, and temperatures between 55 degrees and 60 degrees. Next week’s forecast calls for colder temperatures and rain, also known as great indoor-riding weather. But this week, if I have a window of time to ride, I want to be able to just hop on my bike and go; I don’t want to have to take the bike off the trainer and reinstall my cassette before I can even start pedaling outside. With a dedicated trainer setup, I can just take my bike off the hook on the wall and roll away. Next week, when the weather goes south, I can just hop back on the trainer.

According to recent reports, the Zwift Ride makes it easier to do things like use power-ups, steer the avatar, and toggle through screens, but those features are just an added bonus compared to the other reasons to pick one up. It is a burly, simple, near-flawless machine for riding on the trainer. It’s stable when putting out your max watts. The built-in tool makes it easy to accommodate different riders—including adjusting the reach. Even the bottle cages are designed to fit almost any bottle. The bike’s handlebar tray fits an iPad or other tablet well, but I pair it with a rolling trainer table if I’m using my laptop. You can buy the Zwift Ride itself, or as a package deal with Wahoo’s excellent Kickr Core 2, which gives you everything you need for a stress-free indoor riding season.

Jason Griffin is Bicycling's Senior Health and Fitness Editor, bringing more than a decade of fitness experience and years in the cycling industry to every story. A former personal trainer and bike shop manager, he's lined up for crits, tackled enduros, but prefers getting lost on multi-day bikepacking adventures. Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • There are moments on the trail when Karen Sparks stops running.
  • It has been revealed that karen took up running in the years after she lost her world.
  • Erwin Park rises rather unexpectedly out of ranchland and rolling prairie where longhorn cattle dot the landscape.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This story was originally published in June 2021.

There are moments on the trail when Karen Sparks stops running. She puts her hands to her knees, opens her mouth, and lets the sound that’s been building find release. The noise starts low and feral, then rises from the depths, growing sharp and loud enough to echo under the canopy of oaks where she runs each day. Karen doesn’t care who hears it. The sound fuels her.

It has been revealed that karen took up running in the years after she lost her world. She liked the feel of her feet pounding the earth; the shock and adrenaline needed somewhere to go. But it wasn’t until she discovered this wooded trail in Erwin Park in McKinney, Texas, that she felt something close to peace. Nature is her church. She was raised Baptist but can no longer bring herself to enter a church. She’s been angry with God.

Erwin Park rises rather unexpectedly out of ranchland and rolling prairie where longhorn cattle dot the landscape. Tucked away inside the trees, Karen feels protected. She talks to her kids. She talks to herself. She runs along the dry-cracked mud, next to riverbeds and over trees fallen in the path.

Karen strained her piriformis, a buttock muscle, when she was younger. She’s 43 now, and sometimes when she’s running her hamstrings get so tight it feels like her muscles might rip. Maybe she likes being in pain, or maybe she likes knowing that the pain does not own her. Anyway, she’s in pain all the time. Spiritually, emotionally, physically. When it gets bad, she tries talking to her body. I’m grateful for this hamstring, she claims. I’m grateful for this pain. She thinks about people who can’t do this. Because they’re in a wheelchair or in a hospital bed, or because they’re not here anymore.

She thinks about Reagan and Grant.

On the fifth anniversary of their death, November 1, 2015, she ran a hundred miles on the nine-mile loop in Erwin Park. She’d originally signed up for the Indiana Trail 100, but the pandemic brought an end to that plan, and Karen could not be deterred. So she created her own race, an ultramarathon for one. People told her she was crazy, and maybe she was. But she’d spent previous anniversaries hiding from the world, walloped by grief, and this year she was flipping the script on the tragedy that had come to define her life.

In a recent development, the trail was steep and winding. After sunset, the moon lit her path. Each time she thought about quitting, her mind flashed to the man who took her children. Each step was vengeance. Her feet pounded and pounded, like she could pound him into the ground.

Sources indicate that on the day her children died, Karen could not move. She remembers falling to the floor in the living room of her parents’ house, curling her body around a framed picture of Reagan and Grant that she clutched to her chest. A neighbor had phoned to say the home she once shared with the man she no longer called her husband was burning, and she dialed her father, who was on his way to pick up the kids.

Recent findings suggest that he’s killing my kids, she stated, and she kept repeating the words, because some dark force had overtaken her, and it’s like she knew. Dad, hurry. He’s killing them.

It has been revealed that her father dashed to the scene, where he found firefighters and a home lapped by flames. Karen stayed frozen, and she still gets angry when she thinks of this detail. Why didn’t she go to them? Why didn’t she race to her car and drive 190 miles an hour to reach them? She can’t explain. She only kept rocking back and forth, back and forth. The next thing she remembers is her uncle walking through the front door. He kneeled beside her and whispered in her ear, “They’re gone.”.

It was her best friend, Brandy, who got her running. Brandy was once a lost teenager who shot up heroin; now she’d become a sober woman who found release through her body in motion, and she wanted Karen to find it too.

In a recent development, she did, but often it felt like anguish. She muttered and cussed and yelled. This is stupid. It hurts. Why am I doing this? Karen didn’t like running so much as she needed running. She needed the catharsis, the endurance challenge. She wanted to suffer. She ran a half marathon less than a year after the tragedy, a full marathon the next.

In a recent development, still, the grief escalated. The shock and adrenaline wore off after two years, leaving a fathomless despair. One night in May 2018, she laid out hydrocodone, Valium, and Xanax. The plan was to wash them down with vodka and wine and not wake up.

Industry observers note that her memory of that night is spotty, but she remembers looking at a picture of Reagan and Grant. She was desperate, sobbing. She did not want to die, but she could not understand what she was doing on Earth without them. I need you to intervene, she begged them. Soon after, she remembers getting a text from a cousin checking in on her, then another cousin, then a friend, then her sister. Karen took it as a sign. She threw away the pills.

In a recent development, two weeks later, her father checked her into a residential treatment center outside Nashville that specialized in trauma. It was a serene place, acres of rolling pasture, and Karen spent hours on the wooded trail out back, running. Some people who lose their children don’t make it. Alcohol and drugs take them; the suicide rate is higher than average. Eventually Karen came to accept that if she died, then Reagan and Grant died with her, and she couldn’t let them die twice.

Recent findings suggest that she discovered the trail at Erwin Park after returning home to North Texas. Over the next two years her race distances ramped up quickly, from 50 miles to 100K. Karen, who had once made fun of Brandy’s cracked and blistered feet, was now the one peeling off toenails, running her fingers over the watery bubble of a blister. The fifth anniversary of her children’s death was the first time she ran 100 miles. As the hours went by, she checked her watch, trying to place each of her children’s last moments. This is when he was pouring the gas, this is when he texted.

Recent findings suggest that she could feel Reagan and Grant on that trail. She always does. A cardinal fluttering past, a heart shape in the stumps of the trees, a pair of blue jays—they’re reminders that although she lost her children, they are with her still. Reagan and Grant are the reasons to keep going—not just over the 100 miles, but in the life she is still figuring out how to live.

According to recent reports, karen Sparks had a different life once. She was 25 when she met David Small at the mortgage company where they worked. A clean, good-looking man, a real charmer. He was eight years older. She liked the salt-and-pepper hair, the goatee. She was wearing pink corduroy pants and a floral top that day; he complimented the outfit. Karen needed compliments. Ever since adolescence—the glasses, the braces—she’d struggled with a sense that she was not pretty enough, not thin enough. Not enough.

It has been revealed that karen already had a boyfriend and kept a photo of him at her desk. “He won’t be that for long,” David told her. “I’ll have you.” She laughed, because obviously that was a joke. A bit arrogant, too, though she liked the feeling of being coveted. He was smirking, a micro-movement that struck her then as benign.

Industry observers note that to understand why Karen fell so hard for David Small, it helps to understand how badly she wanted to escape. Garden-variety teenage rebellion had escalated fast. She’d been a cheerleader and athlete, the daughter of a charismatic high school football coach who became the principal, but in her 20s, she watched Brandy rope off her arm with a rubber tube and plunge a needle into a vein. Around that time, Karen was arrested for drunk driving. She knew she needed to find a better path.

And she did, but she didn’t. She traded the nice boyfriend for the charming bad boy at the office. She’d dropped out of college, which was probably a mistake, and the working world had been a series of dull cubicle gigs. More than anything, she wanted a family. She wanted to be a wife and a stay-at-home mother. Motherhood felt like a purpose. She’d never been a star student or athlete, but she had heart. She was the kid on the team who got the “hardest worker” award. And maybe because her own father had been so powerful, she believed that marrying David could give her those things.

Industry observers note that her mother didn’t like the guy, but Karen’s father urged his wife to give him the benefit of the doubt. Duke Sparks is a Santa Claus of a man, significant laugh, big smile. The eldest of 10, with an alcoholic dad, he raised his siblings. Maybe his mistake—he thinks about this all the time—is that he couldn’t stop saving his daughter. Whatever she wanted, he gave it to her, so when she fell for this man, he wasn’t going to stand in her way. When she asked for the fairy-tale wedding, he gave it to her, even though $30,000 was a chunk of change for a school administrator and his schoolteacher wife.

Sources indicate that she bought the gown at one of those big bridal warehouses. Silver-ivory beads embroidered on the straight corset, a long flowy bottom like a princess at a ball. She took bridal photos in front of black-eyed Susans at a Dallas park that was popular with brides-to-be. She sits on the lawn with a tiara nestled in her brown beachy waves, the diamond ring with three bands fitting together like interlocking puzzle pieces conspicuous on her finger as she rests her cheek in her palm. Karen doesn’t recognize the 27-year-old woman in that picture. It’s like she’s wearing a mask.

The newlyweds moved to a one-story in McKinney, about a half hour north of Dallas, and then a two-story a little farther north in the small town of Van Alstyne. In 2006 she had a baby girl named Reagan, and 17 months later a baby boy named Grant, and the way those two came into the world was the way they walked through it: Reagan swift and bold, Grant taking his time, circumspect. Reagan was Karen’s mini-me. The girl of a thousand smiles, with a smattering of freckles. She was a gymnast who loved to climb the walls, climb the refrigerator, climb anything. The summer before the fire, Reagan learned the backstroke and Grant had just gotten comfortable in the pool. Out on the field, though, he was a heck of a ballplayer. He was very particular about his clothes—everything had to match—and had a thing for neons. Those two loved tricking their grandfather into eating Sour Patch Kids. They’d promise him the candy wasn’t sour—definitely not sour, no way was it sour—then when he popped one into his mouth and his face puckered, they’d fall to the floor laughing. They were happy kids. The marriage was rocky, surely they heard things, but Karen is pretty sure they were happy.

David had trouble keeping a job, though. He had trouble keeping the electricity on, keeping the mortgage paid. In a word, he had trouble. He pawned her ring shortly after Grant was born. Karen sat on the steps of their lease-to-own home, weeping. How could this happen? We have to make sacrifices, that’s what he said. He promised it would never happen again, but it just kept happening. Karen’s credit card started getting declined. David once bought the kids scooters for Christmas, only to pawn them. He kept the car parked in the back to keep it from repo men.

After the fire, Karen visited the house. She had to retrace the steps, witness the damage with her own eyes. She pulled back the canvas that investigators had draped over the carpet in the master bathroom. She had to see it: The silhouettes of her children’s bodies, soot outlining their final positions like sidewalk chalk. Some mothers never want to go back, she gets it, but she needed this. What also stands out from that visit is the enormous engagement photo of her in that wedding dress. Flames had licked the canvas, so the picture-perfect image had crackled and turned blister-black.

Why did you stay? Karen could torture herself with this until the end of time if she wanted to. Did you ever think he was capable of such wickedness? Of course not! He never hit her. He never hit the children, never even threatened it. No drinking problem, no drug addiction, no gambling, as far as she can tell. But when Karen scans for warning signs, she thinks about his charm. The subtle manipulation, gaslighting, coercion. How many serial killers, how many con men, how many two-bit criminals get described this way by some innocent bystander? He was so nice, so good-looking, so charming. David’s favorite movies were The Talented Mister Ripley and Catch Me if You Can. So yeah, that was a clue.

Some signs were more obvious, especially to people who weren’t Karen. Her sister trailed him twice to see if he was going to work. (He wasn’t.) Though their memories of the incident are foggy, Karen remembers that her sister tried to show her a photo of him meeting another woman. Karen couldn’t hear it. David loved her. He loved their kids. Karen had gone on antidepressants for postpartum depression after Grant was born, and she wonders if the meds kept her hazy.

Also, Karen did not quit things. The little girl who got “hardest worker” trophies would not give up on her marriage so easily. Resilience would be her strength, and her undoing.

Sources indicate that it was her father who finally convinced her to leave. Duke had run a background check and found David had an outstanding arrest warrant for unpaid traffic tickets. He called his daughter from the football field. He’s driving around with your kids, he told her. If they arrest him, they’re taking those kids to social services.

Sources indicate that that startled Karen. Reagan was 9. Grant was 8. Her instinct to protect them overrode any fear of leaving.

Recent findings suggest that she pulled David into the bathroom one night so they could talk in private. The bathroom had a worn brown carpet that led to a walk-in closet. She leaned against the countertop with the double sink and spoke in a voice more defeated than angry. This was over. No fighting. His voice was calm, too. I’m sorry, baby. I’ll fix it, baby.

The fire began in the garage. He’d poured gasoline through the house, dousing the walls, dousing the furniture. The investigators had never seen so much gas. The children lay on the carpet inside the master bathroom where he and Karen had stood just a month before, when she’d told him it was over.

How he kept the kids compliant is a mystery. No drugs were found in their system, no sign of struggle. The children were arranged the way they usually slept, Reagan on her side, Grant on his tummy. David’s body was curled in a ball at the back of the closet, holding down one of the dogs. That sorry coward had placed his kids closest to the flame.

Sources indicate that karen had finally left him on October 19. Her attorney had recommended that she go without warning, so she moved the kids to her parents’ place. After David was served divorce papers, he told her he didn’t see it coming. He just didn’t think his wife would do this.

“You got me,” he texted her that day.

She shot back, “I learn from the best.”.

In a recent development, halloween had been his first weekend alone with the kids. Karen saw no reason to punish him, even though he seemed to be punishing her. He took Reagan and Grant trick-or-treating, but he didn’t send one photo to Karen of them in their costumes.

In a recent development, then came Sunday, November 1, 2015. He started texting her at 6 a.m. Are you coming to church with us?

Sources indicate that was he kidding? No, she wasn’t going to church with them. She wasn’t playing “happy family” anymore.

It has been revealed that the texts kept coming, all morning long. I need to talk to you. There’s something I need to tell you. Her family told her to ignore him. Do not go back, it’s a trap. Karen had gone back so many times. She stayed firm. The texts stopped around noon.

Her mind runs alternate scenarios of what might have happened if she’d gone that day, and though she’ll never know, she believes he would have killed her. She thinks he wanted to take them all down together. Instead, he took her children, the pets, most of her belongings, her unshakable faith in God, nearly everything she had, and left her the lone survivor.

According to recent reports, from what Karen can piece together, it seems his plan was to blow up the house, leaving nothing but ashes. But the trail of fire never reached the master bathroom. The bodies did not burn. Cause of death, carbon monoxide poisoning and smoke inhalation. Karen hates the phrase “at least”—at least you got them for nine years, at least you were a mother for a while—but this part really is an at least. He’d left a suicide note. Some nonsense about seeing her in heaven. How long had he been plotting this? Some answers she’ll never get.

Was he unstable? Clearly. Narcissistic sociopath turned psychopath, that’s her best guess. Karen has spent the past five-plus years puzzling out the question of why, and she hasn’t gotten far. Part of her trauma therapy at the treatment center was reenacting that day, placing herself in the scene she never entered in real life, a technique known as psychodrama. The benefit was profound, but it never gave her the “why.” There is no word in the English language for a mother who loses her children, the way there is for widows and orphans. It’s like language itself cannot admit the possibility.

In a recent development, the fourth year was even harder than the first three. Grief kept amplifying. She got tattoos. Their names on her outer left forearm. Their birth dates in Roman numerals on her inner right wrist. Angel wings on her ankles, which she got with another mother who’d lost her kids. And on the tender ivory of her inner bicep, the phrase that has become her motto: Love never ends. She dyed her hair magenta and started painting her nails in bright neons. The look is a bit out there for a 43-year-old woman in small-town Texas, but the wildness fits her soul, and she likes to think her kids are proud. She believes they see her the same way she sees them.

Industry observers note that on November 1, 2020, Karen ran the 100 miles by herself, but she wasn’t alone. People had flocked to support her. One woman ran alongside her for 50 miles. Another flew in from Indiana to crew. Karen didn’t even know some of these people. But they had heard her story and wanted to help. At pit stops, her coach and his wife massaged her feet. It felt nearly Biblical. Her feet. Her dad was there from beginning to end, sleeping in his truck at night.

Industry observers note that karen had never seen a pit crew hustle so hard; it felt like NASCAR. They changed her clothes, popped her blisters, fed her when her stomach could take it. Pringles, PB&J sandwiches, ice-cold Coca-Cola. Her favorite was mashed potatoes and ramen. Sounds disgusting, but it went down smooth and easy as night fell.

Industry observers note that somewhere in the dark, she started to hallucinate. The trees came alive. They turned into fairyland creatures, with swooping limbs and kind faces. Karen was Little Red Riding Hood, running from the Major Bad Wolf. She was Katniss Everdeen, an ordinary girl who never asked to be a hero. The sun came up, she scarfed down pancakes and syrup, and she could see the faces of the people who showed up for her, and the feeling was golden.

According to recent reports, around mile 70, she started to crumble. She broke down when she briefly couldn’t find her dad at the pit stop. Duke wondered if it was time for his daughter to call it quits, but he knew her better than that. She would crawl to the end if she had to, but she would finish.

It took Karen 31 hours to complete the run, an hour longer than planned. She beat herself up about the extra time until her team reminded her that what she’d done was harder than most races, not just because of the personal stakes but because she couldn’t feed off the energy of other runners, spectators, all those passing people. Even Karen had to admit: One woman, 100 miles. It was a triumph.

Sources indicate that karen had never wanted this. She only wanted to be a mom. But this loss summoned a strength she didn’t know she had. Back in her previous life, she did not have the courage to stand on her own. This part is confusing, it fills her eyes with tears, because losing Reagan and Grant was the worst thing that had ever happened to her—but it also made her more like the woman she wanted to be.

It has been revealed that she’s working on a memoir with her sister, and she aims to keep racing. Another 100-miler in October, a 200-miler after that; her dream is the Moab 240. Reminders of her loss never go away. Kids playing on a jungle gym. An empty swing. The memories can bring a smile, or they can bring a tear. She has learned to live with both: happy and sad, furious and grateful, lucky and cursed. Sixty-eight months. That’s how long it’s been since her world split open. Every first day of the month marks another notch in that marathon.

Most people want to outrun emotional pain. Not Karen. She runs into the pain. “Run toward the roar” is a line she read in a book about grief, and it’s why she can tell this story to a stranger in a cozy cafe, because she’s learned that sharing the pain is a better path. Allowing herself to be angry and difficult and complicated and hurt, swiping away tears and muttering cuss words only to apologize because she knows this is for a magazine—that’s better than pretending.

Recent findings suggest that it will tell you about her spirit, and the radiance of this woman who never asked for any of this, that as she tells the worst story of her life, a man stops to comment on her smile. Another man stops, an hour later, to compliment her hot pink nails. In other parts of the world, and to other women, such comments might not go over well, but Karen flashes that smile. “It’s them,” she says, finger pointing upward, and maybe that’s true. It’s also true her smile was here before they were. And though she will never stop running for Reagan and Grant, maybe one day she will run for herself. It’s the next step.

3 Restorative Yoga Poses for When You’re Stressed and Short on Time

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that in Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past issues beginning in 1975. This article about restorative yoga poses appeared in the September-October 1995 glitch of Yoga Journal. Find more of our Archives here.

According to recent reports, in a perfect world we would all have time for a long restorative yoga practice daily. But obligations to work, family, friends, and community often leave us with little time for self-care. It is precisely when we are the most stressed that we need to relax and renew ourselves, and bring some restorative yoga into our busy lives.

Traditionally, a yoga class or personal practice session begins with active poses followed by a brief restorative pose. However, the entire focus of this practice is on supported restorative poses.

To relax deeply in this amount of time, you must have a quiet room, but you can get by with a minimum of props. There are only three poses: Legs-Up-the-Wall Pose, Supported Child’s Pose, and Basic Relaxation Pose. Practice them in the order presented. If you can’t find even 15 minutes, practice Basic Relaxation Pose for five.

Recent findings suggest that this pose is simple to practice, even when traveling. Just lie on your back and let a nearby wall support your legs. This pose brings the blood and lymph fluid to pool in the abdomen, refreshing the leg muscles and enhancing the health of the circulatory system. In addition, the pose reverses the energy of the legs from moving down and out to the feet, as in our normal stance, to moving down and back to the pelvis. Nothing feels better to tired legs and feet than being elevated.

Recent findings suggest that setting Up. To begin, sit on the floor with one shoulder near the wall and your thighs parallel to the wall. Roll back as you swing your legs up the wall. Once in position, make sure that your lower back is not rounded and your tailbone and buttocks are not lifting off the floor. If they are, move slightly away from the wall so your lower back is comfortably supported by the floor.

If your chin lifts toward the ceiling, place a standard-fold blanket under your head and neck to support your cervical curve. Make sure your chin is slightly lower than your forehead, but do not force your chin down and flatten the back of your neck.

Recent findings suggest that keep your legs straight but relaxed. Place your arms out to your sides with the palms turned up. Close your eyes. Place an eyebag over them.

Sources indicate that being There. Take several long, slow breaths. As you do, imagine the fluid in your legs flowing down toward the abdomen. With it, all tension drains out of your legs. They begin to feel lighter and softer. Imagine that your brain is shrinking in size as it moves away from your forehead and sinks toward the back of your head and the floor. Feel your entire spine supported by the floor. The position of the arms creates a feeling of being open and free. Enjoy this feeling.

Recent findings suggest that coming Back. Practice Legs-Up-the-Wall Pose for five minutes. When ready, remove the eyebag and open your eyes. Rest for a few breaths before bending your knees toward your chest and rolling to one side. Pause again for a few breaths before slowly coming to a sitting position with the help of your arms.

It has been revealed that benefits. Legs-Up-the-Wall Pose reduces swelling and fatigue in the legs.

Cautions: Do not practice this inverted pose.

According to recent reports, supported Child’s Pose is the familiar posture of rest and sleep for babies and young children. When you practice this pose, not only will it help to relieve tension in your lower back, but it may evoke a sense of security from your earliest days. This pose is one of introversion, one of curling up and reconnecting with feelings of support and release.

Sources indicate that setting Up. Begin by kneeling on a carpeted floor or blanket with your knees hip-width apart and your bolster in front of you. Use more padding under your knees and shins if you need it. To avoid stress on the ligaments of your outer ankles, point your toes directly backward and not toward each other. Sit back on your heels.

If you experience discomfort in your knees, ankles, or tops of your feet, come up and try one or both of the following adjustments. Place one towel, folded lengthwise, into the bend of your knees to create more space in the knee joints. Place the other towel, rolled lengthwise, under the front of the ankles, and let your feet hang over the roll. Experiment with the thickness of these folded and rolled towels to get them just right for you.

Sit back on your heels again. Separate your knees wide enough to place the bolster between your thighs. To enhance relaxation, hold a sandbag across your lower back as you bend forward. The weight of the bag helps to relax the muscles of your lower back.

Your torso should be completely supported by the bolster and your thighs. Your chest should rest easily on the bolster. Let your tailbone drop toward your heels. This action will lengthen your lower back as you relax. Your buttocks do not have to touch your heels.

If you need more support, try one of the following variations. Come up to a kneeling position and place a long-roll blanket on your heels and sit back, or come to a kneeling position and significantly raise the height of your torso support by adding one or more single-fold blankets. If you have difficulty breathing, push the bolster forward so it only supports your breastbone and lets your belly hang free.

Turn your head to one side and bring your chin slightly toward your chest. Turn it to the opposite side halfway through the practice of Supported Child’s Pose. If the side head position is uncomfortable, rest on your forehead and slightly tuck your chin toward your chest. Make sure you can breathe easily regardless of your head position.

Recent findings suggest that place your arms so they reach either back toward your feet or forward around the edges of the bolster. The position of the arms is unimportant; it is crucial that you are comfortable. Close your eyes.

Being There. Take several slow breaths. As you do, let your shoulders move away from the ears. Let your belly relax and feel supported. The counter-pressure of the bolster on the belly may feel especially good if you have menstrual cramps.

Coming Back. Practice Supported Child’s Pose for three minutes. Be sure that you spend equal time with your head turned in both directions. Open your eyes. Reach back with one hand and slide the sandbag off your back and to one side. Place your palms on the floor, under your shoulders. Press your hands into the floor, inhale, and sit up slowly onto your heels. Rest for a moment. Come to a kneeling position and immediately bring one leg forward, placing your foot on the floor. Press your hands on the forward thigh, and inhale deeply as you come to a standing position. Coming out of the pose in this way prevents discomfort in the knees.

Recent findings suggest that benefits. Supported Child’s Pose gently stretches the lower back, relieves shoulder tension, and quiets the mind.

Cautions: Do not practice this pose.

This pose is the heart of restorative practice. Relaxing completely, even if it is only for five minutes, is one of the most key skills you can acquire. When you have learned to relax whenever and wherever you need to, you can use this skill in a variety of situations to reduce stress and its accompanying fatigue.

It has been revealed that the less time you think you have for spending a few minutes a day in Basic Relaxation Pose, the more you need to do it. If you do nothing else for your health every day, make time for this pose. Practice it, for example, at an afternoon break at work, when you first come home from work, after a workout session, or whenever you feel depleted, exhausted, or stressed.

Setting Up. In Basic Relaxation Pose you will be lying on your back with your arms out to the sides and your legs comfortably apart. Give yourself enough floor space to spread out comfortably. Before you lie down, position a standard-fold blanket for your head and neck to rest on.

Recent findings suggest that begin by sitting on the floor. If you have a tendency to get cold, cover your legs with an unfolded blanket. Now turn to one side and lean on your elbow and forearm as you slide onto your side. Then roll onto your back. Coming into the pose in this way is less stressful on your back than leaning back into a reclining position.

Sources indicate that roll the long edge of your standard-fold blanket slightly to support the gentle curve of the neck. Adjust the prop placement so that your neck is comfortable. Your chin should be slightly lower than your forehead. This position quiets the frontal lobes of the brain. If you are using an extra blanket for warmth, now is the time to pull it up to cover your torso and arms. Cover your eyes with an eyebag.

Sources indicate that many people can practice this pose lying flat on the floor. If you have tension or pain in your abdomen or lower back, place a long-roll blanket under the backs of your knees before you lie down. Make sure that your legs are relaxed and the knees supported by the long-roll blanket. If your heels do not touch the floor, place a folded blanket or pillow under them. If your lower back discomfort persists, come out of the pose by following the instructions under Coming Back (below). Resume your practice of Basic Relaxation Pose when you feel ready.

In a recent development, once you have established yourself, observe the position of your body. Your arms and legs should be equidistant from an imaginary line drawn from the tip of your nose to exactly midway between the feet. Most people practice with the palms turned upwards, but if this is not comfortable, turn them down and let the elbows relax. The most important thing is that you feel completely at ease and supported by the props and the floor. If you need to sit up to adjust props and lie down again, follow the instructions for Coming Back and Setting Up.

Being There. Swallow and relax your lower jaw. Soften your upper eyelids and look down toward the lower lids as you close your eyes. Let your cheeks feel hollow and loose beneath the cheekbones. Release the root of your tongue. Your fingers will curl naturally as your hands relax. Let your legs roll outward. Allow the entire back of your body to feel at ease and in complete contact with the floor and the props.

Recent findings suggest that your arms and legs will feel longer and longer, as well as heavier. Feel the large muscles of the legs, buttocks, and trunk drop away from the bones. Now feel the smaller muscles of your arms, neck, and head as they seem to move away from the bones. Let the bones themselves feel heavy and the skin loose, all over your body. Notice that the abdominal organs seem to nestle gently back into your body. Savor the silence.

Recent findings suggest that the Centering Breath. As you continue to rest, notice when you begin to feel lighter. This is a signal that your body has relaxed and that you can begin the Centering Breath: a long inhalation followed by a long exhalation, followed by several cycles of normal breathing.

According to recent reports, begin by slowly inviting the inhalation to move more deeply into your body. Do this by lifting your ribs slightly and spreading your lungs. Let the air come to you. As you inhale, imagine that the breath breathes you. Follow the inhalation with a soft focus on the exhalation. Feel your diaphragm, lungs, ribs, and muscles of respiration contracting to press the breath out in a steady and focused stream. When your exhalation is finished, breathe several normal cycles of inhalation and exhalation.

According to recent reports, then inhale slowly and deeply once again. At the fullness of inhalation, pause slightly before melting the inhalation into an equally long and steady exhalation. The inhalation is the receptive part of the breath; the exhalation is the active part. Once again, take several normal cycles of breath.

In a recent development, once you have established the rhythm of the long breaths, pay particular attention to the quality of these breaths. What is their texture? Is the beginning of inhalation as soft as the end of inhalation? Is the end of exhalation as smooth as the beginning? With each cycle, allow your breath to become more and more refined, like the texture of fine silk.

Remember, never strain or force the breath. If at any time you feel even slightly agitated or out of breath, simply return to normal breathing. Once you feel calm, resume the cycle of long, slow inhalation and exhalation, followed by several normal breaths.

Recent findings suggest that the success of the Centering Breath is not measured by how much air you can take in or let out. So go slowly, gently, and be present with the process. If you feel fatigued, anxious, or light-headed during practice, it is an indication that you have practiced long enough. Let your breathing return to normal, and, in the future, take longer breaks of normal breathing between each round of long inhalation and long exhalation. Do not practice the Centering Breath if you have a fever, a bad cold, sinusitis, or more serious respiratory diseases, such as pneumonia.

Repeat the Centering Breath for up to 10 rounds. Be sure to leave some time for normal breathing before coming out of the pose.

Coming Back. Remain in Basic Relaxation Pose for five to 20 minutes. To come out of the pose, bend one knee and roll onto your side. Let the eyebag fall off by itself. Gradually open your eyes. Rest in this position for a few breaths. To sit up, press the floor with the elbow of your lower arm and the palm of the hand of your upper arm. Sit quietly for several breaths before standing up and resuming your normal activities.

According to recent reports, benefits. Basic Relaxation Pose lowers blood pressure and heart rate, releases muscular tension, reduces fatigue, improves sleep, enhances immune response, and helps to manage chronic pain.

Recent findings suggest that black Friday sales are notorious for flooding inboxes with endless discounts on triathlon gear you might not actually need. Industry observers note that to separate the signal from the noise, we asked our very own Triathlete editors to share the items sitting in their online shopping carts this holiday season. From reliable daily trainers and high-end smartwatches to cold-weather layers and budget-friendly pool essentials, here are the Black Friday deals our team is actually buying with their own money.

Industry observers note that have you ever found that pair of shoes where it was immediate love at first stride? You just knew you’d found yourself in a latest, long-term relationship, and for the next several weeks, you were in the honeymoon phase – enjoying running more and convincing yourself that running in carbon shoes was fine because this was the only shoe you wanted to run in. Forever.

Industry observers note that that was me with the New Balance SC Elite V4. That might surprise a few people, as it’s not the fastest or flashiest of shoes – and very few pros wore it. Yet it just ticked all the boxes: a wide toe box, stable, grippy, and breathable. They’re the not-intimidating super shoe I recommend to everyone looking to try super shoes. And to top it off, they lasted two seasons and far more miles than you’re ever supposed to put on them.

That’s why the SC Elite V5 is on my shopping list. It’s not only well past time to replace my current pair, but the new version promises to be lighter and faster, with a couple of small problems, like the short tongue, addressed. Alex Yee and Laura Philipp both wore this shoe to great effect, and now I think it’s my turn.

But I can’t just run in these for every session. Sigh. I must also shop for a daily trainer that matches the love I have for the Elites, and that’s why I’m shopping for the FuelCell Rebel V5. After temporarily trading my trusty Adidas EVO SLs for a friend’s new Rebels for a couple of laps around the track, I was immediately hooked. Again, even though they might not be as popular as the SLs, it’s all about your relationship with the shoe – and I knew I’d just found my next pair of daily trainers.

With both on sale at Running Warehouse for way less than they deserve, it’s time to stop talking about relationships with shoes and just get them. Otherwise, my wife will say I should just go on dates with them instead.
