As someone who tests a lot of endurance-focused smartwatches (pretty much all of them that have been made in the last decade), I know a good watch — and a good deal on a watch — when I see one.

Industry observers note that when the Suunto Race 1 came out in 2023, I reviewed it for Triathlete. At the time, I gave it 4.5 out of 5 stars, only dinging it for a slow raise-to-wake/processor that was slightly behind the competition. Pros included a giant, bright AMOLED touchscreen, excellent offline mapping and a useful rotating digital dial, and shockingly solid battery life for a massive-screened AMOLED smartwatch. The other major pro was what I considered an incredibly thrifty price — $500 at the time for the titanium model with more storage than the even cheaper (and heavier) steel $400 version.

Three years later, I still consider the original Suunto Race a menace to the rest of Suunto’s line: The Race 2 somehow had less battery life than the original, but cost way more; and I don’t even consider the Race 3S a worthy challenger to either of the previous models in function or price.

Don’t be turned off by the age of this watch; pick it up now, be satisfied for years, and take the money you save and put it toward some holiday gift-giving.

– Chris Foster, editor-in-chief.

I live in Arizona, where sunshine and heated pools are abundant, so swimming all winter is something I actually get excited about. Sashaying onto the pool deck in new gear just makes it even more fun.

And just for funsies, I’ll throw in this $8 swim cap decorated as a crown – because if I’m going to rule lane four this winter, I might as well dress the part.

Industry News: Otso’s Waheela R Is a Gravel Race Bike Built Around Rider Choice

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1678 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that otso might not be a name you see as often as Specialized or Trek, but you’ve likely come across its sister organization, Wolf Tooth Components.
  • Industry observers note that the Waheela R sits next to the Waheela C in Otso’s lineup as the racier bike with a more focused mission.
  • It has been revealed that that longer, slacker geometry is the part I noticed most while riding.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that otso might not be a name you see as often as Specialized or Trek, but you’ve likely come across its sister organization, Wolf Tooth Components. The Minnesota-based bike brand was founded in 2016 by the engineers behind Wolf Tooth, and the two companies share a home and a practical approach to bike design. Otso’s small lineup includes gravel, mountain, and fat bikes, offered with a level of custom options that puts most big brands to shame.

Industry observers note that the Waheela R sits next to the Waheela C in Otso’s lineup as the racier bike with a more focused mission. Otso gave it a longer front end, a slacker head tube angle, aero-shaped tubing, and internal storage, all to build a bike that can be raced hard over rough terrain.

It has been revealed that that longer, slacker geometry is the part I noticed most while riding. The Waheela R felt composed at speed and gave me confidence on steep, loose descents. But it never felt like a handful when I slowed down for a tight turn. I also appreciated the choices Otso gives riders when setting up the bike, from cable routing to the parts that come on a complete build.

Industry observers note that there are some compromises, particularly for riders who need one of the two smaller frame sizes. But after spending time on the Waheela R, I came away thinking that Otso got a lot of things right.

There’s nothing particularly flashy about many of the Waheela R’s frame details. It has a threaded BSA bottom bracket, a round 27.2 mm seatpost, an external seatpost collar, and a UDH derailleur hanger. In a world where it sometimes feels like every new bike comes with a proprietary part you’ll eventually have to track down, I find that extremely refreshing.

Perhaps the biggest example of Otso giving riders a choice is the cable routing. If you want a completely clean front end, you can route the lines through the handlebar, stem, and headset. If you’d rather keep them out of the headset entirely, there are ports at the head tube. Or you can do what I did and take the middle ground, running the lines under the stem and into the headset.

It has been revealed that as far as I know, this is the only production bike that lets you choose between fully internal and external headset cable routing right out of the box. While brands might point to the small amount of extra weight added to the frame to accommodate this feature, I still think it can be worthwhile on more bikes, particularly ones aimed at regular riders rather than world tour pros.

In a recent development, the down-tube storage is another detail I like. Its opening sits above the bottle cage, so you can get into the compartment without removing your bottle. More importantly, the door isn’t also responsible for holding the weight of the cage and bottle in place. The compartment feels well sealed and has enough room for a flat kit and an emergency jacket.

There are plenty of useful mounts, including space for three bottles, a top-tube bag, and a partial frame bag. Otso also includes fender mounts, though you won’t find cargo mounts on the fork legs. For a bike designed primarily around gravel racing, I think that’s a sensible decision.

The frame is 1x-only and clears a round chainring up to 50 teeth. Rear tire clearance is 50 mm on medium through extra-large frames, but drops to 45 mm on the extra-small and small. That smaller-size limit of just 45 mm is the one frame detail that feels like a big miss for Otso.

Industry observers note that in general, while more tire clearance is good, I’m okay being in the minority of tech writers and saying that for most people 50 mm is plenty. At the same time, 45mm-frame clearance isn't enough in 2026, and I would probably advise riders considering the two smaller frame sizes to look at other options because of that one detail.

Industry observers note that the Waheela R has a longer front end and a slacker head tube angle than many gravel race bikes. A medium has a 405 mm reach and a 70.5-degree head angle. For comparison, a 54cm ENVE MOG has a 389 mm reach and a 71.25-degree head angle, while a 54cm Specialized Crux 5 has a 388 mm reach and a 71-degree head angle.

Sources indicate that the Otso also has a longer wheelbase: 1,058 mm on a medium, compared to 1,027 mm for the 54 cm MOG and 1,026 mm for the 54 cm Crux. The BMC URS is closer to the Otso’s approach, with a 410 mm reach, 69.5-degree head angle, and 1,070 mm wheelbase on a medium.

One thing to keep in mind is that frame sizes don’t always line up between brands. The medium Waheela R is closer in stack and reach to a 56cm Crux 5 than to a 54 cm. Stem length, handlebar reach, and spacers all affect the final fit, so it’s worth looking closely at the geometry chart before ordering.

Sources indicate that I spent a lot of time riding the Waheela R on all kinds of terrain, from smooth gravel roads and flowy singletrack to steep, loose doubletrack. If I could reasonably tackle something on a gravel bike, I rode the Otso on it. And just about everywhere I took it, the Waheela R was very enjoyable to ride.

According to recent reports, the longer front end and shorter stem gave the bike a stable, confident feel, particularly when I was moving swiftly over rough ground. On steep, loose descents, I felt comfortable relaxing my grip on the bars and letting the front end roll and stabilize through rocks and ruts. The Waheela R never felt nervous or like it needed my constant attention to navigate every trail imperfection.

What impressed me was that the Waheela R didn’t feel sluggish when I slowed down. It was still easy to steer through tighter turns on singletrack, and I never found myself fighting the bike to get it pointed where I wanted to go. I probably wouldn’t choose it for a cyclocross race, but that’s also not what Otso designed it for.

The bike was just as capable going uphill. On steep, loose climbs, I felt like the longer front end gave me room to move forward and keep the front wheel planted without giving up too much rear traction. It’s a subtle thing, but it helped me stay seated and keep moving when the grade got very steep.

The Waheela R also has the stiffness and responsive feel I expect from a gravel race bike. It felt eager to accelerate when I pushed on the pedals, and I never found the ride particularly harsh. That said, I’d still rank the Specialized Crux 5 ahead of the Otso for comfort. The Waheela R strikes a good balance for a race bike, but it isn’t the smoothest gravel bike I’ve ridden.

According to recent reports, the Waheela R is very competitively priced, especially given how much freedom Otso gives you to customize the build. The frameset price is $2,950, but it’s the complete bike prices that really shine. A complete Waheela R with mechanical Shimano GRX 600 starts at $4,250. A SRAM Force XPLR AXS build starts at $5,450.

In a recent development, of course, you can spend more if you want to. Otso offers upgrades including ENVE wheels and cockpit components, along with a range of Wolf Tooth parts and anodized colors. But what I appreciate most about the configurator is the ability to choose things like stem length, handlebar width, and seatpost offset when you order the bike.

In a recent development, that can save you the expense and frustration of buying a complete bike, only to immediately replace parts to get the fit right. Depending on the build, you can also choose your wheels, tires, gearing, and cable routing. Some options add to the price, but you get to decide where you want to spend or save your money.

It’s the kind of flexibility I wish more brands offered. Whether you want a relatively straightforward GRX build or a Force-equipped bike with ENVE wheels, Otso lets you put together the bike you actually want from the start.

In a recent development, the Waheela R is a fun, capable gravel race bike, but what sets it apart for me is how much choice Otso gives riders. You can route the cables through the handlebar and headset, keep them entirely out of the headset, or choose something in between. Add in a threaded bottom bracket and a standard round seatpost, and you get a bike that will be easy to live with for years to come.

In a recent development, that flexibility extends to the build options. Otso lets you choose your stem length, handlebar width, seatpost offset, wheels, and other parts when you order. The pricing is good, too. Even a Force AXS build decked out with ENVE wheels and components can come in under $10,000.

Recent findings suggest that the biggest miss is tire clearance on the two smallest frame sizes. While medium through extra-large frames fit tires up to 50 mm, the extra-small and small are limited to 45 mm at the rear. For riders who want more tire volume for rough courses or the option to run wider rubber in the future, that will be a deal breaker.

It has been revealed that test Editor Dan Chabanov got his start in cycling as a New York City bike messenger but swiftly found his way into road and cyclocross racing, competing in professional cyclocross races from 2009 to 2019 and winning a Master’s National Championship title in 2018. Prior to joining Bicycling in 2021, Dan worked as part of the race organization for the Red Hook Crit, as a coach with EnduranceWERX, as well as a freelance writer and photographer.

Before “cloud” was associated with On’s trainers and Phil Knight cofounded Blue Ribbon Sports, which eventually became Nike, there was Asics. The brand was founded over 75 years ago as Onitsuka Tiger, and would eventually merge with the Asics Corporation in 1977. The Asics “tiger stripes” logo on its shoes derives from the 1950s Onitsuka Tiger Mexico 66 shoe model. Its Gel-Cumulus and Gel-Nimbus legacy models were released in 1999.

According to recent reports, though the organization is Japanese, the origin of Asics’s name is actually a Latin acronym, anima sana in corpore sano, for “sound mind in a sound body.” This ethos is exemplified when wearing, running, and racing in an Asics shoe. The brand’s dynamic cushioning provides comfort and a responsive ride for all running experiences. Well-received by wear-testers, we’ve included Asics trainers in multiple buying guides, including Best Running Shoes and the 2026 Shoe Awards.

Runner’s World has offered running advice and gear recommendations since 1966. We assembled a 300-plus-runner local group of varying experience levels, paces, and foot types to test the latest shoe releases and give their honest assessments on fit, comfort, and ride.

The shoes included on this list were all vetted by wear-testers and RW staff. I have also included my own experience testing some of these models during all kinds of workouts and in a couple of races.

RW contributor Michael Charboneau provided insight on Asics shoe tech and answered frequently asked questions about Asics trainers.

Industry observers note that the Novablast 6 gets an injection of fun that is awfully reminiscent of the original. For this patch, though, Asics cored out a hole in the forefoot and filled it with A-TPU, a foam that’s bouncier than PEBA. The effect is that the carrier (the bulk of the midsole) delivers a predictable, stable ride, yet the forefoot feels explosive and propulsive. It makes this everyday trainer suitable for days when you want to pick up the pace.

“The Asics Novablast 6 is a bouncy do-it-all shoe that excels with faster paces,” remarked tester and Runner’s World Editorial Assistant Michael McDonough. “Compared to other up-tempo daily trainers I’ve tested, like the. New Balance Rebel v5 and Nike Pegasus 42, it has more cushion and a softer feel, yet is still light and bouncier than both.”.

Testers liked the reworked knit upper, improved AsicsGrip rubber outsole, and responsive trampoline pod of FF Turbo Squared foam in the forefoot.

Sources indicate that “Cushioning is the strongest feature of this shoe,” said tester Trevor Conde. “The Novablast is a high-cushioned trainer and it delivers on that. The shoe has a bit more give than most of my go-to trainers, with a higher amount of sinking and compact cushioning during the foot strike phase.”.

According to recent reports, the GT-2000 underwent a makeover with its 14th iteration. Asics has carried these changes over to the GT-2000 15, ensuring the cushioning feels even softer with an added 2 mm of FF Blast Max foam. One tester noted they had the same feel as the Hoka Clifton, saying the Asics shoe was just as comfortable.

Industry observers note that the outsole has the same flame-like pods as the previous version for better traction and stability. The GT-2000 15 also has Asics’s 3D Guidance stability system, which involves high sidewalls for a secure fit and a wider platform for support.

“I’ve had the Asics GT-2000 13 and 14 models, and I was just has happy with this pair as I’ve been with the others,” said tester and overpronator Sophie Kahler. “I found it to be a solid sneaker for a beginner runner like myself who is looking for a mid-price, versatile shoe with good support. I tested it on road, treadmill, and gravel trail at my usual pace around 9:30 to 10:00. I also did a lot of walking in the shoes and found them comfortable for hours.”.

For an even cheaper option, check out the GT-1000 14 ($115), which also has the brand’s 3D Guidance System.

Shop Men’s at amazon.com | Shop Women’s at amazon.com.

According to recent reports, the Gel-Cumulus is a long run favorite for its plush, supportive cushioning. It buffers miles of pounding in a surprisingly lightweight package. The shoe’s midsole is FF Blast Max, which promotes soft landings with high rebound. The foam—along with Asics’s PureGel tech—provides arch support for both neutral runners and underpronators.

“Compared to other daily trainers I have tested, the Asics Gel-Cumulus 28 is a perfect, stable, trainer,” said Caroline Lennon, a heel-striker who trains at 8:30 pace. “I found myself not interested in reaching for any other shoes in this period, no matter whether I was running on the treadmill, trail, or road. They were exceptionally comfortable and I never had any pain, discomfort, or nagging injury crop up in my time with these shoes.

Sources indicate that “They don’t feel flashy, light, responsive and fast,” she continued. “But when I was waking up, and bleary-eyed pulling on my sneakers for a pre-dawn run, they felt like the comforting warm hug my feet wanted. Like getting back into bed. The cold streets/sidewalks didn’t feel nearly as jarring underfoot, and despite my feeling slow, I actually ran faster than I was expecting every time I wore these.”.

Since its release 27 years ago, the Gel-Nimbus has delivered a premium cushioned, long-lasting ride. The Gel-Nimbus 28 is updated with 20 grams shaved off its weight, a feature testers were keyed in on when they ran in the shoe.

“I really like having a lightweight shoe that offers enough support for mostly road surface miles,” noted Courtney Kazmierczak, an intermediate runner who trains at 9:15 pace with a forefoot strike. “The shoe feels like a feather when you hold it and honestly, putting it on I was doubtful that it would have enough cushion based on the weight of the shoe.” Kazmierczak shared that she had recent heel pain before testing the shoe and was surprised her runs were absent of discomfort in that area.

The Gel-Nimbus 28 has a much softer version of the brand’s PureGel tech in the midsole. The Gel tech combined with FF Blast Plus foam results in high energy return workouts and support that lasts for miles.

Industry observers note that “The forefoot cushioning, like I mentioned in the overall rating. It was spot on,” stated fellow forefoot striker Dave Brattley, who runs at 10:00 pace. “I’m still able to feel the road while still minimizing the impact. It made these shoes a real pleasure to run in.”.

Year after year, the Gel-Kayano lands on our list of the best stability shoes for its comfortable fit and smooth ride. The latest version introduces Asics’s new stability tech: FluidSupport.

Replacing the 4D Guidance System, which made the shoe feel stiff, FluidSupport enhances cushioning with a dual layer of foam. FF Blast Plus and FF Blast Max are combined in the midsole; what you get is a softer top layer of foam and a denser bottom layer. Working in tandem with the shoe’s geometry, FluidSupport provides guidance only when you need it.

The result is a more flexible trainer that delivers high energy return on your runs.

Recent findings suggest that the Magic Speed 5 is the cheaper but still capable carbon-fiber-plated racing shoe for the first-time marathoner or 26.2 vet looking for a speedwork trainer. FF Blast Plus foam cushions your landings along with a layer of the brand’s lightest and bounciest FF Leap foam. Asics also reduced the offset to 7mm and the heel height and forefoot height for a more stable ride.

Industry observers note that testers felt the shoe was too firm for long runs, but liked its responsiveness for shorter efforts during their training. Midfoot striker Gabrielle Kelenyi, who trains at 7:45 pace, stated the Magic Speed 5 wouldn’t be her first choice of shoe in terms of comfort (the arch felt too pronounced for her foot), but the functionality was there.

“Without extra effort, I was going 15 to 30 seconds faster per mile on my runs,” she mentioned. “These shoes offered good control during wet runs and up and down small hills. The lace closure was secure. Overall, I wore these for shorter runs (6 miles) and they gave those runs some extra oomph. They were not comfortable enough for longer runs (8+ miles).”.

Other testers, like Stephanie Petrides, appreciated the arch support and overall cushioning.

“I have very flat feet and tend to give my knees and ankles a good pounding because of it, but the cushioning made everything very comfortable,” said Petrides, an overpronator. “The shoe was definitely not too soft and didn’t make me feel like it was slowing me down.”.

Recent findings suggest that I raced in the Metaspeed Edge Tokyo at the 2025 Sydney Marathon and didn’t expect to run 3:05 after combatting a week of being a tourist and jet lag. The shoe is more aggressive than the Metaspeed Edge Paris. Its bounce derives from a newly introduced layer of FF Leap foam, which is super light and responsive. The carbon plate is sandwiched between this top layer of Leap and FF Turbo Plus.

According to recent reports, the Edge is made for cadence runners, with the plate at a lower angle in the forefoot area compared to the Metaspeed Sky Tokyo, which has a more equal distribution of foam with its carbon plate placement. We highlighted the Edge version here, but both models are favored by testers and can be worn by the same runner (some prefer the Sky for long races and the Edge for shorter races, like 5Ks, and vice versa).

Recent findings suggest that “I think that the Metaspeeds are my all time favorite super shoe,” said tester Anthony Calantoni. “I have worn over 10 different pairs at this point and still find these to be the best feeling all around. They have definitely made improvements from the first edition which feel great.

It has been revealed that “I think the increased padding on your foot is the biggest improvement from previous models. The old shoe you could feel the plate and the hardness was real, especially in a marathon. These have definitely improved in that area and you can feel it in most steps. I think I also love it because it still feels like a normal shoe but just with some enhancement of the speed.”.

Asics Metaspeed Edge Tokyo Review.

The Sonicblast is your prep shoe before showtime, or that trainer with just a little more oomph when you want to push the pace during workouts. A Pebax Astroplate is sandwiched between 46mm of FF Blast Max and FF Turbo Squared foams, to stabilize the ride as the shoe propels you forward. FF Turbo Squared is Asics’s high-performance A-TPU foam, which delivers aggressive rebound.

Testers loved the bouncy, high energy return ride and praised the shoe’s supportive cushioning.

In a recent development, “The best part of the shoe was the ride of the shoe for me,” remarked tester Tegan Kovacs, who’s been using the Sonicblast 2 for structured long runs. “It was very comfortable and honestly just plain fun! The shoe was comfortable and foamy enough to take on longer distances, and delivered a propulsive ride when you kicked it up a notch.”.

While testers like the Sonicblast 2’s propulsive ride, some were wary of sharp corners due to the shoe’s tall stack height.

It has been revealed that “I found that taking a turn does require a little more care to counter some of the instability of the higher stack height, but it wasn’t enough of a concern for me to worry too much about it,” noted editor Ashley Tysiac. “Because the cushioning is much more firm rather than plush, I could still easily navigate a fork in the road or a turn on the greenway without feeling like I was going to turn my ankle.”.

Shop Men’s at amazon.com | Shop Women’s at amazon.com.

Recent findings suggest that the Blast series hits the trail. Testers loved the comfort the Blazeblast provided fit-wise and on the run. The shoe has FF Blast Max cushioning to provide a plush, high-energy-return ride. The trampoline pod outsole and midsole design promotes propulsion during toe-off.

The AsicsGrip outsole was satisfactory for our testers who ran the shoe on the road, towpaths, and semi-rocky terrain.

“The only shoe that I can kind of compare this to were the Hoka Mafate Speed 4,” remarked tester Anna Piskorska. “Both of them are very light and have a great flexibility at the midfoot. The Asics give you enough cushion throughout the foot. There’s a noticeable bounce feeling, which allows you to swiftly lift off and pick up speed instantly.”.

Some testers wanted longer lugs for dicier trail efforts. “For a shoe with trail running as a mission, the tread is a bit lacking with the 2.5mm lugs as they will serve you well on mild inclines but anything wet or steep (or wet and steep!) is likely going to be troublesome,” said tester Eric Bartosz. “Just like my Kawasaki, it’s fine for some easy trails, but I would need to change tires for anything more demanding or technical...and that’s OK!”.

Still, testers appreciated how the Blazeblast made runs feel easier and faster off road.

Shop Men’s at asics.com | Shop Women’s at asics.com.

According to recent reports, the Megablast has that high-octane, pogo stick bounce that makes it earn our Most Aggressive title. The shoe’s midsole is pure FF Turbo Squared, Asics’s bounciest foam. At a tall 46mm stack height, the Megablast is a lot of shoe at a surprisingly light weight.

Josh Davis, an underpronator who trains at 7:00 pace, described the shoe as bulky but appreciated its bouncy ride.

Sources indicate that “This is a pretty darn good shoe,” he said. “The super high deck broadcasts the FF Turbo Squared foam, and it lives up to its name. For its size, the shoe is pretty darn light and very responsive. I’ve put over 100 miles on it at this point, and haven’t noticed any change in the pop. I liked this shoe for easy runs. I didn’t try to push it in any workouts because the shoe was a bit bulky.”.

Some testers, including myself, felt the ride was too squishy and erratic in a whole lot of shoe. RW contributor and tester Heather Mayer Irvine noted “the junk in the trunk” was her least favorite aspect of the Megablast.

Recent findings suggest that with the Superblast 3 you get the best of both worlds in terms of cushioning and ride. The midsole has FF Blast Plus foam and FF Leap on a trampoline pod-shaped sole, designed to encourage better toe-off.

It has been revealed that runners loved its soft but supportive foam and bounce. Said intermediate runner and 7:45 pacer Erin Dewalt: “I like the combination of lightweight cushion and bounce most. For half marathon and marathon training, when you’re logging lots of miles, foot comfort is paramount. During my long runs, I’d marvel at how comfortable my feet felt even towards the end.”.

Nick Miller, an underpronator and heel striker, named the cushioning as his favorite Superblast 3 feature.

“The cushioning of the Superblast 3 is what truly sets it apart from other shoes I’ve tested,” he stated. “Its substantial stack height provides exceptional impact absorption, noticeably reducing the stress on my legs during runs. This made a clear difference on longer efforts, where fatigue typically builds up, and allows me to recover more promptly between sessions.”.

Some testers, however, including myself, felt the loudness of the shoe was distracting. When I tested the Superblast 3 on my runs, the pavement slapping was comparable to Nike’s Alphaflys.

Industry observers note that asics has cooked up quite a few proprietary features, and you’ll see many different terms when browsing the manufacturer’s running shoe lineup. To help you get more insight into these features, compare models, and find the right shoe, here’s a deeper dive on the main Asics running shoe tech to know.

This tech consists of a squishy, gel-like substance implanted in the midsole, and it absorbs impact forces for a smoother ride. The latest iteration is PureGel, and it’s formulated to be lighter, softer, and more flexible than previous versions of Gel.

Like other shoemakers, Asics has its own proprietary cushioning, called FlyteFoam (FF). Although it’s based on ethylene-vinyl acetate (EVA), the traditional running shoe cushioning material, this foam is formulated to be lighter and more resilient than standard EVA. It doesn’t have quite the same springy feel as the other types of FF below, but it works fine for everyday running. It’s used in Asics’s more affordable shoes.

FF Blast Plus is the next level up. Asics hasn’t released details on the chemistry, but it likely includes olefin block copolymers, which make for a lighter, more flexible and more responsive foam. For a pillowy and springy ride that still holds up to everyday training, FF Blast Plus is the cushioning to go with.

Asics has also released an updated version, called FF Blast Max, that has a lower density, so it’s even softer and bouncier. It gives models a very plush ride. For maximum cushioning that doesn’t sacrifice responsiveness, look for training shoes with FF Blast Max.

Industry observers note that asics’s elite racing shoes have FF Turbo Plus foam. It’s made with polyether block amide (PEBA), an exceptionally light, soft, and bouncy material. The brand took this foam up a notch with the even bouncier FF Turbo Squared. Leap foam, which is made of Aliphatic TPU (A-TPU), is a super foam that’s softer and lighter than FF Turbo Squares. It is used in the brand’s top tier racing shoes. The shoes with this type of cushioning are pricey, but provide excellent shock absorption and springy responsiveness for a smooth, propulsive ride that helps you go fast. For race day, it’s definitely the top choice.

Asics takes a holistic approach to stability in its shoes, with several features working together to support the foot and guide it from landing to toe-off. The latest version of its stability feature-set is called the “4D Guidance System.” The 4D Guidance shoes feature a wide sole, a firm foam layer in midsole under the arch, and a flared sole shape at the heel to create a planted feel while counteracting overpronation, or excessive inward rolling motion in your step.

Some models have an earlier version of the system, called 3D Guidance. It has the same general features as 4D, but lacks the firm arch support foam in the midsole. If you know you need stability shoes, or simply prefer a more guided, supportive design, then you should look for these features.

Industry observers note that asics has developed a well-deserved reputation for manufacturing reliable shoes that can hold up through high-mileage training. Core models like the Gel-Cumulus, Gel-Nimbus, and Gel-Kayano have been around for decades (and continuously improved upon in that time), and they’re great picks if you’re looking for everyday trainers.

That stated, the brand has also expanded into lightweight, responsive racing shoes and even trail shoes, too.

How do Asics shoes compare to shoes from other brands?

It has been revealed that historically, Asics shoes have been known for using multiple layers of cushioning to create a stable, well-cushioned (and somewhat stiff) ride. Core models like the Gel-Cumulus still exhibit this construction, with a moderate drop and layers of Gel and foam in the midsole for a plush feel that’s great for long runs and training miles.

However, newer shoes in the Asics lineup, like the Novablast, utilize more lightweight, bouncy midsole designs that mirror what other top brands are doing in their premium speedwork and racing shoes.

Has Asics created any key innovations in running shoe tech?

The short answer: Yes, lots of them. Asics has been experimenting with running shoe tech for well over half a century. In 1990, the brand opened the Institute of Sports Science in Kobe, Japan, where the firm conducts materials tests and biomechanical research to fine-tune designs.

Sources indicate that this lab has produced and refined many of Asics’s hallmark technologies, like Gel cushioning and super foams, like FF Leap and FF Turbo Squared. For runners, this means Asics shoes are built with proven designs that can help you meet your goals, from sticking to a training plan to nabbing a new PR on race day.

Amanda Furrer, Editor, Running Reviews, studied journalism at NYU and writing at Emerson College. She has reviewed gear and covered other topics in the running space for almost 10 years. Since 2013, she has consecutively run the Boston Marathon. She also has a master’s degree in gastronomy from Boston University and was formerly a professional baker for two years before hanging up her apron.

#149696. 6 Core-Strengthening Exercises to Spice Up Your Routine

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Bicycling ↗ Open Full Page

6 Core-Strengthening Exercises to Spice Up Your Routine

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1269 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The core gets a lot of attention when it comes to aesthetics.
  • Research indicates just how notable core-strengthening exercises are to an athlete’s routine.
  • The authors of that review state that a strong core provides a fulcrum for your arms and legs, allowing for optimal power transfer between the upper and lower body, overall better motion control, and spinal stability.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The core gets a lot of attention when it comes to aesthetics. But your torso muscles—which include your abs, back, glutes, and hip flexors—play a crucial role in cycling that goes way beyond looks.

Research indicates just how notable core-strengthening exercises are to an athlete’s routine. One 2019 study, published in PLoS One, found that an eight-week core training program improved balance and core endurance (which you need to maintain posture through long miles) in the 21 college athletes who participated. Another research review, published in Frontiers in Physiology in 2022, indicates core training should have a place in all athletes’ training programs.

The authors of that review state that a strong core provides a fulcrum for your arms and legs, allowing for optimal power transfer between the upper and lower body, overall better motion control, and spinal stability. The authors also write that these core strength benefits help prevent “energy leaks,” therefore leading to better performance.

To help you gain these benefits of a strong midsection, you need a solid workout to add to your routine. Thankfully, Noam Tamir, C.S.C.S., founder and CEO of TS Fitness in Upcoming York City, created this dumbbell core-strengthening workout.

In a recent development, in addition to the research that proves the benefits of core strength for athletes, the moves Tamir chose for this workout make an ideal mix for those looking to improve performance. Not only will the moves improve your stability in an upright posture, allowing you to ride and breathe more efficiently, but they also target the core from multiple angles, hitting every muscle of the torso.

Even better: While these moves resemble familiar core exercises, each one has a creative spin. This means they not only challenge your body in fun newly introduced ways, but also engage your brain.

Recent findings suggest that how to use this list: Do each exercise below, in order, for the reps listed. Repeat for 3-4 rounds. Rest as needed between exercises and rounds.

Tamir demonstrates the exercises in the video above so you can learn proper form. You will need one light to medium dumbbell for this workout. An exercise mat is optional.

Industry observers note that why it works: The half-kneeling halo exercise focuses on trunk stability. “It works the core at 360 degrees because the dumbbell is moving around the body while you’re maintaining an upright position,” Tamir claims. You do the same thing on a ride—hold a strong posture and upright body position while your arms and legs move.

It has been revealed that how to do it: Start kneeling, right knee on ground, and left foot planted in front, both knees bent 90 degrees. Hold a dumbbell horizontally at chin. Keeping torso and lower body steady, circle dumbbell clockwise around head. Elbows stay close to head. Return to chin. Repeat in other direction. Do 8-10 reps in each direction. Switch leg stance each round.

Sources indicate that why it works: Target the obliques with this rotational move. You’ll also hit the rectus abdominis (those six-pack looking abs) and work on coordination of the upper and lower body, Tamir explains.

Recent findings suggest that how to do it: Start seated on floor. Hold a dumbbell horizontally at chest. Lean back slightly, and lift legs off floor, hips and knees bent about 45 degrees. Bring dumbbell to outside of left hip by rotating torso to right and extend left leg straight out, foot lowering close to floor. Keep shoulders down and back. Next, bend left knee and extend right leg out, lowering foot close to floor and lift dumbbell up and over to the right, rotating torso to the right. Bring weight back down to outside of left hip, as you extend right leg out and pull left knee back in. Repeat. Do 10-12 reps. Then repeat on the other side.

Industry observers note that why it works: This explosive movement focuses on the hips. “The core is not limited to just the abdominal muscles,” Tamir indicates. “You also need the whole body to create power, strength, and endurance.” This exercise gets more muscles in on the action, while the hinge motion helps to improve riding, especially during acceleration, he adds.

How to do it: Stand with feet hip-width apart, dumbbell in right hand down by side. Hinge at hips, by sending butt straight back, dumbbell reaching behind you. Keep back flat and core engaged. Using glutes, drive feet into floor and extend hips. Let the power of your glutes send dumbbell forward and up to shoulder height. Engage core, like you’re hitting a standing plank position at the top. Let the momentum of the dumbbell guide you back into a hinge position. Repeat. Do 10-12 reps.

In a recent development, why it works: This anti-rotation exercise works the deep core muscles, including the transverse abdominis that wraps around your midsection, and the multifidus, the posterior core muscles that protect your spine, Tamir explains. “It also helps to stabilize the pelvis to reduce risk of injury,” he adds, and aids in strong posture by working the back.

How to do it: Start in a plank position, left hand on a dumbbell, shoulders over wrists, forming a straight line from head to heels. Feet should be slightly wider than hips. Pull left elbow straight up, dumbbell reaching to ribcage. Lower back down. Repeat. Keep hips as steady as possible. Do 8-10 reps. Then repeat on the other side.

Why it works: The pullover crunch focuses mainly on the rectus abdominus (the muscles on the front of the torso) which helps to stabilize the spine and, in turn, maintain good form, Tamir indicates.

In a recent development, how to do it: Lie faceup, holding a dumbbell vertically with both hands overhead, dumbbell behind you, arms extended. Bend knees, feet planted on floor. Pull dumbbell overhead and crunch up, lifting head, neck, and shoulders off floor. At the same time, lift feet off floor, driving knees toward arms. Slowly lower back down, dumbbell hovering off floor behind you, and feet hovering off floor in front of you. Repeat. Do 12-15 reps.

Why it works: This is a great move for stabilizing the spine, while teaching abdominal bracing, Tamir claims. The weight on one side also forces the core to resist rotation, which you need for efficiency on the road.

How to do it: Lie face up. Hold dumbbell in right hand over shoulder, arm straight. Extend left arm overhead, biceps by ear. Lift head, neck, shoulders, and legs a few inches off floor. Use legs to rock back and floor, maintaining the hollow body position. Do 8-10 reps. Then repeat with dumbbell in left hand.

It has been revealed that mallory Creveling is an ACE-certified personal trainer and RRCA-certified run coach, who also holds certifications in kettlebell training, sports performance, and more. She has more than 15 years of experience covering fitness, health, and nutrition for a wide range of publications, and nearly 10 years of experience as a trainer and fitness instructor. Mallory stays on top of her continuing education in fitness, as well as the latest science in wellness. She has worked with some of the best experts in their medical fields, and regularly interviews researchers, trainers, athletes, and more to find the best advice for readers looking to improve their performance and well-being. As a freelance writer, Mallory's work appeared in Women's Health, Self, Men's Journal, Reader's Digest, and more. She has also held staff editorial positions at Family Circle and Shape magazines, as well as DailyBurn.com. A former Fresh Yorker/Brooklynite, she's now based in Easton, Pennsylvania.

#149695. This Is the Minimum Amount of Time You Need After a Half Marathon to Run Your Next Race

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1315 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Runnersworld ↗ Open Full Page

This Is the Minimum Amount of Time You Need After a Half Marathon to Run Your Next Race

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1315 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that generally speaking, the shorter your race distance, the more frequently you can race.
  • But jumping right into another race without a solid chunk of rest time means you risk injury, burnout, and potential disappointment in your next race results.
  • Below, run coaches lay out guidelines for when to race again, depending on how you tackled that initial 13.1 miles and your goals for the next one.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that generally speaking, the shorter your race distance, the more frequently you can race. You might only get a few chances per year to run a marathon, but you can stack up multiple half marathons, 5Ks, and 10Ks per season, as long as you balance those harder efforts with sufficient recovery time.

But jumping right into another race without a solid chunk of rest time means you risk injury, burnout, and potential disappointment in your next race results. Even if you feel ready to race again soon after a half marathon, specifically, you might need more time than you think. So what’s the ideal reset time after 13.1 and when should you be able to line up again?

Below, run coaches lay out guidelines for when to race again, depending on how you tackled that initial 13.1 miles and your goals for the next one.

In general, it’s a good idea to take two to four weeks off from high-intensity work after a half marathon before racing again, says Laura Norris, a Seattle-based certified personal trainer and run coach with a master’s in applied exercise science.

You should first take three to five days postrace off completely to clear up any muscle damage and let your body fully recover, then stick exclusively to easy running for the rest of that two- to four-week period.

“There’s new research that highlights the half marathon stresses the heart pretty decently for two weeks postrace,” Norris says. While it’s not the same level of stress as a full marathon, it’s still vital to take sufficient time to recover before tackling another high-intensity effort.

With that in mind, you can make adjustments to your timeline:.

The harder you push, the longer it takes to recover, so Norris suggests waiting those three to four weeks before racing again if you just ran your fastest half marathon, even if you feel good.

However, you can consider your upcoming race distance and goal: If you’re jumping into a Turkey Trot 5K for fun, for example, you can probably get away with just two weeks of recovery, but wait at least the entire four weeks before gearing up for a full marathon, Norris suggests.

After a race where you feel really beat up, you’re extra sore, mentally drained, or fatigued, it’s a good idea to take those first three to five days off followed by two to four weeks of really easy running, Norris claims. But that doesn’t mean you jump right into another race.

In this case, “it might be worth spacing your races at least six to eight weeks apart, maybe even a full training season apart,” she notes. Otherwise, you could enter into a vicious cycle of overtraining, not recovering fully, and entering another race underprepared and beating yourself up again, Norris explains.

It can feel really disappointing to train hard for months for your race and not have results to reflect that work, but it’s crucial to honor your recovery and health more than performance.

The amount of time you give yourself to recover from a bad race depends on the reason the race went poorly, Norris says. If you just had a bad day, dealt with a difficult course, or struggled with fueling, you might stick to three to four weeks before another race.

But if you were dealing with an illness after your event or you undertrained leading into it, then in addition to taking days completely off and a few weeks of easy running, you probably want another few weeks of adding in speed before jumping into another race, Norris suggests. This would give you an opportunity to prepare more for your next race, while allowing your body to heal.

Industry observers note that wait a minimum of six weeks before racing again. “That’s at least two weeks to recover, four weeks to navigate training again, and also a few weeks to make sure that you aren’t impulsively making a decision based on high postrace emotions,” Norris says.

It has been revealed that norris notes that you have to evaluate how poorly you feel and listen to your gut, too. It’s always a good idea to get pain or potential injury addressed by a physical therapist and navigate your timeline from there.

In a lot of cases, you can use post-half marathon fitness to your advantage to tackle another race and see how much better you can do. “If you want to race in a couple weeks once your legs feel better and you’re not sore, it might not be a bad time to do a 5K,” claims Christine Rockey, an exercise physiologist, RRCA-certified run coach, and principal lecturer at Coastal Carolina University.

In a recent development, but there’s a difference between setting your sights on another PR and jumping into a fun family 5K. Here’s how you should prepare in training for your next race, depending on your goal.

Norris suggests slowly ramping back up with about a week of 30-minute easy runs after the three to five days of rest. “They won’t feel great at first, but we just want to get the legs moving now that most of the muscle damage has started to repair,” she indicates.

Industry observers note that then, continue with easy running during the following week, but try to aim for about 75 percent of your peak volume during half marathon training. For example, if your peak long run was 14 miles, you might aim to cover 10.

If you have two more weeks, you can add in some race pace work to sharpen your speed during the first of those two weeks, then give yourself a week to taper. It’s always easier to maintain fitness than it is to build, and you want to avoid being overtrained before your next race, Norris says.

As you lace up for your next race, keep a realistic goal in mind. It’s always good to be an ambitious runner and gain more race experience, but remember to keep your expectations in check, Rockey indicates. “I think if you go in thinking the next five races you do are all going to be PRs, I think you’re going to end up disappointed and you might even get so frustrated that you stop running,” she says.

You have a bit more leeway to do lower volume and run a few short easy runs every other day, for example. Norris says you can coast on 50 percent of your peak half marathon volume and know that you’ll still be fit enough to jump into a last-minute 5K.

Sources indicate that it’s important not to go back to a completely sedentary state if you initiative on racing again. “If you were to sit on the sofa [instead of easy running] and do absolutely nothing for three weeks, you would begin to detrain,” Norris adds. “It might not be that serious, but it would probably make the race not feel as good.”.

Plus, going from the couch to another half marathon can lead to aches and pains, Norris adds. “If you go from doing nothing for three weeks to doing 13 miles, that’s a huge jump in single-session load,” she states, pointing to a study published in 2025 that shows jumping up your single-run volume by more than 10 percent in a 30-day span can increase injury risk.

Keeping up with a couple easy runs in between efforts will help you race your best—even when your best means having the most fun.

Kristine Kearns, a writer and avid runner, joined Runner’s World and Bicycling in July 2024. She previously coached high school girls cross country and at the moment competes in seasonal races, with more than six years of distance training and an affinity for weightlifting. You can find her wearing purple, baking cupcakes, and visiting her local farmers market.

#149694. These Three Offseason Strength Exercises Can Help You Break Through Your Climbing Plateau

These Three Offseason Strength Exercises Can Help You Break Through Your Climbing Plateau

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (885 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that this time of year, it is easy to start to look ahead to 2027—more than a few riders I know are starting to trade their outdoor rides for more Zwift and gym time.
  • For a lot of cyclists, the winter becomes time off the saddle, at least from riding outside.
  • It has been revealed that the workout below is perfect if you are someone who doesn’t want to join a gym or you just want to dip your toe in the water of strength training.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that this time of year, it is easy to start to look ahead to 2027—more than a few riders I know are starting to trade their outdoor rides for more Zwift and gym time. If you’re thinking about winterizing your bike for the season, then it’s the perfect time to start looking at your strength training plan for the offseason.

For a lot of cyclists, the winter becomes time off the saddle, at least from riding outside. For others it takes form as time on fat bikes, skis, or even a pair of running shoes. Regardless of how your winter activities take shape, be sure to add some strength training to make sure you can hit your 2027 goals.

It has been revealed that the workout below is perfect if you are someone who doesn’t want to join a gym or you just want to dip your toe in the water of strength training. Each exercise targets a different part of the body to dial in the strength you need when you are trying to power up climbs next year. The workout can be done as a stand-alone set of exercises or it can be added on to your current strength training initiative.

Industry observers note that so many cyclists want to just spend time in the saddle for training—that’s great up to a point. Eventually we all need to get off the bike and spend some time strength training to help break through those frustrating plateaus. These three overlooked exercises can help you elevate your climbs for 2027.

Industry observers note that today I had my first hill-focused ride after a few weeks focusing on running and trainer rides. The first steep pitch quickly reminded me how much I use my upper body while getting up a hill on the bike. As I climbed, I felt myself pulling on the handlebar with each pedal stroke while gravity was trying to pull me back. Developing the pull muscles is something that will benefit the whole kinetic chain while climbing. Bent-over rows in particular are a great upper-body exercise for this because they engage multiple muscle groups for one movement pattern. Rows can be done with so many different types of equipment: dumbbells, kettlebells, TRX Suspension Systems, elastic bands, and more. Here’s how I recommend doing them with dumbbells.

In a recent development, one of the reasons I love deadlifts for cyclists is because they are exercises that works almost all the muscles through the kinetic chain in one simple move. As we climb, we are pulling energy through our upper body, driving through the hips, and pushing the power through our legs into the pedals. This exercise trains the muscles through your arms, back, and core, while simultaneously working the muscles throughout your legs. Another reason deadlifts are one of my go-to exercises is that they can be done with several different types of equipment. My favorite equipment for this exercise is a barbell, but deadlifts can be done with dumbbells and kettlebells too.

It has been revealed that recovery Tip: Delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS) is very real, and depending on the person, your muscle burn can last for a few days after your training session. Plan accordingly for your rides following a heavy weight day. Listen to your body and add a recovery ride or off-bike activity if that's what you need.

According to recent reports, your core is what ties everything in your body together, so it is integral to grow your stability and power here. While riding today, I was trying to really be in tune with how I was using my core when climbing. When I was in the saddle I felt like the focus from my core was on stability, allowing for a sound upper body while pushing power through my legs and out of the pedals. My simple go-to core exercise to improve climbing is a plank with cross-body knee taps. This works stability through your core while working the internal obliques through the cross-body motion of the knee tuck. This exercise will really show its gains when you get out of the saddle as the climb pitches up.

A quick note on consistency: strength training will give you the best results when you incorporate it in your blueprint week after week. It will offer significantly diminished results if you are sprinkling it in sporadically. If you are able to, try to commit to adding strength training consistently for a four- to six-week block and see how that impacts your rides.

According to recent reports, our strength training program can help get you started with a more in-depth workout blueprint. It’s vital to remember it does not matter where you are in your cycling journey, there are gains to be found from adding some level of strength training to your calendar.

Industry observers note that jason Griffin is Bicycling's Senior Health and Fitness Editor, bringing more than a decade of fitness experience and years in the cycling industry to every story. A former personal trainer and bike shop manager, he's lined up for crits, tackled enduros, but prefers getting lost on multi-day bikepacking adventures. Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.

Latest Update: The 6 Best Folding Treadmills for Runners, Tested by a Treadmill Expert

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The best folding treadmills give you a real running experience without permanently eating up your floor space.
  • Recent findings suggest that if you're like me and you want to be able to run a treadmill at home, but you can’t give away valuable space to a huge piece of fitness equipment?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that we earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

The best folding treadmills give you a real running experience without permanently eating up your floor space. I adore having a folding treadmill at home, because, living in a smaller space, I can easily stash it away or bring it out for a go. And this time of year, when there's sleet and snow? I don't want to miss out on a workout.

Recent findings suggest that if you're like me and you want to be able to run a treadmill at home, but you can’t give away valuable space to a huge piece of fitness equipment? We get it. There’s a solution, though: A folding treadmill gives you the ability to pack up and store your ’mill between runs. Their compact size and light weight comes at a cost: They often don’t have as many convenient features we expect from a top-of-the-line model, nor do they offer huge inclines and top speeds. That said, most can do the basics effectively when you need them to, then fit in your closet when you’re done. The best folding treadmills, as we see them, offer a range of sizes and prices for casual runners and athletes in training.

The dream of shoving your treadmill under your bed between runs is alive in the Echelon Stride-6. This high-performance mill features a full-size, 20.5- by 60-inch running deck that can hit a max speed of 12.5 mph, but still manages to fold up tight. Personally, I store mine upright against a wall, sometimes hidden behind a curtain. It takes up about as much space as a few snowboards or a couple of winter coats. No, I'm not kidding, it's just that compact.

Sources indicate that the Stride-6’s belt features low-response cushioning that creates a ride that feels closer to outdoor road running than treadmill running, which I love when I’m training for road races. Also, as an autistic sensory seeker, sometimes I really enjoy beating the hell out of the deck after a bad day. Are you also a sensory seeker, or have one in your life? If so, this is a solid choice. At full speed, with a 12 percent incline, this machine gives as good as it gets, too.

In a recent development, this treadmill does not have a touchscreen, though. Instead, it syncs directly to a running watch or tablet, for which it has an extra-large holder. The pre-loaded running programs are fine and dandy, but nothing to write home about. Echelon produces a paid workout video library like NordicTrack’s iFit, which you can access via an app, but it’s no different than any other virtual workout platforms without native support on the treadmill.

Let’s talk a little more about the folding mechanism, though, because that’s the reason to buy this treadmill. It is one of only a handful of options that doesn’t require any assembly. Unbox this beauty, unfold it, plug it in, and you’re good. It has an “autofold” feature that makes collapsing the treadmill feel seamless. All that you do is press the foot pedal, and the crossbar and board fold onto the surface of the treadmill. You can then store it flat on the ground or upright, which is a win for anyone who doesn’t have the permanent floor space available.

Recent findings suggest that also, after testing treadmill after treadmill in my house, I can confidently say my cats prefer the Stride-6, and I have no idea why. They're obsessed and I can't figure it out. It is also the easiest to store, fun to run on, and it's by far the easiest to move around.

When this treadmill is folded, it practically disappears. Fully folded, it drops to under 11 inches tall, which is easily flat enough to slide under a bed or stand upright in a closet corner. For anyone training for a marathon in an apartment, a spare bedroom, or a shared space, you know the value there. The SwiftFold mechanism handles it in one motion, and there’s no assembly required.

According to recent reports, what I appreciate is that folding this flat usually means compromising on the machine underneath. This one doesn’t. You still get a dual brushless 4.0 HP motor, a 0–12 percent auto-incline, a 12.5 mph top speed, and a 300-lb weight capacity that matches most treadmills in its class. The 51.18 x 18.9-inch deck is a touch narrow for tall runners, and that is, admittedly an concern.But, when you add the real marathon course maps and an AI coach, along with that magical fold? At around $900 to $1,000 it’s a ‘mill that’s hard to say no to.

Urevo CyberMega Treadmill Review.

I will be the first to admit I was incredibly skeptical about this machine. I mean, it folds up to be smaller than your average card table. I have luggage that’s bigger than the G5i. But, I hear the cawing coming because I need to eat crow. It’s surprisingly stable and fun to run on. It’s really pretty smooth. It is more road-like than cushioned, so if you’re expecting pillowy surfaces, you’ll be disappointed. But if you’re worried you’re going to feel the fold seam, or feel super penned in, you won’t.

Industry observers note that no, this is not a treadmill for tall runners. I’m 6-feet tall, and I’m at the tippy top end of the range of someone who should throw miles on this. But, that being said, if you’re shorter than I am, starved for space, and you want a folding treadmill with serious speed and incline, this is a fantastic option. One thing I will note, though: that first fold when you’re folding it isn’t as soft as you’d expect, and it’s kinda loud. But considering the fact that you could store it just about anywhere, and that it takes less than five minutes to set up and assemble? It’s freaking impressive as all get out. Like, truly wild territory, here.

If you’re looking for a serious running machine that also happens to fold, then you can’t do better than the NordicTrack Commercial 1750. Both Dengate and I really appreciated the feel of running on this machine, which has he called “Goldilocks” cushioning. The deck is firm enough that you don’t feel like you’re running on rubber but soft enough that it wasn’t as hard on our joints as a road run would be. We were also sold on the quick controls for both speed and incline changes, which are both easy to identify and toggle. I found that it stops a bit more abruptly than other NordicTracks: It’s not “knock you off your feet” fast, but there’s a little learning curve.

Recent findings suggest that the Commercial 1750 has a large running surface, which I appreciate as someone who tends to wander on the ’mill a bit. All NordicTracks come with a trial subscription to iFit, the brand’s virtual workout library, which gives you dozens of programs, like marathon training companions, guided runs, and more. It costs extra after the first 30 days, but I think it’s a distinctive and worthwhile option if you like a guided workout. Of course, you can run on this treadmill without iFit, too.

Recent findings suggest that on to the folding: The frame is huge–it weighs over 300 pounds–so it needs the hydraulic lift help that gets it to fold. The process could be a hair easier, but the balanced weight makes it fairly simple. Moving the 1750, on the other hand, is tricky. Sure, it technically has wheels so that you can roll it around, but that requires tipping the machine and balancing it while you do. Once you place it, you can fold it, but you’re better off leaving it where it is.

The Horizon 7.0AT was the easiest treadmill to get started and learn how to use, but its simplicity holds it back from being the outright best. It’s an old-school treadmill with no touchscreen display or video components, and that limits options for programming. That being mentioned, it’s a very affordable option that gets the job done so long as you don’t need a guided workout or on-board entertainment.

According to recent reports, the Horizon 7.0 does exactly what you expect and does a great job of it. It has a 20- by 60-inch running deck that’s plenty large enough for the majority of runners. I wish that it felt a little firmer underfoot, but other members of our team did not have the same complaint. The pre-loaded programs are easy to find if you know your way around a treadmill. (Most of the runners I spoke with are “set and forget” or running with program apps—which you can link through your watch or tablet—so it’s not a worry.) The toggles for speed and incline are intuitive and easy to use.

Folding this one is nice and easy, thanks to a hydraulic assist mechanism. Moving it around is pretty easy, too: The wheels line up in a better place than the 1750. It shrinks by nearly 40 percent when folded, which is genuinely impressive when you consider its massive build and huge incline range. One thing to keep in mind, though: That steep incline lifts you fairly high, so I do not recommend it for basement gyms unless you plan on running flat, or you live in a fancy place with 9-foot basement ceilings.

Read Full Horizon 7.0AT Treadmill Review.

Sources indicate that I’ve never met a treadmill that folds up smaller than the WalkingPad R2. In keeping with the brand, it’s made for walking, with a top speed of 3.7 mph and speed walking at 7.5 mph. And honestly? It’s so compact that you could reasonably put one of these in your home as a more portable complement to a standard, non-folding treadmill without feeling cramped. Use it as an under-desk treadmill or move it around to wherever you can find some free space.

According to recent reports, it’s a fantastic treadmill for anyone who wants to get moving when they’d otherwise be sitting around. It features a smaller deck, super-responsive cushioning, and whisper-quiet motor. You could walk on it during a Zoom call with your microphone unmuted, and people would be hard-pressed to hear it. The cushioning means that you’re not going to wear yourself out while you work, and keeps you from bouncing around so badly that you can’t type.

One little thing I like about this folding treadmill is its smart “automatic mode,” which automatically detects your speed changes depending on where your feet are hitting the deck and adjusts as you go. That alone is worth the cost of the machine.

It has been revealed that folding this treadmill is a cinch, and so is storage, thanks to its low weight and small footprint. Even if you store it in a different room from where you use it, it’s only 55 pounds, so you can just haul it from space to space without any issue.

In a recent development, the team at Runner’s World has been testing all things running for decades. We work year-round on everything from shoes to treadmills. Personally, I have been running for over 20 years, running multiple marathons and ultras, and treadmill training is a huge part of my regimen. And I’ve been professionally reviewing products for nearly a decade.

In a recent development, runner-in-Chief Jeff Dengate designed a rigorous testing protocol to measure a number of critical features in each and every treadmill that we test, and I wrote a specific rubric to test folding treadmills based on that protocol. This year alone, I have run on over 40 models, racking up almost 200 miles in the past several months. Dengate, who is “never not running,” has also put in miles on many of these models. With folding treadmills, there are several specific qualities we examine to separate the best from the just ok:.

Having the ability to fold should not make a treadmill any less useful. While it’s impossible for them to maintain all of the features of certain non-folding treadmills, many or most of them are every bit as good. Some are so gozZod that they even appear on many of our guides.

Even with a compact folding model, it’s key to plan ahead and measure out the spaces where you plan to use and/or store your treadmill. Keep in mind that you need at least 2 feet of clearance surrounding your treadmill in every direction while you’re running. As someone who has put a Cat-shaped hole in the wall of her basement because I lost my footing, I cannot recommend this enough.

There’s a Right Way to Fold and a Wrong Way to Fold.

This sounds like a no-brainer, but a folding treadmill should become more compact and easy to store when folded. There are a ton that technically have a folding mechanism but are not all that much smaller in their folded form. If the folded treadmill is too tall for a room, or if it doesn’t clear very much floor space, it doesn’t make sense.

According to recent reports, A small running platform can prevent you from feeling comfortable at your full running stride, so we generally think that longer is better. (There are exceptions, of course: A walking pad doesn’t need a long belt.) Width is crucial for people with a wider stride or who tend to wander a bit, or those of us who run a bit duck-footed. A narrow belt can feel constricting when you’re running.

Don’t Worry Too Much About Max Speed and Incline.

With folding treadmills especially, you only want as much power as you actually need. A faster max speed requires a bigger motor, which makes for a bigger, heavier treadmill. Most people will be just fine with 10 mph for running, and 3 or 4 mph for walking, so a huge motor isn’t necessary.

Industry observers note that inclines are controlled by a separate motor, so the same rule applies. Most of us don’t want to pretend we’re climbing Everest at the gym, so a 15 percent incline is overkill. It’s nice to have occasionally, but not a dealbreaker to go without.

What are some ways to stay safe on the treadmill while training?

With the treadmill setting the pace for you, it is notable to select a pace that you feel capable of walking or running at, and use the safety equipment provided. Be sure you know where the automatic stop switch is and where the speed adjustment buttons are before starting to run/walk.

Should I adjust my mileage while using a treadmill?

Because treadmill running can be easier than road running, you may need to increase your mileage (or adjust speed and incline) when training on the treadmill to get the same level of workout you get from running outdoors. However, many people find treadmill running far less mentally stimulating, making it difficult to do longer distances indoors.

Is a treadmill a good way for newbie runners or walkers to start?

There are benefits of starting your training on a treadmill. The external pacing of the treadmill allows you to set a desired pace, then not have to think about maintaining it once it’s set. Treadmills are also indoors, which means inclement weather can’t stop you from running. They also can have screens attached, allowing you watch reveals or follow a video workout instead of just listening to music. However, walking outdoors has been shown to be beneficial for mental health with the changes in scenery as you walk, increased vitamin D production from being in the sun, and decreased sensory stimulation with the absence of screens.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A group of friends celebrating the Thanksgiving Holiday with a Friendsgiving dinner. (Photo: Getty Images).

Holiday gatherings are the prime place for awkward small talk as you reconnect with loved ones you really should see more often. And as folks scan the windswept plains for something — anything — to talk about, triathletes are easy targets: “Are you still doing that triathlon thing?” I’ve gotten asked at plenty of family parties.

According to recent reports, I know, my hobby is not normal. It’s one of those activities that claims, “easy small talk,” but also “that’s so weird.” In honor of the holiday season, I asked my colleagues for fun ways to answer the question while enjoying turkey and cranberry sauce. Here’s what they remarked.

Sources indicate that think triathlon is wild? Take on eight sports. You go from kayaking to mountain climbing to mountain biking, then trail running, a swim across a lake to get to your road bike, and after 50 miles of biking, you tie up your road running shoes for a foot-race to your final event: paddleboarding to the finish line.

In a recent development, the only problem is, I can’t say it with a straight face. Triathlon (or a made-up octo-thlon) sounds about as crazy as cooking an eight-course meal with one oven for 15 people to gather around a table that really only seats six.

Once you do it a few times, muscle memory kicks in, and the logistics feel less overwhelming. So yes, I’m still doing that triathlon thing, and you can too.

– Rebekah Brately, associate editor.

Sources indicate that everyone’s doing those Ironman races these days. I’m not sure when it became normal to casually jump into a full-distance race before the shorter ones, but here we are. Some people are even doing multiple, in a row.

In a recent development, I used to be one of the youngest on the start line. Now I’m surrounded by the next generation telling me their HRV scores, how many gels they’re trying to stomach because some pro is eating 200 grams of carbohydrates an hour, and why I NEED to start taking creatine. And don’t forget Bicarb, yes, that bicarb under your sink … don’t get me started.

Oh, and they’ve got an ultramarathon and a Hyrox lined up in the next three weeks, too.

It seems my “crazy weird” endurance hobby has really caught on. You’d better jump on quick before you get left behind with me. Now pass me more yams because … Magnus, carbs, and whatnot.

– Travis Mundell, social media manager.

Recent findings suggest that so first you run, then you hop in the water. No, you don’t take off your shoes, that’s part of it. Then you swim. Really far? No, not at once, but in aggregate. (What does aggregate mean? Don’t worry about it, [nephew name redacted to prevent family squabbling].) Then you get out of the water. Oh, and you can use paddles and a swim buoy; it helps with the shoe problem. And you run again.

Did I mention you usually do it with a partner, so you’re tied together? Most of the running is off-road … Yes, you’re tied together; it’s for safety. I think. And you do it over and over for hours. My time? Honestly, I can’t even remember how long it took me; it was a long time. And there’s like a dozen transitions. Well, maybe “transitions” isn’t accurate; it’s not like in triathlon at all. And you end up swimming and running really far. How far? I can’t remember, and it changes, and it doesn’t really matter.

Oh, and there’s some really cool gear that you can use, like wetsuits that zip down to cool you off and have removable arm warmers and…wait, where did everyone go?

– Chris Foster, editor-in-chief.

In a recent development, you’ve shown such interest in triathlon every time I see you, Uncle Bill, so I signed you up to do a race with me next spring! Don’t worry, it’s a short one – only about 16 miles total. I’ll see you in the pool tomorrow morning for your first workout! [Walks away in search of pie.].

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, these yoga poses are meant to be easily accessible.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Andrew Clark; Design in Canva).

Recent findings suggest that certain seasons come with a lot, and we mean a lot, of socializing. On the one hand, this means a chance to spend quality time with family and friends, which is always a win. But if you deal with any amount of social anxiety, gatherings can also come with stress and general overwhelm.

Industry observers note that if leaving isn’t an option—just kidding, we know you probably want to be there—there are ways to find grounding and calm within your own being. You can practice breathwork, take a walk, even excuse yourself and enjoy a yoga pose or two for a minute. Or, if you resonate with the asanas on this list, perhaps five!

In a recent development, these yoga poses are meant to be easily accessible. Escape for a few moments to try one of the more involved poses or enjoy a super subtle modification mid-party!

Recent findings suggest that holiday gatherings tend to involve a fair amount of standing around—which is where your casual Tree Pose (Vrksasana) comes in. Popping one foot up—whether against your upper or lower leg or, more stealthily, your ankle—can be done at literally any time: while you’re doing the dishes, chatting with loved ones, or experiencing a lull in activity. The reminder that you’re in control of your sense of balance can help you feel steadier on your own two feet in all ways.

Social gatherings can feel all over the place, making grounding of all kinds welcome. Sinking into Squat (Malasana) calls for strength and stability. And though households all over the world perform chores and even eat meals in this pose, if you need some privacy to find stillness in a deep squat, we’re sure that your family will understand if you disappear for a minute or two.

Folding forward can provide a sense of tremendous release and relief. Hinging at your hips in Standing Forward Bend (Uttanasana) and allowing your head and upper body to hang heavy—sometimes referred to as Rag Doll—serves as a subtle inversion, activating your parasympathetic nervous system and encouraging calm. Plus, this pose is normal enough to fold into at any point. Just tell your people that you need a quick stretch.

Finding strength within yourself can make chilling out a little easier. Pressing up—or jumping back—into Plank Pose activates your core, arms, and legs, then asks you to pause. Turning your focus toward this physical task, whether for a few breaths or a full minute, can help snap you out of an anxious spin and get you back into a celebratory state.

According to recent reports, sometimes, the best thing you can do is retreat to a spare bedroom (or the couch or the floor) and lie down for a while. Savasana can certainly provide some calming release, but for something a little more likely to get you out of your head and into your body, try Reclining Bound Angle Pose. It’s a subtle stretch that rejuvenates without being daunting—sort of like a best-case-scenario social engagement.
