📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Recent findings suggest that you wouldn’t think late autumn is the best time to buy an electric bike; after all, the daylight hours are short, and the weather is getting cold in many regions. However, whether you’re hunting for deals or seeking out the latest tech, now is the time to buy. With holiday discounts and fresh e-bikes rolling out to dealers and online retailers, plenty of great commuter, cargo, and e-MTB options are out there—at great prices.

In a recent development, I’m a lifelong cyclist, former product director for bike companies, and was a mechanic at busy shops in Upcoming York City. Plus, I commute daily on an e-bike and ride test dozens of electric bikes each year. Last summer, I even went almost entirely car-free thanks to an electric cargo bike.

Recent findings suggest that whether you’re choosing your first e-bike, upgrading to a newer model, or adding another electric model to your garage, dozens of great options are available—and our editors and staff have tested many of them. No matter your age, cycling ability, or budget, brands offer electric bikes that meet needs.

Tip for E-Bike Buyers: Don’t overpay for an electric bike, but spend what you can comfortably afford. If an e-bike is fun to ride, you’ll use it more often. It’s more cost-effective to buy an e-bike equipped the way you want it upfront than to upgrade it later. Also, remember: you cannot change an electric bike’s motor system if you decide you want more power.

The Aventon Level is our benchmark electric bike. It’s a great e-bike for commuting, running errands, or leisure riding. Over several years, the Level platform has proven to be reliable and low-maintenance. Plus, its price doesn’t break the bank.

According to recent reports, aventon split the 4th-generation Level into two models. The REC features a 750W hub motor with 80 Nm of torque. Aventon also added regenerative braking, increasing the bike’s range up to 75 miles. The pricier ADV edition features a mid-drive motor; it bumps up the torque to 100 Nm and range to 110 miles. Both versions come standard with fenders, a rear rack, lights, and suspension.

Recent findings suggest that another feature users will find quite useful is the Level’s connected features. The Level 4’s ACU (Aventon Control Unit) adds several smart features to the already well-equipped platform. The wheel lock and motion sensor alarm are passive theft deterrents when you stop for a mid-ride coffee or run into the post office. A 4G chip in the ACU enables GPS tracking in Aventon’s mobile app, so you can locate your bike if you forget where you locked it. 4G connectivity also allows you to set geofence restrictions on the bike for teens or housemates.

BUY LEVEL 4 STEP-THROUGH BUY LEVEL 4 ADV.

In a recent development, the relatively affordable seven-speed model Soltera 2.5 from Aventon delivers simplicity and style that is tough to beat. This makes it an excellent choice for getting around town or quick commutes. It’s even better than the original version, thanks to hydraulic disc brakes. A push of the throttle gets you started; then, the brushless hub motor gently assists your pedaling.

Along with disc brakes, the Soltera features integrated lights and turn signals, and the battery is hidden in the bike’s frame (rather than the bolt-on batteries found on many similarly-priced e-bikes). Best for smoother roads and bike paths, the Soltera delivers the essential features a city rider needs in a strikingly light 46-pound package.

Aventon also offers a singlespeed, Soltera 3 ADV with a Gates belt-drive system.

When buying a low-priced e-bike, a simple, low-cost, easy-to-repair, and reliable model usually beats out complicated designs. Lectric’s XP Lite2 is about as basic as it gets. It has a low-maintenance singlespeed drivetrain, a 300-watt hub motor, and a 375Wh battery. With its compact size, 20x2.5-inch tires, and twist-grip throttle, the XP Lite is perfect for zipping through traffic, commuting to the office, or heading to the gym or bar after work.

The XP Lite2 features only one gear and a 300W motor, so it’s not ideal for very hilly terrain. But with the throttle, you can get over small rises and bridges. Lectric also equips the bike with hydraulic disc brakes and front and rear lights. The XP Lite2 is also great for RVers and campgrounds, since it’s lightweight (about 48 pounds) and folds down to 36x16x27-inch dimensions.

Many “step-through” e-bikes don’t actually have a low step design. This makes it challenging for some riders to mount or dismount. However, the CTY e2.1, by REI’s Co-op house brand, has a fully step-through front triangle. The CTY is a great choice for older riders, those with reduced mobility, or others who seek an easy-to-ride e-bike.

In a recent development, REI equips the CTY e2.1 with a 250-watt hub-drive motor that provides smooth pedal-assistance up to 20 mph. It also features a suspension fork to smooth out bumps and potholes, an adjustable stem for a comfortable riding position, and hydraulic disc brakes for better stopping. For less than the cost of some e-bikes online, you can get a quality electric bike backed up by REI warranty and service.

Sources indicate that the Current ADV is the priciest bike in this story, but for a good reason. Some electric bikes look a lot like mountain bikes, but that doesn’t mean they are built for real off-road use. Aventon’s fresh Current is the brand’s first full suspension E-MTB, and it is trail-ready right out of the box. Trevor Raab, Bicycling’s Senior Photographer and Test Team member, mentioned, “The bike’s intuitive ride feel will please experienced mountain bikers and also benefit first-time mountain bikers.”.

Industry observers note that the Current ADV features an aluminum frame with 140mm rear wheel travel and a great-feeling motor with 750 peak Watts and 110 Nm of torque. (It also has a Boost mode that bumps power to 850W and 120 Nm of torque.) Rounding out the ADV are high-end components like a RockShox Psylo Gold fork, SRAM DB8 brakes, SRAM Eagle 70 Mechanical transmission, and a tubeless wheelset with Maxxis Minion EXO tires.

In a recent development, in his full review of the bike, “Aventon Goes Full Performance: The Current Electric Mountain Bike Is Surprisingly Dialed,” Raab particularly likes the Current’s easy-to-use interface. It’s loaded with ride data as well as the ability to tune the motor settings. If you don’t need rear suspension, check out Aventon’s updated Ramblas ADV hardtail E-MTB.

READ AVENTON CURRENT REVIEWMORE GREAT E-MTBs.

Getting into E-MTB trail riding on a budget is tough. Low-priced electric mountain bikes often aren’t built strong enough for off-road riding (or weigh half a rider’s weight), and trail-capable models typically cost more than $4,000. That’s what makes the TrailRush a standout bike—for less than $2,000, you get a trail-ready hardtail you can take on singletrack and have some fun.

Sources indicate that ride1Up equips the 29-inch-wheeled TrailRush with a Brose mid-drive motor. With 90 Nm of torque, it isn’t as powerful as many upcoming, higher-priced E-MTB motors, but it gets the job done. The TrailRush also comes stock with a dropper seatpost, four-piston disc brakes, and tubeless-compatible rims with Maxxis Minion tires.

Of course, to hit this great price, Ride1Up made some equipment sacrifices. The 504Wh battery isn’t as large as some peers (like the Aventon Ramblas), so you get less ride time between charges. Additionally, the 11-36T cassette and 38T chainring limit your ability to climb steep hills.

Compared to earlier iterations of the Aventure, the third-generation model has a smoother ride and feels more like a premium bike (without the high price tag). Aventon’s new torque sensor allows more control over the acceleration of Aventure’s 750W rear hub motor. Lighter-weight testers found earlier models had too much torque, but this Aventure remedied that fault. Additional features include a new head-unit interface, integrated turn signals, a front light, a rear rack, and fenders.

Sources indicate that the Aventure 3 is an excellent fat-tire e-bike for commuters—especially on snowy days and gravel paths. Off-roading, it excels on doubletrack trails and cinder paths, but with this burly bike’s weight and components, it has limited functionality on singletrack and more aggressive mountain trails.

Industry observers note that aventon also offers the Aventure M, a mid-drive version of the Aventure. It keeps the same big, burly character but adds a more premium feel, a smoother, more powerful motor, and an upgraded drivetrain—along with a higher price. Those refinements cost about $1,000 more than the Aventure 3.

Buying an e-bike on Amazon can be risky, especially if you don’t know much about bikes or have limited mechanical experience. However, sometimes you can find a good deal on a decent bike. At $500, the Heybike Cityscape isn’t the pinnacle of e-bike technology, but it lets you get out and enjoy some rides without breaking the bank.

According to recent reports, I combed through dozens of Amazon listings comparing low-priced electric bikes, and this Heybike stood out for its combination of price and features. Then, I saw someone on the local bike path with one and asked them about the bike. The rider liked it and said it has been trouble-free (they noted a local bike shop assembled it for them). Heybike’s U.S. support line is available for warranty service or product questions.

Sources indicate that don’t want to purchase from Amazon? Use this exclusive Bicycling discount link for $100 (applied at checkout) off the Cityscape 2.0, plus free shipping.

Sources indicate that tern’s cargo bikes are the gold standard for practical features, durability, and ride quality. This reputation makes the brand’s GSD (longtail) and HSD (short-tail) cargo models top picks for bike commuters, families, and riders looking to cut their dependence on automobiles.

According to recent reports, the new third-generation HSD improves on its predecessor’s legacy. The HSD (short for “Haul Stuff Daily”) is a shrunken-down version of Tern’s GSD3 model released last year. The HSD3’s frame has a 419-pound carrying capacity (combined bike, rider, and cargo), added stiffness, and improved stability at speed compared to its predecessor. The P10e Sport configuration features the peppier Bosch Performance Line Sport motor and an electronic-shifting ten-speed TRP E.A.S.I. A10 drivetrain. The Sport motor’s 28mph assistance was a welcome upgrade for commuting and running errands alongside car traffic on local suburban streets. The 90 Nm of torque (15 Nm more than the standard Performance Line motor) also provides quicker acceleration from a dead stop and a little more oomph when loaded down with cargo or climbing hills.

Industry observers note that while it’s the second-most affordable HSD3 model in Tern’s U.S. selection, the P10e Sport is certainly not a budget-priced e-bike. But for the extra cost over similar-sized cargo bikes, you get a proven and well-thought-out bicycle. The HSD’s features and design elements feel purposeful. A great example of this is the bike’s stowability: The HSD3 can be tilted and stored vertically, balanced on its rear rack. It also moves easily on its rear wheel when you need to park or store it. The handlebar and stem also fold down, making the HSD3 much easier to transport by car or SUV than almost any other e-bike.

Many riders are attracted to the XPedition’s very appealing price. Currently priced at $1,399 for the single-battery model, it boasts an impressive 60-mile range and a top speed of 28 mph. (The dual-battery model for $1,799 doubles the range to 120 miles.) This makes the XPedition one of the most affordable electric cargo bikes around and a good option for riders seeking an excellent deal on an e-cargo bike.

Industry observers note that “The XPedition’s capability surprised me”, remarked Test Editor Dan Chabanov. “Combined with the Lectric XL panniers ($150) and the Essentials package ($120), I comfortably carried several days of groceries for a family of three or one adult passenger.”.

Industry observers note that however, to reach a price like this, concessions have to be made somewhere. This results in a somewhat cheap feeling to the bike. Most of the XPedition’s parts are bottom-tier—with the notable exception of the brakes. The pedal-assist motor is powerful off the line, but at times, it feels erratic. The XPedition is adequate if you live in a very flat area or don’t need to carry kids or an adult passenger. Despite these faults, if you’re on a budget and looking to ditch the car for errands and trips around town, the XPedition is the cheapest e-cargo bike we recommend buying.

Plenty of commuter e-bikes cost far less than Specialized’s Turbo Vado SL 2, and they can probably do most of these things. So why spend twice as much as many popular options? I dive into the details in my story, “Stop Wasting Money on Cheap E-Bikes. Here’s Why Spending More Pays Off for Commuters.”.

The TL;DR: The Turbo Vado SL 2’s excellent ride geometry, silky-smooth motor, low weight, and premium components make riding fun. Together, these features make you want to ride the Vado every day and use it for more than simply getting to work. And thanks to Specialized’s extensive dealer network, you have somewhere to turn when it needs service.

Sources indicate that “Lightweight e-bike” might sound like an oxymoron to some, but a sub-40-pound weight is impressive when many electric bikes exceed 60 or 80 pounds. And often, e-bikes this light are pricey. Yet, the Velotric Tempo is only $1,499 and boasts a 39 lb. (claimed) weight.

It has been revealed that velotric achieves this weight reduction by ditching the bulky suspension fork (suspension forks on lower-priced bikes often don’t work all that well, to be frank), swapping heavy tires for 700x42c gravel tires, and using a smaller battery. Riders who need to carry the bike up any stairs or load it onto a bike rack will appreciate the reduced weight. However, heavier riders may want to test ride the Tempo before purchase, as lower-powered motors can bog down and reduce battery range for bigger-bodied people.

In a recent development, bicycles are my life, and I’m a dedicated e-bike user and enthusiast. I’ve also worked in cycling for over 25 years. For almost six years, I’ve ridden and tested electric bikes as Bicycling’s Deputy Editor—and I use e-bikes for my daily commute. Before joining the staff, I led product development for top bicycle brands.

It has been revealed that our editors test dozens of electric bikes across every cycling category, and we continually receive new models to evaluate. Our riding involves much more than taking bikes on short spins; we use electric bikes in our daily lives. Commuting, school drop-offs, grocery runs, and daily transportation are only a few of the things we regularly do with e-bikes. We also hit the trails on E-MTB models to test their performance in real-world mountain biking conditions, not simply riding them around town.

It has been revealed that in addition to ride-testing, our editors regularly talk to cyclists of all ages and abilities about their riding needs. This helps us craft our list of Best Electric Bikes: e-bikes that will meet your needs on the street, trails, and around the neighborhood. Two of the e-bikes in this story even made the final cut for our 2026 Bike Awards.

It has been revealed that electric bike prices range from entry-level models for less than $500 to premium machines costing almost as much as a good used car. However, our years of testing have proven that many of the best and most practical models live squarely in the middle.

We find that many standout e-bikes are priced between $1,500 and $3,000. These models strike a good balance between reliability and practicality, without requiring you to overspend on features or technology you don’t need. Electric bikes costing less than $1,000 often take shortcuts to achieve this, either by using lower-quality parts or offering limited service after the bike is purchased.

According to recent reports, of course, you can also spend much more on electric bikes. Premium e-bikes typically offer improved motor performance, higher-quality components, lower weight, or more tech features. However, for most general riding purposes, these bikes are overkill—but they‘re certainly fun!

According to recent reports, → Consider how much cargo you’ll need to carry if your riding involves commuting or running errands. Look for a bike with appropriate racks, mount points, and other accessories.

→ For singletrack and trail riding, look for mountain bikes with knobby tires, adjustable suspension, high-quality frames, and low weight.

→ Pay attention to weight. While fat tire e-bikes and cargo bikes offer versatility, many weigh over 90 pounds. If you’ll need to carry your bike up any stairs or lift it onto a bike rack, a lighter option will be a better fit.

In a recent development, → Bike storage is another consideration. While most e-bikes don’t require excessive space compared to their non-pedal-assisted counterparts, ensure you have access to a power outlet where you initiative to store it for easy charging.

Several e-bike brands, Aventon, Ride1Up, and Lectric, performed well in our ride testing and evaluations. These bikes might require some minor assembly at home, such as installing pedals, a seat, and tightening handlebars. We considered how easy bikes were to assemble in our recommendations. Many bike shops will not assemble or otherwise work on e-bikes they do not sell due to liability issues. The direct-to-consumer brands we recommend have dealers nationwide ready to support you.

Established bike companies, such as Specialized and Trek, manufacture e-bikes and have hundreds of dealers across North America. Additionally, REI sells its house-brand Co-op electric bikes (and models from Cannondale and Tern) in its stores.

Recent findings suggest that there are three electric-assist classes available in the United States, and the use of each class of bike can vary by state, city, and area you are riding. Be sure to check local regulations before buying and before riding your bike.

Class 1: 20 mph max assist speed; throttle is not standard equipment.

Class 2: 20 mph max assist speed; throttle comes standard equipment.

Class 3: 28 mph max assist speed; throttle is not standard equipment.

Industry observers note that what this means: Class 1 motors kick in only when you pedal and stop helping you at 20 mph. Class 2 also offers pedal assist up to 20 mph, but these bikes can also have a throttle-powered mode that allows users to engage the motor without pedaling. Class 3 is pedal-assist like Class 1, but helps you until you reach 28 mph.

Other countries classify electric bikes differently, and many do not allow e-bikes to assist riders beyond 20 miles per hour.

Electric bikes generally feature one of two types of motors: mid-drive motors, which are contained in the frame at the bottom of the bike between the pedals; and rear hub motors, which are built into the rear wheel.

Bikes with rear hub motors are generally less expensive but are also less powerful. Mid-drive e-bikes tend to be more expensive, but are typically more reliable and higher performance. Because the extra weight on a mid-drive motor is centered in the bike and lower to the ground, these bikes are generally easier to handle than bikes with hub motors.

Measured in Newton meters (or Nm), torque is a rotational measurement of force—and the number to pay attention to when you want an idea of an e-bike motor’s output. More torque means more power off the line and more boost to your pedaling.

The heavier the bike, the more torque it needs. Lighter road bikes typically have 30 to 40 Nm of torque, and trail and cargo models (generally) have at least 80 Nm. Most commuter bikes fall somewhere in between.

In a recent development, the size of an e-bike’s battery is measured in watt-hours (or Wh). This measurement represents the energy stored in the battery and how many watts it can deliver each hour. The higher the number, the longer the range, but the faster you go, the faster you drain the battery.

So, if a 504Wh battery paired with a 500W motor gives you one hour of ride time at the highest assist, riding at about half that power will double your range.

Many e-bike brands seamlessly integrate batteries to make the bike look sleeker (and more like a traditional non-assist bike). Most batteries lock to the bike and come with a key that lets you unlock and remove it, which serves multiple purposes: You can remove the battery and charge it off the bike, plus a locked battery deters (and hopefully prevents) a thief from stealing it. An e-bike with the battery removed is safer for hauling on a bike rack and lighter for carrying up steps.

According to recent reports, since e-bikes can maintain higher speeds for longer than standard bikes, you want extra control when riding. Wider tires provide better traction and the freedom to leave the pavement with little penalty, and a suspension fork will help tame some of the rougher roads you might explore. Good disc brakes are a must, too, for slowing a heavy bike at high speed. This is not a place to skimp.

It has been revealed that some e-bikes have an integrated lighting system that turns on when you power up the bike. While this is a great feature, it’s not a deal-breaker if your bike doesn’t come equipped this way. It’s just as easy to attach your own since so many great bike lights are available.

Sources indicate that E-bikes need regular maintenance and repair to stay in good working condition. Because they’re heavier and go faster than non-assist bicycles, e-bikes often require more regular service on parts like brakes, tires, and drivetrain components. We recommend having a good relationship with a local bike shop experienced in e-bike repair to keep your equipment running smoothly.

Industry observers note that E-bikes use electronics for their motors, batteries, and displays. These parts are often proprietary to bike brands or even specific e-bike models, making replacement more difficult than parts on non-electric bicycles. Make sure to use the correct electronic replacement parts to avoid damaging your e-bike (or it catching fire).

Recent findings suggest that established brands usually (but not always) have a good supply of these parts for replacement, even for years after a bike goes out of production. Bosch and Shimano are two e-bike motor manufacturers with some of the most compatibility between bikes and stock parts for previous generations of systems.

Industry observers note that look for e-bikes from brands that offer at least a one-year warranty on electronic components (many brands’ warranties are longer) and make items like replacement batteries for your bike. These parts are usually not cheap (sometimes up to half the cost of a upcoming bike), but it’s the difference between having an e-bike that can be repaired or becomes a bicycle-shaped paperweight if something goes wrong.

Sources indicate that following a dramatic increase in fires caused by the lithium-ion batteries used in electric bikes, there is a push from local officials, regulatory agencies, and advocacy groups across the U.S. for improved safety certification of e-bikes, batteries, and motor units. In September 2023, a Latest York City law took effect requiring that any e-bike sold in the city “has been certified by an accredited testing laboratory for compliance with Underwriters Laboratories (UL) standard 2849”.

Recent findings suggest that however, just because something is marketed as UL 2849 compliant, tested to UL 2849, or even “certified to UL 2849” does not mean it is UL Safety Certified. Ibrahim Jilani, UL’s Global Director of Consumer Technology, notes: “Certification is always earned by a manufacturer and not a given when they undergo a product submittal. The UL Mark, or any authorized certification mark, can only be issued upon successful demonstration of meeting the requirements of the safety standard.” You can find UL’s updated list of products certified to UL 2849 here. You can cross-reference OSHA’s Nationally Recognized Testing Laboratories for a deep dive into the topic.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

A 5-Minute Stretch Routine to Relieve Tight Joints and a Stiff Back

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (703 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Triathlete

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you’ve been feeling ultra stiff lately, a five-minute yoga-inspired stretching routine break to release physical tension can feel like a full-body reset, helping you feel better in your body—and even more productive—so you can do all of your favorite activities.
  • In a recent development, this short practice is ideal when you need a short break during the workday, but it can also serve as a grounding moment before you sit at your desk or when you’re winding down in the evening.
  • Lie on your back with your arms and legs straight, as if you were in Savasana.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you’ve been feeling ultra stiff lately, a five-minute yoga-inspired stretching routine break to release physical tension can feel like a full-body reset, helping you feel better in your body—and even more productive—so you can do all of your favorite activities.

In a recent development, this short practice is ideal when you need a short break during the workday, but it can also serve as a grounding moment before you sit at your desk or when you’re winding down in the evening. You only need a yoga mat and a sturdy surface to practice on. Come exactly as you are.

Lie on your back with your arms and legs straight, as if you were in Savasana. Take some small movements, maybe wiggling your fingers and toes or moving your head side to side. Then let yourself relax for a moment. Inhale as you reach your hands overhead and your feet away from you, stretching your entire body from head to toe. Exhale and release.

According to recent reports, bend your knees, plant your feet on the mat about hip-distance apart, and rest your arms at your sides. Inhale, press your hands and feet into the mat, and lift your hips in Bridge Pose. Exhale and lower your hips to the mat.

Separate your feet slightly wider than your hips. Bend your elbows and draw your arms into a cactus shape. Exhale and allow your knees to lower toward the left. Inhale and return your knees to center. Exhale and lower your knees toward the right. Repeat Windshield Wipers two more times on each side.

Hug both knees toward your chest, grasping your shins or the backs of your thighs with your hands.

Come to a comfortable sitting position. Lift your shoulders toward your ears, then roll them back, down, and forward. Continue drawing circles with your shoulders in one direction for a few rounds, then switch directions.

In a recent development, interlace your fingers behind your head with your elbows out to the sides. Exhale as you draw your navel toward your spine, round your back, and lower your chin toward your chest in a Cat Pose variation. Inhale as you lift upright and arch your back, drawing your elbows back slightly in a Cow Pose variation. Repeat a few times.

Industry observers note that inhale and reach your arms overhead. Exhale and twist your chest toward the left. Place your right hand on your left knee and your left fingertips on the mat behind you. Take a few breaths here.

It has been revealed that still sitting, come back to center and bring your arms into a cactus shape. Open your hands as wide as you can, spreading your fingers apart. Then shut your hands into tight fists. Repeat opening and closing your hands as many times as feels good.

Recent findings suggest that sit on the mat with your knees bent, your feet flat on the mat, and your hands on the mat behind your hips, fingertips pointing toward you or toward the back of the mat. Press into your hands and feet as you lift your hips off the mat. Draw your chin toward your chest and gaze forward. Take a few breaths here, then lower your hips to the mat.

Draw the soles of your feet together. Inhale and lift your chest. Your feet can come closer to you or stay farther away. Exhale and fold forward, grasping your ankles or feet in Bound Angle Pose. You can stack your fists on top of each other and rest your forehead on them. Breathe here.

Lie on your back with your arms resting at your sides and your palms pressing into the mat. Bend your knees toward your chest and straighten your legs so your feet are reaching toward the ceiling. Keep your legs slightly bent if it’s more comfortable. Take a few breaths here, then shake out your arms and legs and lower your feet to the mat.

It has been revealed that lie on your back, resting your arms, legs, hands, and feet against the mat in Savasana. Or find a comfortable seated position. Take a few deep breaths before returning to the day.

I Run With Constantly Cold Hands—These Smartwool Gloves Keep My Fingers Warm Without Sacrificing Dexterity

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that we earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article.
  • Sources indicate that even though I finally embraced wearing leggings last year, I still hesitate when it comes to winterizing my running gear—even when the “feels like” temp is 28 degrees Fahrenheit on a 34-degree day.
  • Sources indicate that of all the runs and races I’ve underdressed for, the one accessory I always regret not putting on is a pair of gloves.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that we earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Sources indicate that even though I finally embraced wearing leggings last year, I still hesitate when it comes to winterizing my running gear—even when the “feels like” temp is 28 degrees Fahrenheit on a 34-degree day. The simplest gear that transforms my getup, doesn’t make me regret overdressing, and helps me stay warm when the weather begins taking its nippy turn? Gloves. My pair of choice is the Smartwool Active Fleece Insulated.

Sources indicate that of all the runs and races I’ve underdressed for, the one accessory I always regret not putting on is a pair of gloves. I’m the kind of person whose hands are constantly cold. (Healthcare friends, I’m sorry for having fingers that refuse to get a quick oxygen read.).

Industry observers note that I could go the mitts route, and I do when I need an extra layer over my gloved fingers (yes, I double up). But the thing about running, especially when you’re training for Boston in the spring, is that you need to be able to spread your 10 digits and use them to retrieve fuel—or lip balm or a Kleenex—from the depths of your pockets, which requires more dexterity than mittens allow.

I like Smartwool’s gloves because of their range of sizes, though I will admit the extra small is still slightly long in the tips due to their unisex sizing. The gloves are double-layer knit and have a blend of merino wool and polyester to thermoregulate your hands and wick away sweat. The overlay panels serve as windproof protection.

Sources indicate that besides warmth and the usage of my fingers, the Active Fleece also provides visibility, thanks to a reflective logo and piping on the back of the hand. Being seen is key when daylight hours are shorter and I need to log that run before dawn or can only fit in a workout at dusk.

The index and thumb have touchscreen-compatible pads. I wouldn’t recommend them for long-winded texts since, through my own experience, messages aren’t always accurate. But it’s nice that I can type into Google Maps or use dictation and send, “PICK ME UP—I MADE A HORRIBLE MISTAKE” with a location pin.

Sometimes the best test is when you’re not running. On our first chilly morning this fall, I got up early on a Sunday and waited to cheer at mile 10 of a half marathon. The precursor to the waiting was pacing every block in a half-mile radius, trying to figure out if I was actually on the race course.

It has been revealed that when the runners came in and I finally found the right sidewalk corner, the stutter in my voice told me I should have worn two extra layers. Despite my frozen core, I was surprised I still had the feeling in my Smartwool gloved hands.

According to recent reports, the best part of that morning besides being able to type out post-cheer coffee shop directions? Sticking it out so I could encourage runners with more cowbell.

Tech Report: 3 Subtle Breathing Exercises You Can Do at the Dinner Table

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (636 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Yogajournal

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that there are certain occasions that call for covert calm.
  • Industry observers note that your breath is a powerful tool.
  • It has been revealed that if you’re already dealing with low-level overwhelm, drawing attention to yourself and your nerves is likely the last thing you want to do.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that there are certain occasions that call for covert calm. You know what I mean. Those times when you’re incredibly stressed, uncomfortable, or anxious but can’t really extricate yourself from the situation. Take, for example, the occasion dinner. If the thought of a large gathering and non-stop (as well as unfiltered) conversation fills you with even a slight sense of unease, subtle breathing exercises might just be your latest favorite mindfulness practice.

Industry observers note that your breath is a powerful tool. Practicing breathwork, even the quiet kind, can affect your physiological, mental, and emotional state, activating your parasympathetic nervous system and easing your entire being out of panic mode. Known as pranayama in yoga, breathwork is a broad category, allowing you to find the breathing that resonates with you and return to it whenever signs of stress arise.

It has been revealed that if you’re already dealing with low-level overwhelm, drawing attention to yourself and your nerves is likely the last thing you want to do. So, rather than jumping up from the table for a quick yoga pose or engaging in a liberating round of lion’s breath, subtle breathing exercises invite you to remain in your chair, appearing engaged as you regulate your nervous system.

According to recent reports, start with a count of 3 or 5 rounds of each of these breaths and see how you feel. If the tension is still palpable, take as many as you need to self-soothe. And if you forget any of the below in your situation, simply lengthen your exhalations.

According to recent reports, also known as diaphragmatic breathing, belly breathing invites you to take your deepest breath possible. At it’s core, this breathing exercise is about (surprise!) inhaling into your belly. This is, of course, anatomically incorrect. But think of the larger goal here, which is to direct your inhalations toward your belly without exaggerating the movement in your ribs. The results is the diaphragm lowers and creates space to breathe into your actual lungs.

In a recent development, belly breathing also gets your breath out of your upper chest, which is the sort of shallow, stunted breathing that often accompanies anxiety. Slowing and deepening your breath signals safety, reminding your animal self that this is not a moment for fight, flight, or freeze—even if it feels like one.

Sometimes evening things out is the answer. Box breathing involves a simple pattern of inhaling for a count of four, holding for a count of four, exhaling for a count of four, and holding for a count of four, thus (figuratively) creating a sort of square shape with your breath. If four is too short of a count for your natural breathing, you can change your number to five, six, or beyond, so long as each part of the breath (inhalation, exhalation, and holds) remains even.

Turning even part of your attention away from the group and toward your own breath gives you a break from the noise while demonstrating the power of your own body and mind. Box breathing is often used for focus, so don’t be surprised if you return to the conversation with more interest and alertness.

According to recent reports, the simplest option on this list, equal breathing is all about matching your inhalations to your exhalations. This is a practice of balance, so track the count of a deep inhalation, and if it feels okay in your body, apply it to your exhalation. It’s also the most adaptable, so feel free to vary the count slightly. You don’t want to stress yourself out, after all.

In addition to providing the aforementioned benefits of breathwork, redirecting your focus places your entire being in neutral, enabling you to consider your current circumstance with more clarity and calm.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

From 55 degrees down to 25, I bring one piece of cold-weather gear on every ride: a neck buff. It isn’t the most exciting item in my kit, and it won’t make a dramatic difference in a gear photo. But it’s useful across a wider range of temperatures than almost anything else I own, and it costs far less than most winter gear cyclists spend serious money on.

It has been revealed that at 55 degrees, I can wear it loosely around my neck and cut the wind without feeling bundled up. As the temperature drops, that little bit of insulation becomes more valuable. Covering your neck makes you feel warmer, and the buff also helps close the gap at the top of your jacket. Cold air sneaking in around the collar can make an otherwise reasonable layering setup feel inadequate. A buff helps keep that draft out.

When it gets really cold, I pull it up over my ears and face. It’s a simple way to add coverage without committing to a heavier balaclava for the whole ride. And if the temperature changes, or I start working harder on a climb, I can pull it back down in a few seconds. It takes up almost no space in a jersey pocket, which means there’s little reason to leave it at home.

Neck buffs grew out of a practical problem familiar to motorcycle riders: keeping cold, wind, and road dust off your neck and face. Riders already used bandanas and other neck cloths; the stretchy tube made that protection easier to wear under a helmet. Skiers adopted it too, which may be why people associate it with snow sports.

According to recent reports, there is no shortage of expensive cycling accessories that promise to keep you warm while riding. Many are quite good. But few come close to the humble neck buff in terms of how practical, simple, and cheap it is. It’s an adaptable piece of kit that’s just as useful on a cool ride that doesn’t quite call for full winter kit as it is on a truly cold ride, when every gap and exposed bit of skin becomes a problem. It’s a small thing, which is exactly why I never leave home without it.

It has been revealed that test Editor Dan Chabanov got his start in cycling as a New York City bike messenger but promptly found his way into road and cyclocross racing, competing in professional cyclocross races from 2009 to 2019 and winning a Master’s National Championship title in 2018. Prior to joining Bicycling in 2021, Dan worked as part of the race organization for the Red Hook Crit, as a coach with EnduranceWERX, as well as a freelance writer and photographer.

According to recent reports, the JLab Go Sport+ headphones are a fantastic option for runners and fitness fans who want reliable, sweatproof wireless earbuds without breaking the bank. The fit is my second favorite bit of these earbuds. They wrap around the shell of your ear without squeezing or pinching, and they sit gently upon the lower curve above your earlobe. The biggest matter with over-the-ear headphones is that sweat can short them out. Casual headphones, on the other hand, have suffered from sweat shock. Not these. These were made with workouts in mind, and they keep all the comfort, all the “leave me alone” energy, and all that great sound. They’re also sweat-resistant and ever so slightly more breathable than your standard over-the-ear cans.

Sources indicate that these are incredibly comfortable, stay put, and the music? It just sounds so glorious. Thanks to a custom high-excursion driver and Apple's H2 chip, your hype music comes in sharp and booming, even in loud environments. Apple's active noise cancellation is among the best of the best, and adaptive transparency mode lets you hear what’s going on around you at a level you can stand when you’re trying to get your workout on. Adaptive audio and conversation awareness are upcoming in this version and automatically blend ANC and transparency, or lower your volume when you start talking. Swift and My Chemical Romance, I like it to sound as emotional as possible to keep me motivated.

No phone, no Bluetooth dropouts, no excuses. On land, the sound is firmly good enough, and yes, the buttons need a firmware lesson in responsiveness. But for swimmers and sweaty eddies? This thing is a boss.

Shokz leveled up with this pair of headphones. Being able to ping your earbuds is honestly so clutch. Forget where they are? Don’t worry, you can find them.

They’re comfy, they can handle a decent amount of sweat and precipitation, they’re feature-rich, and honestly, just a great experience overall.

Choosing the right running headphones can really make your run. With so many options available, it’s important to consider which features are most important for your needs. To help guide your decision, here are some key factors to consider when selecting the perfect running headphones.

In-ear headphones, also known as earbuds, fit directly into the ear canal. They are often compact and lightweight, making them highly portable. In-ear headphones can offer good sound isolation, blocking out some external noise and, depending on the fit, a decent level of bass. They often come with various ear tip sizes to make sure they’re not going to fall out of your ears.

Hook headphones typically feature a design with hooks that wrap around the ears for added stability. This makes them popular for activities like running or exercising, where a secure fit is crucial to prevent them from falling out. Hook headphones can come in various styles, including earbuds with hooks and over-ear, open-ear styles with hooks.

According to recent reports, bone conduction headphones work by transmitting sound vibrations through the bones of your skull, bypassing the eardrums. This allows you to listen to audio while keeping your ears open to your surroundings. This is especially useful for runners who need to be aware of traffic or other environmental sounds.

Open-ear headphones are designed to sit outside the ear, allowing you to hear both your audio and the environment around you. They don't block your ear canal, so you remain aware of your surroundings, which is helpful for safety during outdoor activities. However, they may leak sound, and the audio quality might not be as immersive as other types.

Recent findings suggest that headphones with storage typically include onboard memory for storing music files directly on the headphones. This eliminates the need to carry a separate device for music playback. This feature is particularly convenient for runners or swimmers who prefer not to bring their phones along.

Industry observers note that while our testers experienced no immediate issues with water or sweat damage, prolonged exposure to moisture and salt can harm earbuds not designed to repel these elements. That’s why we found it imperative that we checked out each device’s “IP,” or ”Ingress Protection” rating. This rating consists of two digits:.

Noise Cancellation vs Ambient Awareness.

It has been revealed that picking between noise cancellation and ambient awareness for your running headphones is like choosing your own adventure. If you're dodging chatty pedestrians in the urban jungle, ambient awareness—whether that be found in typical earbuds or open-ear style headphones—might be your best bet, keeping you alert to honks and “behind you” shouts. But if you’re hitting the serene trails, craving that deep focus, or you have really noisy coworkers or hate the sound of grunting gym bros, let noise cancellation be your peaceful respite, blocking out everything but the sound of your own steady rhythm and, perhaps, a suspenseful podcast.

Battery life is essential for running headphones, especially for long distances. Will these headphones endure the entirety of your week’s run plan without dying? I’m terrible at remembering to charge my stuff, so this is crucial for folks like me.

Recent findings suggest that connectivity is also crucial. Most running headphones use Bluetooth, and the range can vary. Ideally, you want a stable connection that won't drop out when your phone is a few steps away. Typical Bluetooth range is around 30 feet, but interference can reduce this. Some newer headphones offer improved Bluetooth versions for greater range and stability.

In a recent development, headphones, like other gadgets, have firmware that controls their functions and features. Manufacturers often release updates to improve performance, add newly introduced features, or fix complications with firmware, which can have bugs or limitations like any software. These updates are crucial for maintaining optimal functionality and ensuring compatibility with the latest devices and technologies.

Many of today's best headphones and earbuds have companion apps that allow customers to manage and upgrade the firmware. Additionally, these updates may introduce latest features (e.g., enhanced noise cancellation, improved call quality, and more customization options), all of which are managed through the partner app. Keeping the firmware up to date via the app ensures that the headphones perform optimally and offer the latest features.

When it comes to running headphones, durability is honestly everything, because, who wants to buy a upcoming pair every few months? Trust us, our team put these headphones through the wringer, testing them for weeks, sometimes even months and years (yep, we’re that dedicated) to find the ones that can actually keep up with your miles. We sweated on them, dropped them, stuffed them in gym bags, and even braved a few surprise rain showers—just to make sure they’re as tough as your training routine. So, when we say these are the best running headphones for durability, you know we mean it.

It has been revealed that to pinpoint the best running headphones, our team put each pair through thorough, real-world testing for weeks—and sometimes even months. (And not for anything, I’ve had a pair of the original Beats Pro for five years, and they’re still rocking.) We had all kinds of runners try them out, from marathoners to casual joggers, to make sure our results would work for everyone. This way, we got feedback on comfort, fit, and performance for every running style and distance.

In a recent development, our tests weren’t just in one spot; we put these headphones through all sorts of situations to see how tough and functional they really are. This meant running in different weather, from sunshine to sudden downpours, and at various elevations to check their performance under varying physical stresses. We also tested them in places with different noise levels—from quiet trails where you don’t need to hear much around you, to busy city streets where safety and clear sound are super key.

In a recent development, through this rigorous evaluation, we were able to pinpoint headphones that could withstand sweat, accidental drops, and general wear and tear associated with regular running. We paid close attention to factors like secure fit, battery life, sound quality, and the effectiveness of features like noise cancellation and ambient awareness in real-world scenarios.

How do you listen to music and run phone-free?

As a loyal Garmin user, I recommend using models like the Forerunner 170 Music edition. The latter has more features if you’re a multi-sport, stats-junkie, but the price is significantly higher. The watches allow you to sync with music providers, such as Spotify. Most earbuds, with the exception of Apple Airpods, are Garmin compatible.

How do you pair wireless earbuds to your Garmin?

Test Editor Morgan Petruny offers a helpful guide on pairing your earbuds to devices. Here are her instructions on pairing them to you Garmin:.

According to recent reports, for a deep clean, fill a glass with a drop of dish soap in half a cup of warm water. Remove the foam or silicone tips from the earbuds, and let them soak in the soap mixture for 30 minutes. Use a cotton swab or Q-Tip to remove excess particles. Allow the tips to air dry before screwing them back on. Use a clean old toothbrush to gently scrub the actual earbuds, mesh cover pointed down.

Cat Bowen, senior editor of commerce; reviews, is a seasoned runner with more than 20 years of distance running experience, including dozens of marathons, half marathons, and even a few ultra marathons. For over a decade, she has tested parenting, fitness, home, and running gear and written in-depth guides to help readers with their next purchase. Holding multiple advanced degrees and right now studying kinesiology, Cat Bowen brings research-backed insight to all of her guides. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As cyclists, the end of November usually means two things: A shift to riding the indoor trainer and scoring Black Friday deals on cycling gear. This year, Zwift combines them for significant savings on the Zwift Ride and the Wahoo Kickr Core 2. These are Bicycling’s two best-tested trainers, available for up to 23% off!

Recent findings suggest that the Ride is an indoor training bike designed for seamless integration with Zwift’s popular virtual cycling platform—it’s a bicycle and trainer in one, you don’t even need to attach your outdoor bike. If you want to use your own bicycle to ride in Watopia or train inside this winter, Zwift also has an great deal on our top-rated smart trainer, the Wahoo Kickr Core 2.

Recent findings suggest that training bikes are promptly gaining popularity among indoor riders. These purpose-built units integrate a bike and trainer for quick set up, easy use, and improved durability. With a training bike, you no longer have to fumble to get your bike on the trainer on a rainy day, swap bikes when a family member wants to ride Zwift, or prematurely wear out components on your pricey road, gravel, or mountain bike.

Until Zwift introduced its Ride bike, price has been the massive downside to training bikes. Popular models are $2,500 to $4,000; the Ride $1,300 everyday price cut that cost in half—Zwift’s Black Friday deal trims drops the price to only $999. That’s a complete, Zwift-ready indoor bike for less than the price of some direct drive trainers.

How does Zwift do it? Instead of over-thinking things, Zwift combines the excellent Wahoo Kickr Core 2 smart trainer with a stripped down bicycle frame. But instead of building up this frame with pricey components that wear out quickly, it uses a robust singlespeed drivetrain and shift levers with built-in controls for use on the Zwift platform.

The Ride also features easily adjustable seat height, handlebar height, and bar reach. If you want to use your own saddle or a different bar, the Ride uses standard sizing for easy swaps. Zwift also recently updated Ride with crank length options and more fore-aft saddle adjustment. This means almost anyone can fit on the bike, and it makes it easy to share the Ride with multiple riders in your home.

Seeing the price, it’s easy to assume the Zwift Ride’s low price means a lower-quality experience. However, in head-to-head testing against much more expensive training bikes, the Ride walked away as our editors’ clear pick for most indoor cyclists.

Wahoo’s best-priced indoor trainer is actually the brand’s best overall. The Kickr Core 2 packs all of the accuracy, simplicity, and power of the range-topping Kickr smart trainer into a better-priced package. As Test Editor Dan Chabanov stated in his full length review, “The Core 2 delivers nearly all of the real-world experience of Wahoo’s flagship trainer at a price that’s roughly 50 percent lower.” And that’s saying a lot: Chabanov is a former elite cyclocross and road racer, and still competes at a high-level in Zwift’s racing leagues.

It has been revealed that the Kickr Core 2 is a great deal at its everyday price of $550, and at $400 it’s a steal! The Core 2 features a smooth 11.9-pound flywheel with up to 1,800 watts max resistance, 16-percent gradient simulation, and quick connections via BlueTooth and ANT+ protocols. For updates and smooth data connection, Wahoo added WiFi connectivity to the Core trainer. It also features Zwift Race Mode for better connection and data transfer when racing online.

It has been revealed that the 30 pound Kickr Core 2 fits bikes with 130mm and 135mm quick release dropouts or thru axle-equipped bikes with 142mm or 148mm dropout spacing. The Core 2 has more stable legs than the original model; they work well for all but elite-level sprint efforts. Compared to the top-tier Kickr, the Core 2’s only downsides are its lack of a carrying handle and that it doesn’t fold as small for storage.

According to recent reports, this version of the Kickr Core 2 also includes Zwift’s Cog and Click system. The singlespeed Cog replaces a traditional cassette and works with 8- to 13-speed drivetrains. This means you can use most bikes onto the Core 2 without worrying about cassette compatibility—it‘s great for riders who train indoors on multiples bikes (for example, a gravel bike one day and a road bike another ride) or for households with more than one user.

According to recent reports, the Click is two small video game-style controllers you mount to your bar to virtually shift your bike in Zwift. The buttons also can award kudos, use power-ups, and scroll menus inside Zwift’s Watopia universe.

As Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and Upcoming England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

Latest Update: The World’s Hardest Beer Run? This Brutal Race Sends Runners Up a Mountain—With a Keg of Beer on Their Back

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that running up a rocky and technical trail more than a mile above sea level is tricky enough.
  • Male entrants in the race shoulder a traditional wooden carrying frame, which resembles a sled but is loaded high with a 30-liter (about 8 gallons) keg of beer, plus other supplies (including large bottles of water) that add up to more than 130 pounds (60 kg).
  • Since 1985, this unique annual race has been taking place on the unforgiving flanks of the High Tatras mountains in Slovakia.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that running up a rocky and technical trail more than a mile above sea level is tricky enough. Imagine doing it with a keg of beer strapped to your back—because this is exactly what competitors in the Sherpa Rallye, held on October 24, had to contend with.

Male entrants in the race shoulder a traditional wooden carrying frame, which resembles a sled but is loaded high with a 30-liter (about 8 gallons) keg of beer, plus other supplies (including large bottles of water) that add up to more than 130 pounds (60 kg). Women commonly carry cases of beer and materials that make their load weigh about 44 pounds (20 kg).

Since 1985, this unique annual race has been taking place on the unforgiving flanks of the High Tatras mountains in Slovakia. It starts just above the town of Starý Smokovec and finishes at Zbojnícka chata, a mountain refuge perched like an alpine eyrie 3.5 miles up the steep and rough track.

The High Tatras are home to Europe’s last remaining group of old-school mountain porters, many of whom take part in the race, which was started by a porter named Viktor Beránek to help bring workers together. They are locally and colloquially known as horský šerpa (mountain sherpas)—although they have no connection to the Sherpas of the Tibetan Himalaya, a distinct ethnic group, and are more correctly called horský nosi (mountain carriers).

According to recent reports, however you refer to them, each season they manually transport heavy supplies to the mountain huts, refuges, and chalets that hikers use for shelter while trekking the local trails. And herein lies the rub, because once the Sherpa Rallye runners reach Zbojnícka chata, they don’t even get to celebrate by supping the goods they have just transported up to the hut—it goes in the stores for use over winter.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, we earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Sources indicate that after months of long runs and tough workouts, you’ve finally crossed the finish line of your goal race. Now, it’s time to recover—and figure out what’s next.

It has been revealed that while you can scale back your running in the offseason, it’s worth making room for strength training. Even a short time in the weight room can help you build a stronger foundation for your next training block.

Recent findings suggest that the good news? You don’t need to spend all your newfound free time in the gym to make progress. By hitting the following minimum amount of strength work each week, you set yourself up to handle more mileage and run more efficiently when it’s time to chase a new goal.

According to recent reports, in the first two weeks after your race, you should focus mainly on rest and getting back into easy jogging. After that, aim to add at least two strength sessions per week to your routine, exercise physiologist Heather Milton, C.S.C.S., previously told Runner’s World. Milton indicates these offseason strength sessions should focus on heavier weights (just make sure you work up in weight!) and a low-to-moderate number of reps.

During these heavy lifting workouts, athletes should aim to complete four to six sets of one to five reps of each exercise, pausing for two to four minutes in between each set, strength coach and physical therapist Lisbeth Hoyt, D.P.T., C.S.C.S., previously told Runner’s World.

While running is your main focus during marathon training (or any race distance, for that matter), strength sessions often help you maintain the strength you already have, Milton explains. But between training blocks, you can put more emphasis on building strength.

“Plus, when you start training for your next marathon, you’ll be in a stronger position to increase your running volume again because you’ve strengthened all of the areas of your body that were impacted by your previous race, which can help prevent injuries,” Milton adds.

You might associate heavy lifting with short sprinters or football players—athletes who focus on quick, explosive movement, rather than steady endurance. But building stronger muscles through heavy lifting supports long-distance running, too.

For starters, lifting heavier weights helps you build muscular strength, which translates to improved running economy, New York City-based strength and run coach Yusuf Jeffers previously told Runner’s World. Meaning, heavy lifting can help you use less energy to run at a given pace.

Research backs this up. A review published in Sports Medicine in 2023 examined several types of strength training in middle- and long-distance runners, including lifting heavy, submaximal lifting, isometric exercises, and plyometrics. The researchers found that lifting high loads—at least 80 percent of a person’s one-rep max—had the greatest effect on improving running economy at faster speeds. (Plyometrics worked particularly well for improving economy at slower speeds.).

It has been revealed that the benefits extend beyond your muscles, too. Hoyt explains that strength training can support connective tissues and bone health.

In a recent development, it’s important to remember lifting “heavy” looks different for everyone. If you’re newly introduced to strength training or you’re unfamiliar with a particular movement, start by learning proper form and gradually work up in weight, Hoyt notes.

Hoyt suggests focusing on movements such as squats, deadlifts, lunges, and rows, encouraging athletes to move slowly and with control.

According to recent reports, matt Rudisill is an Associate Service Editor who has been with Runner's World since 2025. A Nittany Lion through-and-through, Matt graduated from Penn State in 2022 with a degree in journalism and worked in communications for the university's athletic department for three years as the main contact and photographer for its nationally-ranked cross country and track & field teams. Matt was also heavily involved in communications efforts for Penn State football, men's basketball, and women's gymnastics. In his role with Runner's World, Matt has interviewed Olympians, world champions, and countless experts in the field to create service content that helps runners of all ages and experience levels train smarter and race faster. When he’s not out jogging, Matt can be found tweeting bad takes about the Phillies or watching movies.

#149675. Industry News: Best GPS Bike Computers of 2026: 10 Editor-Tested Picks for Navigation, Training Data, and Battery Life

Industry News: Best GPS Bike Computers of 2026: 10 Editor-Tested Picks for Navigation, Training Data, and Battery Life

📅 25 Jun 2024 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2945 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Sources indicate that bike computers are one of the best equipment upgrades you can make for your road, gravel, and mountain bike rides.
  • In a recent development, I use a cycling computer on virtually every ride.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Sources indicate that bike computers are one of the best equipment upgrades you can make for your road, gravel, and mountain bike rides. Head units display common metrics like speed, distance, and power, and track and record your data, so you can download it and crunch the info after your rides. They’re also great for ride navigation and following pre-planned routes. Today’s leading head units put features from turn-by-turn GPS navigation to real-time performance analytics at your fingertips.

In a recent development, I use a cycling computer on virtually every ride. I do this to test more devices and log the many miles I pedal on different bikes and equipment. An upside of always riding with a GPS-equipped computer is mid-ride exploration and changing rides on the fly. Now, if I’m curious about a road or potential shortcut, I can check whether it goes where I think. And rerouting features on many computers let me cut rides short and head home if weather changes.

According to recent reports, many new bike computers integrate with popular platforms such as Strava, Trailforks, and Garmin Connect. Our favorite models offer real-time hill profiles on climbs and feature data-rich maps for precise navigation, even when descending switchback roads at speed. Some models even feature solar charging and real-time weather alerts. But beyond the fancy features, every bike computer does the same basic job—record your ride and display the data you need.

Since our editors and test team use cycling computers on nearly every ride, we’re constantly riding the newest models. Brands offer dozens of cycling-specific computers, and many have similar shapes, screens, and button layouts. However, as our testing has proven, the differences are in the details. And picking the right cycling computer for your needs makes rides much more enjoyable.

Buying Advice: Modern cycling computers operate a lot like cell phones (the Hammerhead is actually an Android-based platform). So, think of their operating systems like using a mobile device. What works for someone else might not be right for you, but that doesn’t make it a bad computer. Try computers before buying (if possible), because you cannot change the interface without getting a fresh device.

The Wahoo Elemnt Bolt V3 combines excellent features at a great price, making it a strong option for a wide range of cyclists. In his review of the Bolt V3, Test Editor Dan Chabanov dug into the revamped computer’s details. Its features include a 2.3-inch high-resolution display with 16 million colors for increased clarity and improved battery life (up to 20 hours). The Bolt’s interface still prioritizes information in an easy-to-read format and uses buttons rather than a touch screen.

Recent findings suggest that the Bolt displays grade and climb profiles that show difficulty by assigning different background colors depending on the hill’s gradient (red being the steepest). This makes it easy to see at a glance what the climb ahead of you will be like.

It has been revealed that wahoo computers feature an easy setup process and an intuitive companion app that connects to third-party tools. The Bolt V3 has 32 GB of onboard storage, which is enough to store maps for the United States and thousands of routes. The Elemnt Bolt V3 gives you everything you need (and nothing you don’t).

Garmin introduced the all-new Edge 850 late last year. It features a slightly larger and brighter screen, an integrated bell, voice prompts, and more. However, it also adds $150 to the price. For this reason, we’re still massive fans of Garmin’s Edge 840.

Industry observers note that while the Edge 840 features less functionality than the newer Edge 850, it costs significantly less and has a longer battery life. The 840 provides riders with all the data they need to manage a training program and track progress. These include VO2 max output (when paired with a heart monitor), recovery time, training load, and heat and altitude acclimation. It also offers cycling dynamics like position, right/left balance (when paired with a power meter), and bike setup. The Edge 840 provides plenty of detailed info if you like charts and analyzing data.

Industry observers note that overall, the 840 is an excellent option for riders who love training and digging into data. It offers a reasonable balance of price and features in the generally pricey Garmin bike computer lineup. If you need more battery life, choose the 840 Solar, which extends usage up to an impressive 32 hours.

If you want the maximum possible battery life for a cycling computer, Coros’ recently rolled out Dura 2 is your standout choice. Although the newly introduced Dura costs double the original, the Dura 2 features a sleeker design, improved maps and navigation, and clean pairing with devices such as power meters, heart rate monitors, and electronic drivetrains.

Like the original Dura, the second-gen model gets exceptional battery life, and that’s without considering its solar charging capabilities. Coros claims the Dura 2 achieves up to 120 hours of use on a single charge. In Dan Chabanov’s testing, he still had 77 percent battery remaining after 30 hours of ride time—that’s frankly exceptional for a cycling computer.

However, with its great battery life and solar charging come a couple of downsides. Notably, the price: the Dura 2 costs $499 compared to the original model’s $250 price tag. The other notable miss is the Dura 2’s rerouting. It requires a connection to Coros’ smartphone app, and we found it hit-or-miss in our testing.

If you don’t have the budget for a Wahoo, Garmin, or Hammerhead computer, you still have a few solid options. For only $100, Magene offers a full-color touchscreen, turn-by-turn navigation, and even has a hill gradient feature and Strava segment integration (with a firmware upgrade). That puts the mighty little C506 in the league of its big-name competitors at a fraction of the price.

Recent findings suggest that the low price, however, means the C506 isn’t quite as polished as the pricey head units. For example, you must pair your smartphone to upload routes. Some users also report touchscreen lag and software bugs. However, to its credit, Magene’s firmware upgrades have added a lot of functionality and improved shortcomings. If you have a limited budget and don’t mind a few usage quirks, the C506’s price and low weight make it hard to pass up.

Sources indicate that since launching two and a half years ago, Hammerhead’s Karoo computer has consistently remained my go-to head unit for road and gravel rides. Why? Because it’s the right size, has excellent navigation, pairs well with SRAM components, and features my favorite user interface.

It has been revealed that the Karoo’s navigation and touchscreen are best-in-class. On-the-fly route planning is easy—I love its ability to navigate to any Google Maps destination (shared via the Hammerhead app) and use the feature often. The Karoo’s UI is very intuitive, and it’s easy to find functions or customize the screens (compared to the bloated interfaces on some competitors’ cycling computers).

While the Karoo doesn’t look much different from its predecessor, the Karoo 2 (yes, it’s called the Karoo even though it’s the third-gen), it offers many solid updates: A dedicated power button, improved battery life (up to 35 hours), an ambient light sensor, and automatic backlight control.

Hammerhead’s smartphone app offers automatic ride uploads and live tracking—you can send a link to family or friends to track your ride progress. Another Hammerhead strong suit is its bi-weekly software updates that remedy bugs and add useful features. Combined with the ability to sideload third-party apps, the Karoo’s function constantly improves.

For AXS-equipped bike owners, the Karoo integrates tightly with SRAM’s electronic components. For example, you can program AXS shift buttons (including the bonus buttons on Force and Red hoods) directly from the computer. Read more about this integration in Senior Test Editor Matt Phillips’ story “SRAM Debuts its Upcoming Red AXS Road Group.”.

If you only need a cycling computer for the basics (speed, distance, heart rate, power, etc.) and don’t want a cellphone-sized device hanging off your bar, the Cycplus M2 is a great option. This tiny computer covers all the bases at a fraction of the cost of significant-name competitors. It also has great styling that won’t look out of place on lightweight bikes, and it's small enough to use on the trail.

According to recent reports, while the M2 lacks amenities such as a touchscreen display or mapping, it features a 70-hour battery life, GPS tracking, and ANT+ and Bluetooth connectivity to your power meter and HRM. Cycplus’s app will also sync your rides to Strava to track your progress.

According to recent reports, overhauled in 2025, Wahoo’s Elemnt Roam is consistently one of our favorite cycling computers. Updates to the Roam V3 over the V2 include a larger touchscreen display, dual-band GPS for enhanced connection in mountains and dense woods, 64GB internal storage, and improved battery life.

In a recent development, in addition to the V3’s larger size and weight, Wahoo added a speaker for voice navigation and an integrated bell (activated with a quick two-finger tap on the screen). However, Wahoo removed the V2’s fan-favorite LED status lights. Additionally, we found the screen brightness a bit dim in our testing compared to Garmin and Hammerhead displays.

As Chabanov noted in his detailed review of the Roam, beyond its overall solid reliability, the Roam is a standard mid-tier bike computer. It features a slew of handy navigation features, including turn-by-turn directions, navigate to start, back on track, mountain bike trail integration, saved locations, retrace route, and take me to.

Sources indicate that after using the Edge 1050 for almost six months, the best word to describe Garmin’s range-topping computer is “big”. This computer is big in size, features, and price. But all of this bigness provides an experience unlike anything found on other cycling computers—and if not for the 1050’s price, it would be vying for the Best Overall Computer title.

There is no getting around the Edge 1050’s size, and at 2.4” x 4.7” x 0.6”, it takes up a lot of real estate on your bar. In fact, the 105 is so long that it’s incompatible with many standard mounts. However, the enormous size makes it easy to read data, follow routes, and scroll screens.

Recent findings suggest that navigation features include turn-by-turn directions, maps showing the popular routes locals use, and recalculation when you stray from your course. And while they might not like the 1050’s dimensions, mountain bikers will love its integration with the Trailforks app. However, this is merely scratching the surface of the Edge 1050’s superpowers; if you want to see the data, the 1050 is probably logging it, and Garmin most likely has a screen for it buried in the long list of data fields.

The Edge 1050 also offers some thoughtful safety features, including the ability to automatically send an emergency message to your specified contacts when it detects a crash, group messaging, and a ‘follow my ride’ feature that shares your real-time position with friends and family.

Recent findings suggest that if you like these features but want a smaller package (and slightly lower price), check out the Garmin Edge 850. You can dig into the details on the 850 in Dan Chabanov’s full-length review.

Sources indicate that like Garmin’s Edge 1050, Wahoo goes similarly huge with its Elemnt Ace. The screen’s 3.8-inch size is impressive, as is its battery life (up to 30 hours). Plus, the Ace features Wahoo’s signature user-friendliness. Matt Phillips summed up his full review of the Elemnt Ace, saying, “If you crave big and bold, this is your cycling computer.”.

Industry observers note that the Ace’s super-sized screen offers room for large and easy-to-read data fields. The touchscreen function is also excellent, even while wearing gloves. Wahoo’s signature page zoom function—use the up and down buttons to zoom in on fewer fields or out on more fields—rapidly makes prioritized fields even larger. This helps if you want to concentrate on one metric or have vision challenges. It also provides a very significant map (or a large map plus additional data fields) and spoken turn-by-turn directions.

It has been revealed that compared to most cycling computers, the Ace is overkill in almost every way. However, if you want one computer with a big screen and impressive battery life, then the Ace is your ticket.

Do you wax nostalgic for the days of simple cycling computers—but still want to upload your rides and training data to Strava? Then the Omata is the computer for you. Years ago, our computers only displayed the basic riding metrics like speed, ride time, distance, and elevation. Your rides weren’t interrupted by constant pinging from notifications, messages, navigation, and target training zones.

Silca’s Omata computer is to your rides like a vinyl turntable is to listening to music. Sure, you can stream your favorite band on Spotify, see the songs’ lyrics in real time, and skip tracks you don’t like, but digital audio lacks the tactile experience of a record player. That’s what riding with the Omata is like; it features dials to display your current speed, distance traveled, elevation gain, and riding time—nothing more, nothing less.

Yet, behind the scenes, the Omata also captures critical riding data, like power, heart rate, and GPS route. This means you can still track your rides and get Strava kudos from your friends. However, the Omata comes at a steep price—$800—but it‘s an experience you will not find in any other device.

It has been revealed that one of the biggest differences between GPS cycling computers is the technology ecosystem you’re buying into—much like choosing a smartphone. While you can pair most sensors, regardless of brand, with most computers via Bluetooth or ANT+, these devices work best when used with their corresponding companion apps. Although some budget-friendly computer options require an app to unlock full functionality, premium models from brands like Hammerhead, Wahoo, and Garmin let you perform most tasks without an app.

Recent findings suggest that while bigger isn’t always better, a large, easy-to-read display—like the one on the Wahoo Elemnt Ace—makes navigation and data viewing significantly more convenient. When testing the gargantuan Elemnt Ace, Matt Phillips initially found the screen’s sheer size off-putting, but he eventually grew to appreciate it.

Navigation capabilities vary widely. Even budget models, such as the $120 iGPSport BCS300T, support turn-by-turn directions with downloadable routes. High-end models such as the Hammerhead Karoo and Garmin Edge models take it further, allowing on-the-fly route changes—such as finding a coffee shop—without adjusting settings in the companion app.

Industry observers note that battery life used to be a major concern, but modern bike computers are built to last. Most can handle a full week of riding without recharging.
