A good pair of mountain bike shorts should stay out of your way through long climbs, rough descents, and everything in between. The right fit leaves room to pedal and wear knee pads without bunching or snagging, while a secure waistband and well-placed pockets keep the shorts comfortable on the trail. We’ve tested options for different budgets and riding styles, from lightweight shells to shorts with a padded liner. These are the pairs we’d choose for our next ride.

The Pearl Izumi Summit Shorts scored well across the board, with a comfortable fit, effective water repellency, and well-placed pockets. At 191 grams, they’re relatively light and breathe well (though the Velocio Ultralight MTB Shorts below are yet lighter and more breathable). The Summits still move enough air for all-day trail rides without noticeable moisture buildup.

According to recent reports, their four-way-stretch ripstop nylon has held up through multiple seasons of testing and riding, resisting tears without feeling rough or abrasive. For nylon, it’s surprisingly soft.

It has been revealed that A lined mountain bike short at this price is rare. The Ally has a forgiving fit and plenty of waist adjustment (Velcro sizing tabs and belt loops), which makes it easier to wear than many shorts. On the bike they feel relaxed and comfortable (but not floppy), and move with you well. The included liner means you don’t need to buy a chamois separately. Plenty of pockets let you stash a phone and ride essentials, though all those zippers can feel like a lot—and like potential failure points over time. The unisex sizing means there’s no separate women’s version.

With a 13-inch inseam in the men’s version, the Landfarer covers the tops of most knee pads without feeling heavy. Patagonia also uses recycled nylon in the fabric and makes the shorts in a Fair Trade Certified™ factory, so the vibes are good. The range of waist sizes can help you find a tailored fit, but the elastic waistband has no adjusters. The low-friction fabric and forgiving waist can let the shorts slip more easily, so make sure you get the right size.

I tested the latest version, which features a newly introduced elastic waist that greatly improved the fit and made it more forgiving of weight fluctuations. The Flexair keeps things low-key and streamlined. Its low-profile cut and ratchet closure make for a clean look and a secure fit on the bike. Stretch fabric and laser-cut perforations help keep the shorts light and ventilated, but there’s no liner. The waists run small, so try them on if you can and be prepared to size up.

The 10-inch inseam will suit most riders, though it may not pair perfectly with all knee pads.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • It has been revealed that bicycle helmets have saved my life more times than I can count.
  • While some lids from decades past were bulky and sometimes looked silly, modern road, mountain, and commuter helmets combine safety, performance, and style.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

It has been revealed that bicycle helmets have saved my life more times than I can count. I’ve ridden and raced bikes for most of my life, so unfortunately I’ve hit the deck many times on trails and on roads. That’s why I wear a helmet anytime I kit up, clip in, and head out for a ride.

While some lids from decades past were bulky and sometimes looked silly, modern road, mountain, and commuter helmets combine safety, performance, and style. While a helmet’s primary role is to protect your head and brain in a crash, the best bike helmets also look great, and some even improve your speed.

Helmet technology has improved considerably in the last decade. Plus, safety features once limited to high-end helmets have trickled down to affordable models. Rider safety has also improved: independent testing by Virginia Tech has prompted more manufacturers to incorporate anti-rotational features across all helmet styles, categories, and price levels. Additionally, high-tech materials, improved ventilation, better straps, and more aerodynamic shapes make today’s lids lighter, cooler, and faster than those from only a few years ago.

Picking the perfect helmet can be challenging. Brands offer scores of models in every possible riding category. Whether you ride on asphalt, gravel roads, or dirt trails, you can find a helmet that matches your style, fit, and budget needs.

Expert Advice: Buy the helmet that feels the most comfortable on your head. You are more likely to use a helmet that fits and feels great, and that’s the first step in keeping your noggin safe if you crash.

Elite road and gravel helmets offer low weight, excellent ventilation, and great looks. However, those benefits usually come at a high cost. Giro’s Agilis Mips helmet is a great option if you want a pro-level look and performance without the associated price.

Sources indicate that weighing 299 grams (size medium), my Agilis is only 15 grams heavier than Giro’s premium Aries Spherical model—and the Agilis costs $230 less. The Agilis is very well-ventilated, comparable to the priciest lids on all but the hottest of rides.

Giro offers eight color options for the Agilis, so you’re sure to find one that matches your riding kits, bike, and personal style. This helmet features Mips technology to protect your brain from rotational forces in a crash, and Giro’s Hardbody co-molded shell to better protect it from small bumps and dings when not on your head. Plus, the Agilis is equipped with Roc-Loc dial system to ensure a proper fit.

According to recent reports, with a five-star rating and 8.14 STAR score, the P2R A20 Mips places third in Virginia Tech’s road helmet rankings (and eleventh overall). That ranking is great for any road or gravel helmet—but for a helmet that costs only $60, it’s downright amazing.

P2R somehow hits the A20’s low price without cutting many corners on features. It has nice straps with adjustable quick clamps that offer plenty of adjustment. P2R also includes a USB-rechargeable light that magnetically clips into the rear vent for commuting or extra visibility on the road. The one downside we found with the A20 Mips is that it feels optimized for rounder head shapes. While it fits me well, a couple of others who tried it stated the A20 fits a little snug near their temples.

TOP 5 RANKED VA TECH ROAD HELMETS.

Although it costs less than $80, I reach for the Lazer Tonic KinetiCore as often as helmets triple its price. The Tonic looks good and fits great, and at only 247 grams, it’s lighter than many more expensive lids I own. Plus, it features 18 vents for good airflow on hot days. Another thing I like about the Tonic KinetiCore is the options: Lazer offers it in nine colors and four sizes. This means you’re almost guaranteed to find one that fits your head and personal style.

Overall, the Tonic KinetiCore looks, feels, and rides like much pricier helmets. It combines low weight, ventilation, and protection into an affordable package. The Tonic uses Lazer’s proprietary KinetiCore system; it reduces weight and integrates rotational impact protection. This is a solid lid for your daily road and gravel rides or even commutes.

Sources indicate that for the Aries Spherical, Giro improved ventilation and aerodynamics over its previous range-topping Aether model. It is an excellent, pro-level road lid for road riders seeking superior performance and fit. It’s lightweight, super-adjustable, and is offered in tons of colors—including Visma-Lease a Bike and Canyon-SRAM special editions.

Industry observers note that the Aries also has excellent safety features—I know how well the Aries Spherical works because I personally crash-tested it late last year. Giro incorporates its Spherical nested-shell (ball-in-socket) design for rotational-force protection in a crash and improved energy dissipation. The Aries also uses Giro’s Aura reinforcement bridges to keep the foam in place during impact. These features earned the Aries an excellent five-star rating from Virginia Tech. It ranks in the top fifteen overall and fifth in road helmets.

The Smith Network Mips employs many features from the manufacturer’s pricier models, along with some truly novel ones. It retains the honeycomb-like Koroyd panels that absorb energy upon impact. The Network also features an optional fabric visor for the convenience of a cycling cap without the added bulk.

Since Smith (a sunglass manufacturer) makes this helmet, it has great eyewear integration. Color options are another upside to the Network; there is one to match virtually any rider’s style.

Industry observers note that P2R’s A70 Pro is probably the best deal for a performance road helmet. At only $100, the A70 punches well above its price. It packs the fit, finish, and adjustability we expect from much pricier lids. Plus, this P2R helmet features a Mips liner and earned a four-star rating from Virginia Tech’s helmet lab.

Industry observers note that for the price, it’s an excellent helmet, but it has a few downsides. While it wasn’t noticeable while riding, the A70 Pro is a bit heavier than competitors’ pricier aero helmets. Fit-wise, the A70 fit our test riders’ medium-sized heads, but medium is the smallest size available. Lastly, we lost two pairs of glasses from the helmet’s sunglass port, so maybe don’t use that feature.

In a recent development, aero helmets are a good way to save watts and boost your speed. That’s why you see so many pro racers choosing these sleek lids, even on the warmest days of Grand Tour events. Giro’s new Eclipse Pro is one of the best choices available, and one of the year’s hottest pieces of cycling equipment.

Weighing 280 grams (claimed), the Eclipse Pro is light for an aero helmet, and competes with some brands’ lightweight models. And thanks to improved aerodynamics, Giro claims the Pro is 17% faster than its predecessor, the Eclipse Spherical. Giro also packs the Eclipse Pro with safety features, including its Spherical (anti-rotational), Aura II (reinforcement), and Progressive Layering (dual-density EPS foam) technologies.

According to recent reports, riding POC’s Cytal Mips in 100-degree heat on Stage 5 of the 2026 Tour de France, I learned first-hand how well this helmet ventilates your head. Senior Photographer Trevor Raab backed up my findings in his test riding. He noted, “On fast-paced hot rides, it offered a noticeable increase in cooling as well as remaining comfortable while slowly slogging up climbs.”.

Industry observers note that like other POC helmets, the Cytal combines Scandinavian style and excellent safety into one package. Although the Cytal’s fit runs large, it’s easy to dial in with its adjustable retention system and different padding options. Raab has an approximately 58cm head and falls between sizes (medium and large). Similarly, I consistently wear a size medium from other brands and found the medium was a little large on my head. If you can size down, it may offer a more streamlined and aero fit.

According to recent reports, expert Advice: Most riders know they should replace a helmet after they crash. But did you know that your helmet can expire? Helmets don’t have an actual best-by date, but the general rule of thumb is to replace your lid every three to five years. So, if you’re wondering, “When did I get this helmet?”, it might be time to replace it.

TLD’s full-face helmets have been the go-to choice of top downhill, freeride, and enduro riders for decades. Since launching the A1 trail helmet more than ten years ago, Troy Lee Designs has led the mountain bike market in comfort, fit, and style. The A3 Mips, the brand’s top-tier trail helmet, takes what makes TLD lids legendary to a upcoming level.

Senior Test Editor Matt Phillips has ridden the A3 for countless hours on the trails of Durango, Colorado, and gives it a ringing endorsement. He indicates, “The TLD A3, since its launch a couple of years ago, has risen to the top of my favorite MTB helmets list. The style and color options are a highlight, of course—it’s a TLD. But what makes this helmet a standout is its secure fit and comfort. It locks onto my head and doesn’t wiggle or bounce, yet produces no pressure points. I also appreciate the adjustable visor when the sun is low (or high), reasonably solid eyewear docking, and the super-effective sweat-diverting brow strip, which keeps glasses and goggles dry.”.

Smith recently released the Pilot, and for only $95, it’s a great overall package. The Pilot features Mips protection, a fit dial, and lightweight straps. The helmet also has great compatibility with glasses and goggles (which only seems right considering eyewear brand Smith makes it). Senior Photographer Trevor Raab tested the Pilot and provided some ride notes.

“Helmets can get expensive, and there are lots of premium features driving the price up on MTB lids. The Pilot gives you everything you need and nothing you don’t without breaking the bank,” Raab said. He additionally notes that “the straps with adjusters that wouldn't seem out of place on helmets costing 2x the price.” The only drawback he has found is the Pilot’s fixed visor: “For those who like to fine-tune their peak, it’s a bit of a drag, but I’m not complaining at this price.”.

The Schwinn Intercept is a $30 helmet and is ranked four stars in Virginia Tech’s STAR testing. That’s a higher ranking than several helmets that VA Tech tested, some of which cost hundreds of dollars more. Though it’s inexpensive, the Interceptor still features a dial-adjustable fit system and a removable visor. It’s a one-size-fits-most model with a claimed weight of about 350 grams—surprisingly light for an affordable helmet.

In a recent development, finding a trail-style mountain bike helmet that looks good, has a 5-star rating from Virginia Tech, and is priced less than $100 is a tall order. However, Endura pulled it together with its Hummveee Mips model.

Sources indicate that british-brand Endura is best-known for its excellent riding apparel, but its mountain bike helmets are also worth a look. The Hummvee features a Mips liner to protect against rotational forces in a crash, a removable visor, and in-mold construction to improve durability. While it’s a one-size-fits-most helmet, Endura offers this lid in three color choices: black, red, and white.

In a recent development, if you’re commuting by e-bike, you’ll want to wear a helmet. However, not all commuter lids are rated for e-bike use. Unit 1’s Aura smart helmet not only passes NTA8776 and EN1078 safety standards, but it also earned a five-star rating from Virginia Tech’s helmet lab and ranks third among all commuter helmets.

The Aura also has several built-in features to increase your visibility to drivers. These include 350-lumen head and taillights, turn signals, crash detection, and a Fidlock buckle. It even pairs with Bosch e-bikes.

Industry observers note that this tech comes at a price—in both dollars and grams. At $260, it’s not the cheapest commuter helmet, but it’s arguably the best equipped. The Aura’s 469-gram weight (measured, size medium) is noticeable while riding, and it can feel a little heavy the first few times you wear it.

Inspired by vintage motorcycle helmets, the Thousand Heritage is trendy and comfortable. Recently updated, the Heritage 2.0 retains its faux-leather strap and now features larger vents on the top and in the back to keep you cool. It also has a rear dial so you can adjust the fit for your head shape and hairstyle, and we had no trouble managing the helmet’s magnetic buckle with just one hand. The Heritage’s logo also hides a unique feature: It pops off to reveal a small channel through which you can run a lock to secure the helmet. This is handy if you don’t want to carry your lid around once you reach your destination.

According to recent reports, our team thoroughly vetted each helmet on this list. Collectively, we log tens of thousands of miles each year wearing these helmets (and dozens more), in all kinds of conditions. Our test team rides on pavement and gravel, trail rides and bike park laps, daily commutes, and quick spins around town.

We evaluated each helmet based on performance, value, fit, comfort, ventilation, aerodynamics, adjustability, and looks. We also consider Virginia Tech safety ratings when available. The result is a selection of helmets that deliver the best experience across every budget and riding style.

You probably already know where you like to ride. Perhaps you ride on paved roads, or maybe on gravel and dirt. Other cyclists prefer riding mountain bikes in the woods or on the rail trail with the family.

Helmets are generally grouped by cycling discipline—road, gravel, mountain, commuting, or recreational. But don’t feel boxed in by those labels—You can wear a mountain bike lid for gravel rides, commute in a lightweight road helmet, or don a commuter helmet for weekend rides on the bike path. The best helmet is the one that you will wear—something that fits well, feels good, and meets your budget.

However, it’s still helpful to understand what those category designations actually mean in terms of helmet features, ventilation, and protection:.

Sources indicate that you can spend as little as $30 for a helmet or more than $400 on a high-end race lid. Generally, pricier helmets are lighter and better ventilated. However, all helmets sold in the U.S. must meet the same CPSC safety standards.

Recent findings suggest that for a deep dive into Virginia Tech’s independent helmet testing program, read Matt Phillip’s excellent story, “Virginia Tech’s Upcoming Helmet Ratings Raise the Bar. Here’s How the Tougher System Could Affect Your Next Choice.”.

All helmets sold in the U.S. must meet a Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) standard. However, the standard was adopted in 1998. For example, it does not give specifics for mitigating rotational forces on the brain. It also does not lay down any standards for a full-face helmet’s chin bar.

According to recent reports, voluntary and third-party tests go beyond the CPSC standard. We like Virginia Tech’s STAR tests, which were developed with a more modern understanding of head injuries than the CPSC’s test. VA Tech’s protocols evaluate a helmet’s ability to mitigate linear acceleration and rotational velocity, then assign a ranking of zero to five stars. A helmet receives more stars if Virginia Tech’s testing indicates it does a better job of reducing injury. VA Tech only recommends helmets that receive four or five stars.

Outside of CPSC and VA Tech’s STAR, most reputable helmet makers have their own in-house test protocols. The specifics of those tests and the results are often proprietary and not shared with the public.

Remember, no controlled test can replicate every possible real-world crash, but wearing a helmet is always better than not wearing one. Additionally, manufacturers’ understanding of what makes an effective helmet improves every day, which means helmets are always improving.

Sizes vary by brand, and most companies offer fit guides to help you choose the best size for your head. Measure your head’s circumference to determine the best size. If you fall between sizes, choose the most comfortable helmet.

Industry observers note that the correct size helmet will sit low and straight on your forehead. The retention system should take up some of the slack so the helmet sits securely on your head—you shouldn’t rely on cinching down the chin strap to hold the helmet in place. The right helmet will fit comfortably, and the retention system will easily snug up the fit.

Consider these other factors when choosing and purchasing a upcoming helmet.

Typically, road helmets are the lightest and best ventilated helmets. In some cases, the vents even also enhance cooling (over wearing no helmet at all) by directing airflow through carefully designed shapes and vents and over your head. This also helps prevent your sunglasses from fogging. Other helmets with increased coverage, such as full-face and mountain bike helmets, often have fewer vents.

Sources indicate that however, don’t get tricked into thinking that “more vents are better.” You can’t judge a helmet’s cooling ability only by its number of vents. The Giro Synthe, for example, has only 19 vents but is widely regarded as well-ventilated, while the Kask Valegro has a whopping 37 vents. The size and design of the vents, plus thoughtful internal channels, are more notable than the quantity.

Weight needn’t be your biggest concern because when it comes to a helmet, the one you wear will always win out over the one you don’t. It comes down to comfort—you’re more likely to wear a helmet that won’t get in the way or weigh you down.

Recent findings suggest that lightweight helmets tend to feel more comfortable, especially on long or challenging rides. Both material choices and design aspects contribute to weight savings. High-tech helmets often save grams by incorporating intricate internal bridges and supports that allow airflow and keep the helmet together in a crash. But be prepared to pay a higher price for these innovations. Opting out of “extras” like visors and mounts will also reduce weight.

While we don’t recommend adorning your helmet with too many accessories, extras such as visors, GoPro mounts, and lights certainly have their place and time.

If you find yourself riding in the dark, light mounts can make your life easier and safer by illuminating the path ahead and providing a rear-facing blinker light to help drivers see you in low-light conditions. Bike commuters especially should consider light mounts to make the morning and evening transitions as smooth as possible. Helmet-mounted bike lights work great in conjunction with handlebar-mounted lights because they move with you when you turn your head.

Sources indicate that for those who ride during daylight, visors provide a built-in sun shield, especially for mountain bikers or rec riders. Road riders may use a cycling cap under the helmet and eschew any helmet-related extras.

Most modern helmets come equipped with safety technology such as Mips, KinetiCore, Koroyd, and WaveCel.

These technologies are engineered to help reduce the forces transmitted to your brain from impacts and collisions in different ways. However, no system or technology can guarantee a better outcome in every situation.

Sources indicate that when researching a helmet’s protection, consider rotational and direct-impact forces. Choose a lid that uses a time-tested safety system. Look for positive reviews from actual users, not only quotes from brands. Full-spectrum protection might cost more than the most bare-bones helmet, but it’s worth the price for frequent riders and anyone who ventures off the beaten path onto gnarly singletrack or into heavy traffic.

It has been revealed that mips (Multi-Directional Impact Protection System) is the most widely know helmet technology. It comes in several versions and is used by numerous helmet brands.The most common Mips tech uses a liner inside the helmet that allows your head and helmet to move relative to each other in the event of a crash. Upon impact, the helmet can move without pulling on your head, which claims to reduce brain trauma. Mips Spherical found on some Giro models is variant. The MIPS SL pads in the Specialized Prevail III is another example.

KinetiCore uses blocks and channels in the helmet’s EPS foam designed to create crumple zones that absorb energy under impact impact.Lazer claims KinetiCore improves ventilation, reduces weight, and limits plastic use in its helmets.

In a recent development, koroyd uses miniature tubes thermo-welded to create a honeycomb shape. The material crumples in on itself upon impact. Smith typically applies Koroyd in a zonal manner, built into particular places on the helmet to optimize weight and space savings while protecting the most vulnerable parts of your head. Smith’s latest helmet models employ Koroyd and Mips for a double dose of leading-edge protection.

Sources indicate that used in four Trek helmet models, Wavecel is a 15mm-thick grid of layered polyester intended to crumple, flex, and glide on impact. Trek claims this system reduces forces on the rider’s head.

In addition to standard road, mountain, and commuter helmets, some brands offer full-face and e-bike-rated helmets.

Only the Netherlands has an e-bike-specific helmet standard (adopted there in 2017). NTA 8776 is a standard designed to protect against higher-impact speeds and covers a slightly larger part of the head.

Recent findings suggest that in the U.S., there are currently no helmet requirements specific to e-bike use. However, several manufacturers sell commuter helmets built to the NTA 8776 standard. Two of our favorites are the Specialized Mode and the Smith Dispatch MIPS.

The helmets in this story are “half-shells” and cover the top of the head. Their coverage usually ends around the eyebrows and top of the ears, though some—particularly mountain bike helmets—extend to the back of the rider’s head.

Another style of helmet is the full face. As the name suggests, this style covers most of a rider’s head and has a chin bar to protect the rider’s jaw. A full-face helmet covers the ears and the back of the head, with a large opening in front that allows a rider to wear goggles.

Full-face helmets protect more of the rider’s head—particularly the mouth and jaw—but are heavier and less ventilated than traditional cycling helmets. Full face helmets are primarily used by mountain bikers—especially downhill and enduro racers—but all riders can benefit from the extra protection they provide.

Sources indicate that as Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and Upcoming England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

#149668. Industry News: How To Afford a House These Days

📅 03 Feb 2024 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2438 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Mrmoneymustache ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: How To Afford a House These Days

📅 03 Feb 2024 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2438 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The other day, an MMM reader stopped by and left the following comment on one of my older posts about the principles of FIRE:.
  • “While I still find some of MMM’s advice relevant, it seems like every FI blogger out there worked in tech 20 years ago, pulled down a 6 figure salary and bought a house for a bag of potatoes before 2019.
  • I wasn’t smart enough to find FI when I was young so I sometimes feel like a lot of their advice is not going to help me or others who don’t already own a home and don’t have six- figure salaries in this post-pandemic world.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The other day, an MMM reader stopped by and left the following comment on one of my older posts about the principles of FIRE:.

“While I still find some of MMM’s advice relevant, it seems like every FI blogger out there worked in tech 20 years ago, pulled down a 6 figure salary and bought a house for a bag of potatoes before 2019.

I wasn’t smart enough to find FI when I was young so I sometimes feel like a lot of their advice is not going to help me or others who don’t already own a home and don’t have six- figure salaries in this post-pandemic world.

Sources indicate that A lot of the ideas given to young folks are “house hack” “buy a fixer upper” but that is still out of reach and/or complex to navigate with current prices and interest rates. Most townships around me do not want you to chop a house up into ADU’s or multiple units. My cousin owns 60 acres of land but he is not allowed to live on a trailer on that land.

I don’t know what the next generation of FI bloggers will offer, perhaps they are already out there and I just don’t know who they are, but I’d like to hear from them.”–.

As with every critique of our ideas, I thought about this comment for a while. Tried to determine if there were any Principles of Mustachianism that were genuinely going obsolete, versus the more common side effects of Complainypants and/or Excuse-itis, two afflictions which have been weighing down our critics since the beginning.

Industry observers note that after all, this isn’t the first time FIRE has gone obsolete. Over my retirement I’ve seen it:.

So what’s the situation right now?

Our commenter focuses on two things: the solid salaries of tech workers, and the major increases in house prices (and interest rates) in the most recent four years.

According to recent reports, the first one — high salaries in general – is still a factor and I don’t expect that to change. Some jobs just pay more than others, and there’s a lot you can do to increase your income and switch jobs, and I’m all for it. However, ever-increasing income is not my usual focus here on MMM, because I have seen first hand that most people can waste almost any amount of income and still have very little to show for it.

In fact, the very existence of software engineers and doctors and other high earners who are my age and still feeling financial stress is proof of this: it’s mathematically impossible to earn so much for almost 30 years and not have an absolute shit-ton saved, unless you are also spending an absolute shit-ton of money the whole time.

Sources indicate that so instead, we focus on how to streamline your spending and live joyfully and efficiently without compromise. We focus on reducing waste, while maintaining or even increasing all of the other benefits that come from spending money more purposefully. These skills are essential even for the highest earners, but they become even more valuable as you move down the income ladder.

So now for the second issue: housing. Does the state of housing here in 2024 screw up the whole FIRE blueprint?

As with any question, let’s start by looking at the data: how much have US house prices actually risen – adjusted for inflation – since 2019?

In a recent development, it turns out that our own St. Louis Fed makes this extremely useful  information available here.

So there’s our answer: houses “feel” about 25% more expensive right now than they did at the start of 2019 relative to the average salary and the price of everything else. Although interestingly enough,  they are only up about 10% since the last peak in early 2006, a full eighteen years ago! So housing is a blow, but not a FIRE-extinguishing one.

However, this nationwide data masks some much bigger increases in certain popular cities, including my own: Plain old Longmont Colorado now sports a hilariously high $540,000 median home price. So houses are about triple the price they were when I started writing in 2011, which means they’ve risen much faster than the average salary. Which means houses are much further out of reach for the average person in my area.

House Shopping With Your Middle Finger.

The solution to this is the same as most other problems: to stop thinking in the way our culture likes to train us (as a victim of outside forces beyond our control) and go back to thinking like a Mustachian.

Houses are just like any other manufactured product, and as such they come at a wide variety of prices, subject to supply and demand.

Recent findings suggest that and just because you happen to live in a certain place (even if you were born and raised there), doesn’t mean you’ll automatically be able to afford to buy a house there. Just as a baby born upon the Apple campus in Cupertino today doesn’t automatically get a new iPhone Pro Max every year.

With every purchasing decision, you need to go through the same series of choices:.

According to recent reports, so when it comes to houses, you run the numbers, then decide between renting or buying or house hacking. You might start by doing the analysis right in your own city, but also keep in mind that there are lots of other cities and even countries in the world, and there are happy people living in all of them.

But Wait: I don’t want to move to a whole newly introduced place!

It has been revealed that at this point, people get defensive. We all have ties to our current location, and the stronger the ties the more difficult it becomes to consider moving.

But there’s a difference between genuine, positive bonds to a place and just plain old fear of change. So it’s my job to at least make you question your assumptions, because not doing so is what got you where you are, and it’s also what got our country where it is.

In a recent development, and on a country-wide basis,  I notice that our general fear of relocating creates a very irrational pattern of house prices. They are ridiculously high in some places and ridiculously cheap in others. There does seem to be a general correlation between niceness and cost, but not a perfect one (especially since everyone has their own definition of “nice”).

And that’s where the opportunity lies.

I moved to Longmont in 2005 because it met our young family’s needs at the time, at the right price with homes about $200,000. Today, at the $540,000 price level (houses average about $450 per interior square foot) it has to compete with a much broader range of cities which offer nicer amenities at equal or lower prices.

Let’s do a hypothetical search using another amazing tool: FRED’s list of the top 1000 metro areas with price per square foot, and plot some of them based on my own judgment of their desirability:.

Recent findings suggest that I’m biased towards Colorado because I have so many ties there, and I also highly prioritize sunny climates. My chart suggests that if I wanted to save money, I might start looking around in Albuquerque, whereas Denver would give me a nicer life in the same price range as my current city of Longmont. And if I were willing to spend even more on housing to live somewhere even nicer, I should suck it up and move to Boulder.

Just for fun, I pulled the data from that same FRED website into a separate google spreadsheet (which I’ll share here) and sorted it by cost per square foot. Then, I highlighted a band of affordable cities with housing centered on the $100 per square foot range, which would mean a 2,000 square foot house is about $200k.

As an added bonus, I added a column to calculate the change in house prices over the past year, just in case it helps us see if a city is on the way up or getting cheaper at the moment.

A chart like this is just a starting point – you’d need to read more about any place and then go visit in person before considering a move. But the idea is to start with data, and then do some fun research based on what you learn.

The Earth Awaits: Casting a Worldwide Net.

House prices are a valuable metric, because they influence the cost of living more than almost anything else for the typical Mustachian. After all, biking and nature are always close to free, Costcos are available nationwide, and we probably care less than average about the costs of other services like valets and salons.

According to recent reports, but there’s still plenty of value in looking at the bigger picture, considering more data points, and also being open to renting versus buying your housing. For this, I’m a major fan of a FIRE blogger-created site called The Earth Awaits, and we can take it for a test drive right now with the following search criteria:.

My total monthly budget: $0-$6000.

Apartment type: Two bedroom (outside city center).

Temperature range: January lows not colder than 10F.

The exact parameters don’t matter too much, as long as you don’t make them too narrow. The notable thing is the resulting list, which is meant to give you ideas to research further. For example, that first simple search gave me this list:.

Hey, that’s interesting. I like how the site shows the population right on the main list, because that provides a big clue to the “feel” of a city. I personally like the feel of a 50k-200k person town, so I might look into Fayetteville, Columbia or Athens. I’ve also been to Chattanooga and really like that place – who knew it was only about as expensive as Columbus Ohio?

According to recent reports, in the end, your physical environment – the people, access to nature, urban features and the weather patterns – is probably the most vital factor to get right in creating a happy life. The cost of living there is only one of the factors, and definitely not the most important one.

According to recent reports, but if you choose carefully, you can probably slide yourself in the right direction along that “Nice for the Price” scale in order to get more from your life. Even if it just means making a move within your own city to live along a walking path, a little closer to work or to the people or places you care about most.

The key is just to remember that housing is like almost everything in life: It’s a choice that you get to make, and there are great rewards for putting some solid thought and effort into that choice.

Another Fun Example: Doing the Analysis on Tempe/Phoenix Arizona vs Denver.

This is a fun exercise, because I’m right now living in the Phoenix area (more on that here)  that is way different than the Denver metro area where I normally live. We can start with the rough measure of housing cost per square foot across each region:.

In other words, pretty close. Denver metro* is about 10% higher on average, but the variations from one neighborhood to another within any major city are much larger than that anyway.

So the other factors are more crucial. Both are surrounded by beautiful mountain recreation and get lots of sunshine, but the climates are famously quite different. Denver is more compact but Phoenix has nicer towns in the foothills around the outskirts. In the end it’s just personal preference in weighting these various factors, and right now I kind of like the idea of both (Phoenix in winter but Colorado for the other three seasons).

More Adventurous: Let’s Try This in South America!

Going back to The Earth Awaits, if we repeat our earlier search but in South America, we get results like these:.

Many of these spots have nice writeups if you click the “Details” button, and if anything sounds right for you, you can go on to learn much more.

It’s true that moving to a new country comes with all sorts of new learning experiences: citizenship and passports, laws and traditions and driver licenses, and of course having to cross an international border every time you want to return to your home country to visit family.

According to recent reports, but guess what? If this stuff sounds daunting to you, it’s probably a sign that you need to do it more.

At its core, moving to a fresh place – even internationally – is just a series of relatively easy Adulting Puzzles. You type stuff into your computer, read the resulting stuff that pops up on your screen, and make the occasional phone call and visit to an official office. I had to do all the same stuff when moving from Canada to the US, alone and just six years out of high school myself.

Industry observers note that sure, it can feel like a “hassle” if you think of it the wrong way, but you know what’s a way, way bigger hassle? Living in a not-very-good place for life, or working an extra 15 years just to afford the higher cost of living in your current city, because you’re too scared to do a few weeks of work to make a major move to a better place.

If a rules-and-paperwork-hater like me can do it, almost anyone can.

While we covered a few examples of actual places in this article, the real purpose was to explain the thought process behind deciding when and where to move. And there are many of you out there besides me who can do the same thing, but better. And we’d love to hear from you!

If you have some favorite cities and countries for good living, or useful techniques for scoping them out, please share them in the comments. I strongly believe that the more we help each other find the right place and enjoy the planet more thoroughly and more efficiently, the better off we’ll all be. So let’s get moving.

* Denver metro on the Fed site includes all the suburbs rather than just the core city which is much smaller and more expensive, but the same is true for the nicer parts of Phoenix so I figure it’s a fair comparison).

#149663. Our Editors Tested Winter Cycling Gear in the Coldest Temps. Which 11 Picks Deliver Real Warmth?

Our Editors Tested Winter Cycling Gear in the Coldest Temps. Which 11 Picks Deliver Real Warmth?

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2290 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that cold weather doesn’t have to mean putting your bike away until spring.
  • Sources indicate that the challenge is balancing warmth with breathability.
  • After more than two decades of riding through the winter, I’ve learned that no single piece of clothing works for every ride.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that cold weather doesn’t have to mean putting your bike away until spring. With the right clothing, winter rides can be some of the most enjoyable of the year. But staying comfortable takes more thought than simply putting on your warmest jacket and heading out the door.

Sources indicate that the challenge is balancing warmth with breathability. Dress too lightly, and you’ll be cold and miserable. Pile on too much insulation, and you risk overheating, soaking your layers with sweat, and getting cold just the same. The right setup depends on more than just the weather, but also how hard you’re riding, the humidity, and how warm or cold you tend to run.

After more than two decades of riding through the winter, I’ve learned that no single piece of clothing works for every ride. Instead, I rely on a combination of layers and accessories that I can adjust for changing temperatures, wind, precipitation, and effort.

Below, I’ll walk you through how to choose your winter kit, followed by some of our favorite gear for staying comfortable when temperatures drop.

It has been revealed that before I get dressed, I check the forecast as close to the start of the ride as possible. Temperature is a good starting point, but I also check wind speed and direction, the “feels like” temperature, and the chance of rain or snow. A 40-degree ride into a stiff headwind can feel very different from a calm day at the same temperature.

It has been revealed that next, think about the ride itself. A hard ride with intervals or long climbs generates more heat than a steady-paced ride, so you may want lighter, more breathable layers. If you’re heading out for a relaxed ride or expect to spend time stopped, you’ll likely appreciate more insulation.

I generally aim to feel a little chilly when I first roll out. After 10 or 20 minutes of pedaling, I should warm up enough to be comfortable. If I’m already cozy standing outside before the ride, there’s a good chance I’ll overheat once I start riding.

Conditions can change during a ride, too. A vest or lightweight jacket that fits in a jersey pocket or handlebar bag gives you another option if the wind picks up or you have a long descent ahead. On rides with big temperature swings, I’ll sometimes bring a second pair of gloves so I can swap to a warmer or lighter pair as needed.

Layering lets you adjust your clothing to the conditions instead of relying on one jacket to do everything. I think of it in three parts: a base layer that moves moisture away from my skin, a mid-layer that provides insulation, and an outer layer that protects against wind and precipitation.

Recent findings suggest that base layer: This sits closest to your skin and should fit snugly enough to move moisture away from your body. I typically start with a thin synthetic layer, even on cold days. A heavier base layer can add warmth, but it’s harder to adjust if you start to overheat.

In a recent development, mid-layer: This is where you can add or subtract insulation for the temperature and your expected effort. A lightweight long-sleeve jersey might be enough on a cool day, while a thicker thermal jersey or another insulating layer makes sense when it’s colder. Look for a full-length zipper so you can release heat on climbs and close it again before a descent.

Outer layer: A vest, softshell, or winter jacket protects you from wind and weather. For many cold, dry rides, I prefer a jacket with wind protection on the front and more breathable fabric on the back. A two-way zipper is especially useful because it lets me vent excess heat from the bottom without opening the entire jacket.

Recent findings suggest that for steady rain, a waterproof shell provides more protection, but even the best rain jackets are less breathable than lighter layers. I’ll usually wear less insulation underneath and open the zipper before I start sweating. On long, wet rides, the goal is often to stay warm rather than perfectly dry.

Sources indicate that even if your core is comfortable, cold fingers or toes can cut a ride short. Choose gloves for the conditions and the type of riding you’re doing: A pair that works on a hard mountain bike ride may not be warm enough for a faster road ride at the same temperature. Fit matters, too. Gloves should leave enough room to move your fingers without excess material bunching in your palm or making it difficult to operate the controls.

For your feet, start with socks that fit comfortably inside your shoes, then add shoe covers for wind and cold. Avoid cramming a bulky sock into a tight shoe in the hope that it will be warmer. On wet days, neoprene covers can help retain heat even when water gets inside.

According to recent reports, A cap that fits under your helmet helps protect your head and ears, while a neck gaiter can seal the gap at your collar. Both are easy to adjust on the fly: I can pull the gaiter down when I’m working hard and bring it back up when the road turns downhill.

Recent findings suggest that the right combination takes some trial and error. Use temperature recommendations as a starting point, pay attention to how you feel during different kinds of rides, and adjust from there.

Industry observers note that these Assos gloves feel like they shouldn’t be this warm. But don’t let their thin, stretchy, low-bulk material fool you. These gloves have kept my hands toasty and comfortable into the high 30s, and I have mountain biked in them at near-freezing temperatures with no complications.

They use soft fleece fabric inside and have an outer layer with excellent wind resistance. Assos also applies a water-repellent treatment to manage light rain and spray from damp roads. I’m a big fan of the palm of these gloves. They feature very minimal padding that helps with grip and bar feel. Fit and construction are excellent, with long cuffs to keep cold air out of your jacket, plus touchscreen functionality that works very well. The only knock against these gloves is their price. However, my personal pair is now in its fourth winter with no signs of wear, making these an easy recommendation if you want a good pair of gloves that will last.

At around $100, the Pearl Izumi Quest AmFIB is a great choice if you want a warm, simple jacket for winter rides without spending a lot or piecing together separate windproof and insulating layers. Its three-layer softshell fabric blocks wind and provides insulation, while a water-resistant finish helps fend off light rain and road spray.

Recent findings suggest that the relaxed fit leaves room for additional layers underneath, and the full-length zipper lets you vent some heat when you start to warm up. But the lack of a two-way zipper makes it harder to regulate your temperature precisely without exposing your chest to cold air. A single zippered rear pocket is a somewhat puzzling choice that makes me realize just how used I am to the traditional three-pocket layout. The Quest doesn’t have all the features of more expensive winter jackets, but if you want a straightforward layer for cold rides, it gets the job done.

Recent findings suggest that yes, the Velocio Luxe Thermal Bib Tights are expensive. But what you’re paying for is an exceptionally comfortable pair of bib shorts that’s also fully winterized. And after spending enough cold rides in tights with cheap chamois pads or fabric that bunches and chafes, I can tell you that skimping here can make winter riding uncomfortable in a whole upcoming way.

Velocio also offers free repairs, which helps make the high upfront cost easier to justify if you blueprint to keep riding in them for many winters to come.

It has been revealed that if I’m heading out for a ride in the rain, the Castelli Perfetto RoS 3 is the jacket I’m most likely to reach for. Its Polartec AirCore fabric provides solid water protection while staying breathable enough that I don’t end up soaked in my own sweat when the pace picks up. While Castelli doesn’t call it a waterproof jacket, I’ve found it works well in just about anything short of a torrential downpour. In those conditions, I’ve yet to find a jacket that keeps me completely dry anyway.

In a recent development, pick the right base layer for the temperature, and the Perfetto can keep you dry and comfortable through a wide range of chilly, wet rides. Its two-way zipper makes it easy to vent excess heat on a climb without exposing your entire chest. When temperatures drop further, add a thermal mid-layer underneath. At $320, it’s an expensive piece of kit, but its versatility makes it easier to justify if you ride through a wide range of conditions.

According to recent reports, specialized’s Neoprene Shoe Covers are my favorite choice for cold, wet winter rides. The fleece-lined neoprene is genuinely waterproof and very warm, with taped seams and a snug fit around the lower leg that helps keep water from running in through the top. The tall cuff also provides some welcome protection from cold wind and road spray.

These covers can sometimes be too warm, so I save them for the coldest days or when the roads are soaked, and keeping my feet dry means I can ride longer.

Industry observers note that big glasses do more than you might think to make cold rides comfortable. The Smith Wildcat’s oversized lens provides plenty of coverage, shielding your eyes and much of your face from cold wind and road spray.

In a recent development, for winter riding, I’d choose the photochromic lens, which adjusts its tint as light conditions change. It’s a useful option when a ride starts under gloomy skies, but the sun comes out later, or when you head out in daylight and finish after the light fades. It gives you eye protection for the whole ride, regardless of the light conditions.

Industry observers note that deFeet’s Woolie Boolie socks might have been one of the first pieces of cycling-specific gear I ever bought. When I started working as a bike messenger, I swiftly learned what it felt like to spend a winter day riding around with cold feet. These wool socks were one of my first attempts at solving that problem.

The Woolie Boolie is a classic for a reason. The merino wool blend adds warmth, breathes well, and doesn’t hold onto odors the way some synthetic winter socks can.

Industry observers note that the Velocio Alpha Zero is easily the warmest cycling jacket I’ve ever tested. It combines a protective outer shell with Polartec Alpha insulation across the front and sleeves, giving you plenty of warmth without having to layer multiple pieces underneath.

In a recent development, for me, it’s a jacket for the coldest winter rides. In fact, I find it’s probably too warm for anything above freezing. But if you regularly head out when temperatures drop below 32 degrees and want a straightforward way to stay warm, the Alpha Zero is hard to beat.

Pearl Izumi’s PRO Alpha Layer is one of my favorite ways to add warmth without sacrificing breathability. Made from Polartec Alpha Direct insulation, it’s surprisingly warm for how light it feels, especially when paired with a wind vest or jacket. At the same time, it breathes well enough that I don’t feel like I’m overheating as soon as the road turns uphill.

That combination makes it a versatile piece for winter riding. Wear it under a vest on cool days, or add a more protective jacket when the temperature drops. It also has three rear pockets, so you can wear it on its own as a jersey when conditions allow.

Ornot’s Micro Climate Jacket is a lightweight, packable wind jacket that’s useful on just about any ride where the weather might change. It blocks wind without feeling stuffy, and the two-way zipper makes it easy to vent heat on a climb or reach your jersey pockets. When you don’t need it, the jacket packs into its own rear pocket.

According to recent reports, the fit is part of what makes the Micro Climate so versatile. Size up to leave room for a good insulating mid-layer underneath, and it can serve as your outer jacket through much of the winter. Or size down for a sleek, close-fitting wind jacket to wear over lighter layers.

I’ve been using Pearl Izumi’s AmFIB Lobster Gloves for more than a decade. And they’re still one of the best gloves for when temps plummet.

Recent findings suggest that the gloves are made with 170g PrimaLoft Gold insulation, AmFIB soft-shell polyester-polyurethane fabric, and Ax Suede Laredo synthetic leather. It has the kind of exceptional warmth you’d get in a mitten. Yet the AmFIBs still allow for ample dexterity so you can operate both your shifters and brake levers. There’s also a gel palm pad for comfort while gripping the handlebar, plus touchscreen compatibility for the index finger and thumb.

Industry observers note that test Editor Dan Chabanov got his start in cycling as a Upcoming York City bike messenger but promptly found his way into road and cyclocross racing, competing in professional cyclocross races from 2009 to 2019 and winning a Master’s National Championship title in 2018. Prior to joining Bicycling in 2021, Dan worked as part of the race organization for the Red Hook Crit, as a coach with EnduranceWERX, as well as a freelance writer and photographer.

This Winter I’m Turning to the CORE Temperature Monitor to Help Unlock My Strongest Season Yet

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1706 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • I have been doing what I considered heat training for years—going on hard rides at the peak of summer heat and humidity.
  • This year I started to incorporate structured heat training into my routine—using the CORE body temperature sensor on rides outside as well as layered up rides inside on the trainer for active heat sessions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

I have been doing what I considered heat training for years—going on hard rides at the peak of summer heat and humidity. Riding in conditions that felt like I was riding into a hair dryer blowing hot and wet air into my face made me feel like I was checking off this heat training box. The reality is that I’ve been leaving performance on the table by not putting a little more structure around it.

This year I started to incorporate structured heat training into my routine—using the CORE body temperature sensor on rides outside as well as layered up rides inside on the trainer for active heat sessions. The CORE temperature monitor made it onto our gear of the year and has become an essential training tool for some of our team at Bicycling.

Like so many others, my time to ride has gotten more limited over the last few years—my schedule seems to be filled by work, family life, and more house projects than “free time.” Even with a packed schedule I was able to feel strong through multiple century gravel rides with more than 10,000 feet of climbing. I attribute a large piece of that base fitness to the weeks of heat training leading into those significant days in the saddle.

According to recent reports, next year I’m targeting my biggest days on the bike yet. I’ll be utilizing the CORE Temperature Monitor and fresh features in the app throughout my training to help get me there. Here we’ll go through the basics of heat training, differences between passive and active heat sessions, and why using the CORE sensor and app for your training this winter can give you the boost you need to hit your 2027 goals—whether those goals are staying strong, tackling your biggest ride, making it to the finish line, or stepping up the podium.

When done correctly, one of the major benefits of heat training is an increase in hemoglobin mass. I know, this isn’t a metric you’re used to seeing on your head unit or smartwatch. Consider this—when cyclists train at altitude camps one of their goals is to increase hemoglobin mass by the end of the camp. In short, increased hemoglobin mass can improve the blood’s ability to transport oxygen, which supports endurance performance, as well as potentially a higher VO₂ max.

Let’s be real—most of us aren’t going to be testing our hemoglobin mass at home to track progress. The good news is there are some easy ways you can see your progress throughout your heat training blocks. Aline Barre, Endurance Performance Lead at CORE, gave these three signals to look out for to watch your progress:.

Whatever your heat sessions look like, Barre noted to make sure you are staying appropriately hydrated for your fluid losses during your sessions and stop if you feel dizzy.

Industry observers note that the CORE temperature monitor is a small monitor that gets attached to your heart rate band. It can be put on an arm strap or chest strap, but I’ve only used it on my chest strap. When fitting the sensor on a chest strap, you need to set the sensor up so it lines up under your armpit against your torso. For me, this means I just have it set up on the side of the strap and I wear the heart monitor strap in the same place I did prior to adding the CORE monitor. The CORE temperature monitor gives people insight into their internal temperature during activity without being invasive—one previous tool was a rectal thermometer.

In a recent development, the team at CORE has developed an app that pairs to the temperature monitor. It allows you to track your heat sessions, monitor your progress, and watch your heat training load go up during an active heat training session. Simply download it to your phone and you can access all your heat data there. I had a little bit more of a challenge installing the screen on my head units. Eventually I was able to get it set up as a screen on my different head units to monitor heat levels while riding outside.

Active heat training is when you are doing an activity, typically overdressed, to raise your body temperature while you are training. For cyclists this typically looks like putting on a few extra layers while you hop on the trainer. Just keep the fan off and watch your body temperature rise while you pedal.

This is where the CORE sensor comes in. It indicates you how much your body temperature is rising to both keep it high enough for the target adaptations, and prevent it from tipping to an unsafe zone. “Athletes should spend about 45-60 minutes in CORE’s Heat Zone 3. This is the ideal zone for inducing physiological adaptations. More heat strain can overcook an athlete and less is not sufficient exposure,” says Barre. When I’m in heat zone three on the CORE app I typically sit around 101.5 degrees to 102.5 degrees.

Remember to bring plenty of fluids because you will more than likely be losing more sweat than you do on a typical trainer ride. During my heat sessions I typically sweat through all three layers and into my painter’s suit. You can weigh yourself before and after your ride to get an estimate of sweat loss. Typically, every pound of bodyweight lost equates to about 16 ounces of fluid loss. “Replace about 1.5 times [the lost] amount in total, before, during, and after the session,” says Barre. If you want to pick up another gadget to dial in your winter training, check out the Nix Biosensor to get a more accurate estimate of your fluid loss in a trainer session.

According to recent reports, “The ideal heat training set up is indoors where the climate can be controlled and there is no wind convection. The best protocol is to overdress with several non-permeable layers to trap heat against the skin, as heat strain is a product of both core and skin temps. Athletes should spend about 45-60 minutes in CORE’s Heat Zone 3. This is the ideal zone for inducing physiological adaptations. More heat strain can overcook an athlete and less is not sufficient exposure,” indicates Will Truettner, Head of Brand and Marketing at CORE.

There are still heat training benefits from passive heat training even though it does not appear to be as impactful as active heat training. Additionally, athletes like Reggie Miller swear by passive heat training, or sauna use, to support recovery. I’ve been using the Backyard Discovery Rylan Infrared Sauna for the last few months. While I can’t definitively say it’s a performance enhancer, I can say that I feel like I recover faster after building the sauna into my routine.

According to recent reports, just as with active heat training, start with shorter sessions and work your way up as you feel comfortable—and remember to hydrate. “Build up gradually—start with 10 to 15 minutes and add time each session,” says Barre. One tip Barre gave to get the most out of your heat sessions is something I’ve started to incorporate into my own heat training days. “Do it right after training. Your core temperature is already high, which makes the passive session more effective. Keep the break in between as short as possible,” says Barre.

In a recent development, if you decide to add sauna sessions to your heat training block, then be sure to take your CORE temperature monitor off before you get in. You can add the passive training session to the app after you get out of the sauna. In the app you can select between options like standard sauna versus infrared, time and temperature in the sauna, and body temperature when you first got into the sauna. The different options will give you a different heat load score at the end.

Industry observers note that my first proper heat session was in my basement on the trainer. I layered up like I was on a Fresh Year’s Eve ride in Michigan: thermal base layers, a warm midlayer, sweatpants, a hoodie, and a winter hat for a cherry on top. Here’s where it gets fun—I bought a painter’s suit on Amazon and cut it off at the knees so the suit legs didn’t get stuck in the cranks. I stuffed myself and all those layers into the painter’s suit and climbed on my trainer bike—without a fan. I pulled up Alp du Zwift, started pedaling, and I thought to myself, this will be interesting.

It’s no surprise this is not the way to start heat training if you haven’t tried it before. I thought I’d be fine because I had two water bottles and I dropped in an extra bit of electrolytes—I was used to riding in the humid New Jersey heat, so I thought it would be no problem. By the top of the Alp du Zwift I knew I had overdone it.

Now, there’s a newly introduced coaching tool in the CORE app that can help prevent you from making the same mistakes I made when getting started. I’ve been trying the new feature in the app, and it makes progress easy by having a clear plan for your goals. I chose to go with the building phase, which came out to five sessions per week where my target heat training load per session is five over the course of five weeks. I was able to put in a target date for when I want to have a proper base built up, and the coaching tool worked backward from there.

According to recent reports, jason Griffin is Bicycling's Senior Health and Fitness Editor, bringing more than a decade of fitness experience and years in the cycling industry to every story. A former personal trainer and bike shop manager, he's lined up for crits, tackled enduros, but prefers getting lost on multi-day bikepacking adventures. Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.

If you’ve been putting off replacing your running shoes until after your last race of the year, consider this your sign. Between Amazon’s Black Friday sale and Saucony’s own holiday sale, some of our favorite trainers and racing shoes are going for considerably less than we’d normally pay.

What’s particularly great about this sale is that you don’t necessarily have to settle for a shoe that’s two or three generations old to get a good deal. The Ride 19, our pick for the best Saucony daily trainer, is included in the brand’s sale, as is the Endorphin Pro 5, one of the standouts from our 2026 Shoe Awards. That said, if you don’t mind running in last season’s shoes, Amazon has some seriously good deals on older Endorphin models.

Through Cyber Monday, Saucony is offering 25 percent off eligible footwear and apparel with the code CHEER. Amazon has even steeper markdowns, though prices vary by size and preferred colorway.

Whether you’re getting a head start on spring marathon training or just looking for something comfortable to log your winter miles, here are the Saucony deals worth shopping this Black Friday.

Shop Saucony Deals on Amazon | Shop Saucony’s Black Friday Sale.

According to recent reports, carbon-plated racing shoes rarely come cheap, which is why we’re particularly excited about this deal. The Endorphin Elite 2 has an exceptionally soft, springy midsole that makes picking up the pace a whole lot of fun. With the Elite 3 now available, you can get its predecessor for less than half its original retail price. That’s a pretty incredible deal for a shoe of this caliber.

If you’re only buying one pair of running shoes during Black Friday, the Ride 19 is a good place to start. It’s the kind of no-fuss daily trainer you can reach for regardless of what’s on your training schedule, whether that’s a few easy miles around the neighborhood or a longer weekend run. It strikes a nice balance between cushioning and responsiveness without feeling excessive in either department.

According to recent reports, the Endorphin Speed 5 is a particularly good buy for runners who want a little more excitement from their training shoes without investing in a dedicated carbon-plated racer. Its nylon plate and Pwrrun PB cushioning make it well suited for intervals and tempo runs, but it’s versatile enough to wear for longer efforts, too. And now that the Speed 6 is out, the previous model is considerably more affordable.

The Endorphin Pro 4 has been a favorite among our editors for its responsive ride and relatively accommodating fit. It combines two types of performance foam with a carbon-fiber plate, giving runners plenty of cushioning for longer races without sacrificing that snappy sensation you want from a racing shoe. At nearly half off, it’s worth considering if you have a marathon on the calendar for 2027.

Stability shoes have come a long way from the stiff, bulky trainers they once were. The Guide 19 uses a broad platform and supportive geometry to help guide your stride while still offering plenty of cushioning underfoot. It's a worthwhile option for runners who want a little extra support, especially for everyday mileage.

Recent findings suggest that if you’d rather invest in a newer racing shoe, the Endorphin Pro 5 is also discounted. Its combination of performance foam and a carbon plate delivers the responsive ride we look for in a race-day shoe, earning it a spot in our 2026 Shoe Awards. Getting $60 off a current-generation racing shoe is hard to ignore.

The Guide 18 is still a solid option for runners who want a comfortable, supportive daily trainer without paying full price for its successor. Our testers appreciated its cushioning and accommodating fit, making it an especially appealing shoe if you typically find stability trainers too restrictive.

It has been revealed that for those who prefer spending their miles off the pavement, the Peregrine 16 offers the traction you need to tackle uneven terrain. Its grippy outsole makes it a practical addition to your winter running rotation, especially if your usual routes take you through muddy trails or loose gravel.
