  • I relearned this lesson earlier this month, when I found myself at the top of Bear Mountain, the only notable multi-mile climb close enough to bike to from New York City.
  • It has been revealed that though I’m relatively new to road cycling, I’ve done some long gravel rides and recently tackled the Maratona dles Dolomites in Italy, where I buried myself to finish a 66-mile route that featured over 10,000 feet of elevation and one 8-mile climb up the Passo Valparolo.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

They say pride comes before the fall. In cycling, I’ve found pride usually comes before the first true descent.

I relearned this lesson earlier this month, when I found myself at the top of Bear Mountain, the only notable multi-mile climb close enough to bike to from New York City. Its peak was situated about halfway into the 105-mile route of the Best Buddies Challenge New York, an event the organization had brought back for a second year to fund its programming for teenagers and young adults with intellectual and developmental disabilities. The riders gawking at the intermittently vermilion canopy who were pedaling alongside me had each raised at least $1,800 to reach this particular vista, plus access to several deliciously well-stocked aid stations, SAG vehicles, and the promise of a raucous finish-line party.

It has been revealed that though I’m relatively new to road cycling, I’ve done some long gravel rides and recently tackled the Maratona dles Dolomites in Italy, where I buried myself to finish a 66-mile route that featured over 10,000 feet of elevation and one 8-mile climb up the Passo Valparolo. By comparison, the Best Buddies Challenge century, with 2,000 fewer feet of climbing stretched over a much longer route, seemed plenty doable when I signed up in September.

The first indication I had erred came before I had pinned my bib number to my jersey. At a pre-ride reception, I sat down with Alberto Contador (yes, that Alberto Contador), who was returning to the event for the second time. He was confident I could handle Bear Mountain, but warned me that the end of the ride reminded him of La Flèche Wallonne, a notoriously difficult Belgian one-day race known for its repeat ascents of the relatively short, brutally steep Mur de Huy. “The last 30 miles is all up and down…save energy,” he remarked.

By the time I slid into the fourth aid station, which marked the 33-miles-to-go point in my own ride, this advice was well out of my mind. I was supremely confident in my ability to finish strong. Sure, I had gone a bit deeper in the tank to maintain contact with random groups throughout the day in valleys and on shallow sections, but there was so little left to go.

How hard could the rest really be?

The Best Buddies Challenge is relatively newly introduced to New York City, but the concept of the charity ride is not. The Five Boro Bike Tour, which raises money for Bike New York’s free education and mechanics program, has given city cyclists the chance to experience streets without car traffic since 1977. On the West Coast, Washington’s Cascade Bicycle Club’s Seattle to Portland Bicycle Classic now generates about $1 million each year to fund the organization’s community programs, cycling education, and statewide cycling advocacy work. Even the ride I did in the Dolomites this summer offers charity entrants, who have, over the years, raised over $2 million for road safety, food security, disease research, and rural education.

Sources indicate that among non-endurance athletes, these rides often draw comparisons to running events like the Latest York City Marathon. There are certainly similarities—sanctioned routes, feed stations, distances that sound absurd to normies—but cyclists don’t tend to give even long charity rides anything close to the same level of credence as runners do to marathons.

That kind of resistance perhaps comes from those strains of cycling tradition that prize grit and ardor and self-reliance. Conquering Mur de Huy during a race takes superhuman levels of tenacity and determination—charity rides, by contrast, even those that span 100 miles, are much more comfortable affairs. Do some riders dismiss these events because they’re too soft? It’s possible.

Industry observers note that beginner-friendliness is often baked into the event programming of charity rides. Breakthrough T1D Rides, held to fund research for type 1 diabetes, are actually four-day retreats. Participants spend only one day on the bike. Anthony Geraci, national director of Ride & Endurance Programs, claims most of these rides feature “out-and-back” courses. Turn around whenever you feel done with your day! “We always say it’s not about the miles, it’s about the mission.”.

Sure, you could cross-stitch that phrase onto a throw pillow. But it’s also the kind of mentality that cyclists might need to achieve some personal goals, whether that’s riding in a new destination or tackling their first century. In this way, charity rides can be catalysts for remarkable personal achievement.

They also create the conditions for extremely impressive fundraising. Best Buddies International CEO Anthony Shriver (yes, that Shriver) told me that its cycling events account for about 10 to 15 percent of the organization’s annual revenue. Similarly, Kris Rauh, vice president, event experience and operations for NMSS, states its 49 Bike MS events generate about $52 million in revenue annually for the organization.

In a recent development, indeed, she continued, many of the people signing up to do their first Bike MS have no personal connection to the disease in its name. “They come to us mostly because they want a challenge on a bike … they don’t come to us as fundraisers,” she said.

According to recent reports, for charity rides like Bike MS and Best Buddies, it’s important to connect participants to their mission and the impact of their work. As I ascended Bear Mountain and pushed myself on the way back, I wasn’t just riding with Contador and Chris Froome (who was also participating this year) but also plenty of folks who volunteer for or participate in Best Buddies programming. In fact, individuals with intellectual and developmental disabilities often held key roles during its rides. At the Challenge Newly introduced York, a “Buddy” gave a speech while we waited in the start pen, a different “Buddy” sang the national anthem, and still others staffed the aid stations. “From the moment you wake up at 4 o’clock in the morning, you should know you’re doing something that’s going to enrich another human being’s life,” Shriver remarked.

Recent findings suggest that the combination makes these kinds of charity rides feel a lot different than a standard criterium or gravel fondo. And it seems to hold enough appeal to keep the organizations hosting them going. Best Buddies, which has substantial fundraising minimums for riders, gets a 30 to 50 percent return rate, Shriver says. According to Rauh, at Bike MS that number is closer to 60 percent. That’s a lot of people returning to charity rides each year.

About two-thirds of the way into my own Fresh York Challenge, I was actively questioning how this could be possible. Though I had been correct that all the long climbs were behind me, the “rolling” terrain I had imagined was actually a freak show of sharp pitches. I cracked on a climb my Garmin did not categorize, attempting to hold serve over a bump with a gradient of 18 percent.

Recent findings suggest that I unclipped and shuffled my cramping legs up the embarrassingly short walk to the summit. I felt ashamed by the level of hubris I had brought into the event. If it had been just a regular ride, or even a race, this might have been my day. With hours left to a finish that I felt confident most of the participants had already crossed, it would have been totally within my prerogative to pull the quick-release lever off my front wheel and stuff my bike in a Lyft bound back to Brooklyn.

But as I munched on some blissfully salty crackers that quieted my screaming hamstrings, I realized that getting to the end would be an accomplishment for me regardless of how fast I was able to do it. And, importantly, my path to the shuttle bus that would take me back to the city included one final rest stop. Resolved never to underestimate a “ride” again, I got back in the saddle and held the limpest zone 1 pace of my life until I had made it to the aforementioned support tent. With less than 10 miles left, I slumped into a folding chair and sucked down a can of Sprite.

It has been revealed that immediately, I was engaged by Matt, who was participating in the ride as a volunteer. He asked if I was okay, and when it was clear that I was mentally wrecked, but physically fine, gently encouraged me to get moving. With Matt, another volunteer named Ian, and a pair of other riders who had also had similarly tough days, we set off on the last stretch to the end.

Chatting in my bunch, really the only bunch I had been able to hang on to the entire day, made the miles go by faster and the remaining climbs feel shorter. And when the sugar from my soda hit, I realized I was actually less dead than the pair of participants I had just encountered. Ian and I forged ahead, buoyed by the knowledge the end was near. I managed to stay upright enough up the finishing hill to attempt a celebratory pose as I crossed over the finish line: ninth to last. It was the longest ride I’ve ever done and it challenged me to push myself harder than I might otherwise have done. That’s worth something.

Does anyone have a cool $2,000 I could use to try again next year?

#149632. The Ultimate Life Coach

The Ultimate Life Coach

📅 18 May 2024 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2060 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Almost  nineteen years into early retirement now, I’ve come to realize that the complete freedom of this lifestyle can be a double-edged sword.
  • You’ve already heard me raving plenty about the upside: having the freedom to raise a son from the day he was born to beyond his eighteenth birthday with no compromises.
  • But if I can indulge you to play me a brief Tiny Violin of First World Problems solo, even this perfect life comes with one flaw: I never have to do anything I don’t want to do.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Almost  nineteen years into early retirement now, I’ve come to realize that the complete freedom of this lifestyle can be a double-edged sword.

You’ve already heard me raving plenty about the upside: having the freedom to raise a son from the day he was born to beyond his eighteenth birthday with no compromises. And then to put thousands of hours into everything else I value as well: family, health, friends, adventures, building stuff, and even writing the occasional blog post. No complaints about any of this.

But if I can indulge you to play me a brief Tiny Violin of First World Problems solo, even this perfect life comes with one flaw: I never have to do anything I don’t want to do.

Sources indicate that to most people, this sounds like a dream come true. Especially if you combine total freedom with plenty of money, life is just a non-stop blissful playground of self actualization, right?

Well, maybe, but maybe not. In reality, the answer depends on who you are.

Freedom and money reveal a person’s true strengths and weaknesses, and the result is a spectrum with “Unlimited drugs and booze on the couch” at one end, and “Create and manage a series of nonprofit foundations which employ thousands of people to research and invest in medical advances and clean energy” at the other.

Industry observers note that for most of my journey so far, I seem to have found the balance pretty naturally. My Dad job was very intense for the first decade, but somehow I also had time to build and restore quite a few houses in the neighborhood, take plenty of intense trips to interesting places, give some talks and make some videos, and still write a few hundred blog posts.

But in these last few years, I have started slowing down, and it has become more and more difficult to wrangle and focus myself to get these things to happen as often.

Instead of constantly bouncing around the construction site building cool things, or falling into laser focus on the keyboard finishing an article that I just had to share with you, I found myself retiring to the couch earlier and earlier each afternoon, seeking distraction on the phone and wishing I had the energy and focus to do those other more enjoyable things.

Sources indicate that so I fought back, by learning more about health and wellness. Trying to study and train my way into more energy and focus and motivation. And you’ve seen some of the results here, in articles I’ve shared about daily habits, steering clear of excessive comfort, and more.

And all of these things really work, IF you take the knowledge and actually put it into action. And therein lies the problem:.

I kept learning effective latest things, and successfully incorporating them into my life. They would work for a while, but gradually my brain would invent various excuses to stop doing them consistently, leaving me with plenty of knowledge but far too little accomplishment to show for it.

Until finally, just a few months ago, I realized that I had been sabotaging my own progress by turning my biggest life advantage into a disadvantage:.

I have been using my freedom too much – in order to avoid doing things that I didn’t feel like doing.

According to recent reports, see, freedom is great if it frees you from leaving your children at 5am so you can drive an hour through a traffic jam to sit in an office building for nine hours. But that same freedom goes to waste if you then just plunk the kids down in front of a playlist of cheap cartoons while you lounge in the corner to scroll Facebook all day.

You need to use it to do things that are even more valuable than the job you just quit. And if you can’t do that, you might as well just keep the damned job.

This is what I was doing, while lying about it to myself. I would focus on the easy things which are still good for me, like taking care of the house or hanging out with friends who live nearby. But I avoid doing the harder things – which for me means the things that require more planning, energy or focus. Even though these are the things that allow me to lead the life I enjoy most.

Let’s use workouts as an easy example. I already know that on a minute-for-minute basis, this is the single most effective thing almost anybody can do with their time because it drastically improves every other area of life. But despite knowing this, I was still following this pattern:.

“I want to get in a really good weight training workout today.But I don’t feel like doing a workout because it’s hard.So I’ll try to grease the wheels for myself so it’s easier to achieve. I’ll pick the perfect time of day when the weather is nice, and my energy level is high. I’ll set up my gym in advance the night before.And when that golden moment of perfect conditions hits,I’ll hit the gym!“.

But between you and me, that moment didn’t always come. Some weeks I’d achieve it 2-3 times, some weeks I’d get “busy” and make excuses like “well at least I walked a lot today”. Some days I would complete a great workout, but when recording it in the journal I’d see that the previous one was over a week ago.

And the results of this lackluster effort were exactly what you’d expect: lackluster fitness.

It has been revealed that then something changed and I learned that there’s a much better way to get those workouts done. It’s by replacing the long, meandering, frankly wussypants dialog above with this one:.

It has been revealed that I want to work out today.I don’t feel like it.^^^ AHA!! I JUST CAUGHT MYSELF TRYING TO SELF SABOTAGE! ^^^I am now already putting on my shoes and walking to the gym.

I’m using workouts as an example because this is the behavior I managed to change most successfully, but the exact same technique applies to everything else that you or I want to do, but fail to do regularly.

The key is learning to watch over yourself like an Eagle and identify that exact moment of hesitation.

And then instead of using it as a trigger for excuses, you use it as a trigger for action.

Industry observers note that it’s so counterintuitive at first, but then obvious in retrospect. Hesitance feels shitty in the moment, and it really can ruin your life if you listen to it too often. But the ultimate solution is usually to run directly towards, rather than away from, the stuff you don’t want to do.

So really, Hesitation can be the ultimate life coach.

Using Extremely Badass People as Fuel.

According to recent reports, as part of writing this article, I shared the idea around with friends to test it out first. And I was initially surprised to get mixed results. About half of them could relate with me: they felt they were underachieving in life and wanted to do more. The other half though I was crazy: these people feel they are already doing too much, raising multiple kids and managing multiple businesses and training for ironman triathlons in the mountains.

The overachievers go through life nicely buzzed but often stressed. When hearing them describe their schedules, I was absolutely not envious. At the same time, they weren’t impressed with my schedule either because it’s too easy. We could both benefit from making adjustments towards the center.

Impressive overachiever friends are one thing, but the thing that really flipped the switch for me was hearing a podcast interview with our planet’s most extreme example of driving yourself beyond your former limits, David Goggins.

I learned about his life story with a mix of awe and horror. Severely beaten as a child, he grew up with a looming wall of psychological demons and challenges, but his reaction was the unique part: he has been driven to compulsively seek out and overcome extreme hardship, not just to unimaginable levels but hundreds of times beyond that.

From pushing through several near-death experiences just to qualify for a Navy SEALS career, to breaking his own legs, heart and lungs from the constant exertion of things like running 240 miles over four days without sleeping, to setting a world record of 4025 bar pull ups over 24 hours (shredding his hands to look like ground beef in the process), the man does things I would never have thought are even close to possible for a human.

And that flipped a switch for me, by putting my own incredibly easy, under-achieving life into perspective.

Because while I absolutely do not want any part of the Goggins life, and I would gladly live my life never having run more than 10 miles at a single stretch, I do find it incredibly helpful to learn that pretty much all of our barriers are entirely mental, not physical or placed upon us by the outside world.

It has been revealed that sure, we do have different starting points and different amounts of luck. But instead of thinking of life like this:.

I now realize that things are more like this:.

And that’s a really empowering way to think about life, that feels like the sky has opened way up.

Industry observers note that so the podcast was just an introduction. I wrote down the particularly concise quote “You already fuckin’ know what to do.” on a piece of cardstock, stuck it to my bathroom mirror, and started acting on it immediately.

Suddenly, I was able to hit the gym every single day because I had two ways to approach it: wanting to put in a workout, and not wanting to put in a workout, either of which became a trigger to work out immediately.

And of course, once I finally put in the effort, it started working. Even though I’ve been sorta into this type of training since I was a teenager, I have mostly floated along on a plateau for years. But with this change in attitude, I gained ten pounds of lean weight over the first four months, returning to the strength and flexibility that I had at age 25, and every single joint in my body feels like it has been upgraded to a study, well oiled spring.

I also used the “catch yourself at the moment of hesitance” trick to get myself to run instead of walk more often (over 20 runs since I got back to Colorado last month), get over to the MMM-HQ coworking space for more work and socializing visits, and even to sit back down at the computer to write this post for you. While I’ve found that too much blogger work (and internet “success”) is a bad thing, there is still a right level that works for me. But it takes a lot of discipline to be willing to do it, because of all the other easier and more thrilling activities I could be doing with this same stretch of time.

Sources indicate that for me, fully internalizing this one powerful piece of inspiring profanity has been transformative. But I still find that returning regularly to the well makes all this work even better. So I downloaded both of the Goggins audiobooks and worked through them in little chunks on my morning walks over the period of a month. Then I moved on to Peter Attia’s Outlive, and Jocko Willink’s Extreme Ownership.

In a recent development, while the intellectuals fret about the perils of “Bro Science” or the “Toxic Masculinity” of today’s tribe of health podcasters and question their motivation, I simply absorb the messages that work for me and discard the rest. Find people who make you reach a little higher, and feed on their energy.

And for me, being exposed to successful, strong, athletic people who squeeze a lot of work out of themselves is a big source of inspiration. It helps me do more with my day, which is exactly what works for me right now at this phase of life.

And I wish you more of what works for you too!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

According to recent reports, when it comes to holiday gifts for the runner on your list, here’s the hard truth: No one needs another water bottle or foam roller. Instead, go bold and give shoes. But not just any pair. Choose ones that give their toes more room to move—and could make them a better runner by strengthening their feet.

Altra is famous for its roomy toe box, and here’s why that matters: Research found that wider designs better accommodate the foot’s natural shape than standard running shoes. That extra toe room can reduce stress on the feet and allow a fuller range of motion, reducing the risk of injuries not only in the feet, but also the lower back, hips, knees, and ankles.

Industry observers note that along with its signature Altra Fit (roomy toe box and low drop), Altra offers a model for nearly every fitness enthusiast on your list—including you. Here are some top options.

Chilly mornings, humid evenings, slushy roads—when the daily run is a non-negotiable, there’s no such thing as bad weather, only the wrong shoes. The right ones are the Altra Experience Flow 3 GTX, with a waterproof upper to keep the feet dry and comfy and a grippy outsole for traction on wet surfaces. A low 4mm heel drop with a rocker shape adds a bit of propulsion, so your everyday runner can get more momentum with less effort.

Getting started can feel intimidating for many people, and the sheer breadth of gear choices adds to that overwhelm. Make it easy for the newbie on your holiday list and give the Altra Experience Flow 3, which has swiftly become a fan favorite. The Experience Flow 3 is lightweight, bouncy, and stylish, and it also boasts a rocker shape geometry for a smooth heel-to-toe transition.

Seasoned runners often have two distinct categories of shoes: Ones for long training days and others for race day. The Altra Torin 9 does both jobs, making it a solid choice for the performance-seeking runner who appreciates the ability to wear the same shoes at any distance and still be comfortable. Responsive and soft, with a grippier outsole than the last version, this shoe combines two types of foam for stability and cushioning. There’s also an updated heel shape for improved fit, a secure midfoot that stays in place mile after mile, and the signature toe box that lets toes move freely. This is Altra’s longstanding, bestselling road shoe for a reason.

Trail running is experiencing a massive surge in popularity, with a recent report showing that U.S. participation has jumped by 57 percent since 2019. That means the trail runner on your list may be fresh to the sport, even if they’re not new to running. Because trails can be muddy, rocky, and root-laden, they require a specialized shoe like the Altra Experience Wild 3. Extra grippy for outdoor terrain while still being lightweight, the Wild 3 offers a rocker shape geometry and a super-practical GaiterTrap—a built-in attachment system that allows trail gaiters to lock onto the back of the shoe. There’s also room for the toes while still having the secure midfoot for natural movement around all those trail obstacles.

In a recent development, if your giftee has been conquering terrain for years, they’ve probably heard about the Altra Lone Peak 9, the shoe that put Altra on the map for trail running. It’s been Altra’s bestselling trail shoe for over a decade, and each version gets better. This ninth generation has been reengineered for more durability, with a revised midsole foam that offers lighter weight than previous iterations. A roomy toe box, space through the midfoot, ripstop mesh upper for high-mileage performance, and ultrasticky grip in practically all conditions? Legendary.

Sources indicate that many gym goers like to warm up with a treadmill session before transitioning into strength work, and that usually requires a shoe change. Not anymore. The Altra Escalante 5 is the brand’s beloved cross-trainer, and it shifts from running to lifting like a pro athlete. Strength training shoes require less soft arch support and cushioning because their main job is to provide stability rather than to absorb impact. The Escalante 5 has a low stack height, streamlined design, and zero drop. That keeps the feet completely flat, mimicking a natural barefoot position favored by serious lifters, while still providing good lateral support for cross-training and functional workouts.

According to recent reports, packing multiple shoes for a vacation or business trip is about as appealing as trying to sneak liquids past airport security. If your gift recipient is the type who looks for a run soon after stepping off the plane, there’s the Altra FWD VIA 2. Softer and more responsive than the previous version of the model, it also boasts a mesh upper for increased breathability, a roomy toe box, and rocker shape geometry. Whether someone is running through the airport, sightseeing for hours, or putting a workout on the vacay itinerary, this is the perfect travel partner.

Elizabeth Millard is a freelance writer focusing on health, wellness, fitness, and food.

Latest Update: Assault Fitness AssaultBike Pro X Review (2025): Assault’s Best Bike Yet?

📅 15 Dec 2023 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2764 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Breakingmuscle

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that the Assault Bike ProX is one of the best cardio machines presently offered, as it provides a full-body, low-impact workout that can still be high-intensity.
  • Here at Breaking Muscle, our experts include athletes, strength and conditioning coaches, and certified personal trainers who are intimately familiar with this fan bike.
  • At Breaking Muscle, we know exercise equipment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the Assault Bike ProX is one of the best cardio machines presently offered, as it provides a full-body, low-impact workout that can still be high-intensity. Popular in the CrossFit community, this fan bike consists of a belt-driven system and a heavy-duty steel frame, making it a great tool to build both endurance and strength.

Here at Breaking Muscle, our experts include athletes, strength and conditioning coaches, and certified personal trainers who are intimately familiar with this fan bike. We put it through hours of strenuous cardio workouts to see if it could take on the challenge. In this Assault Fitness AssaultBike Pro X review, we’ll highlight our results, how well the bike ranked in testing, and how it compares to other fan bikes.

At Breaking Muscle, we know exercise equipment. We have a product testing team that has put hundreds of machines through the wringer, using them for everything from gentle warm-ups to high-intensity interval training (HIIT) workouts. Many of our staff members are home gym owners themselves and use these products nearly every day.

In a recent development, with the knowledge we’ve gained over the years, we created a proprietary scoring system that we used to rank the AssaultBike ProX in various categories. Not only did we evaluate how the bike performed on its own, but we also compared it with nearly 30 other exercise bikes to see how it stacked up against the competition.

Recent findings suggest that from the founders of the AssaultRunner (one of the best treadmills to train with), the Assault Bike ProX is made with a heavy-duty steel frame finished in a black powder coat that helps keep it corrosion-resistant and capable of standing the test of time. It is a top-tier fan bike that can provide a brutal workout for any athlete.

In addition to its tough and durable frame, it incorporates a belt-driven system for a quiet, smooth training experience. It also requires less upkeep than chain-driven systems, which should come as a relief to busy individuals who can’t be bothered with complicated maintenance protocols.

At the time of writing, the Assault Bike ProX costs $899. Fortunately, there is also an option to finance it at around $82 a month through Affirm. For comparison, the Assault Bike ProX is more expensive than the AssaultBike Classic at $699 but cheaper than the Concept2 BikeErg, which costs around $1,100.

According to recent reports, the Assault Bike ProX also provides free shipping, which is a big deal for equipment this size. Buying an air bike from another brand could set you back another $100 in shipping costs.

All of the above considered, we’ve rated this bike 4 out of 5 stars for its shipping rate, finance options, and value.

Recent findings suggest that the Assault Bike ProX weighs 125 pounds, has a max user weight of 330 pounds, and boasts a heavy-duty steel frame with a corrosion-resistant black powder coating finish. We love this type of frame and finish because it means less maintenance over time.

Sources indicate that it’s also similar to what you would see with the Rogue Echo Bike, which has a black powder coating and almost looks like it was built from scraps of a heavy-duty squat rack! But the Assault Bike ProX isn’t as bulky as the Rogue Echo Bike, making it more compatible with small spaces, which our product testers enjoyed. For comparison, the ProX is 51.73 inches long, 24.52 inches wide, and 52.51 inches high, while the Echo Bike is 55 inches long, 29.5 inches wide, and 52.25 inches high.

The Assault Bike ProX provides a wide padded seat that can adjust to 11 different heights and six different directions either forward or backward. These adjustments were the same on the Assault Bike Pro, which the ProX replaces. The rubber handles on the ProX help you maintain your grip and keep your hands comfortable throughout the workout as well.

It has been revealed that this fan bike also comes with footpegs at the base of the handlebars for you to place your feet. This gives you the option to do an upper body-only workout, which is great for injury recovery or arm day.

Based on the quality and construction of the Assault Bike ProX, we rated it 5 out of 5 stars.

Recent findings suggest that we gave the AssaultBike Pro X 5 out of 5 stars for delivery and assembly because of how straightforward it was to build. The bikes arrived at our testing facility 75 percent built, so all we had to do was attach the LCD console, pedals, handlebars, seat post, and saddle. Assault Fitness provides all the tools needed to build your air bike, and it should take roughly 35 to 45 minutes.

According to recent reports, when testing the Assault Bike ProX, we noticed a smoother and quieter ride than what we’ve experienced with other air bikes, like the Titan Fan Bike or the AssaultBike Classic. This is predominantly thanks to the belt-driven system. A belt-driven system requires less maintenance than a chain-driven system, but it is also harder to use. When you pedal, the steel fan wheel generates resistance based on your effort. The harder you pedal, the more resistance is applied.

However, once you stop pedaling, the fan wheel will stop moving, requiring more effort to get it started again. This might be tough if you’re not prepared for a high-intensity workout. Due to this, we gave the Assault Bike ProX a 4 out of 5-star rating for performance.

In a recent development, the Assault Bike ProX’s LCD monitor provides seven built-in training programs and a competition mode for those ready to take on the challenge. Through the Assault Fitness App, which we’ll review below, there is also an option to follow instructor-led programs or create customized workouts.

According to recent reports, all in all, we give it a 3 out of 5 star rating in this category. The included workouts aren’t as robust as what you’d see in a more interactive bike like the Peloton. However, we do appreciate having them and think they can be valuable for people who may not know where to start.

Sources indicate that while the AssaultBike Classic was only compatible with the Polar T34 heart rate chest strap, the Assault Bike ProX is compatible with other brands, like Garmin. You can link a heart rate monitor through the bike’s Bluetooth features. However, you need to purchase a compatible one separately, which is why we only rated it 4 out of 5 stars here (though to be fair, this is common for most exercise bikes).

The Assault Bike ProX comes with a five-inch by eight-inch monitor, which is a common size amongst other fan bikes. This high-quality LCD monitor is powered by four AA batteries, which Assault includes with your purchase. The console is great for tracking stats such as calories, distance, heart rate, speed, watts, and RPM. It also connects to the Assault Fitness App.

Sources indicate that our product testers loved that it could track power output in addition to distance and speed, which is a great measure of energy expenditure to quantify workout intensity. The Rogue Echo Bike monitor doesn’t provide feedback such as watts and RPM on its monitor, which gives the Assault Bike ProX the edge.

All things considered, we’ve given this bike 5 out of 5 stars for its display and tracking capabilities.

When testing the Assault Bike ProX, we noticed a ton of conveniences. First, the air bike requires no electric outlet, and we loved being able to use it anywhere. This feature is also a welcome benefit for commercial CrossFit gym owners, as you don’t have to worry about your members tripping over power cords.

According to recent reports, other conveniences include a device holder and a water bottle holder. Some fan bikes like the Titan Fan Bike also include these conveniences. Others, like the Rogue Echo Bike, don’t (though they are available to purchase separately). We always appreciate it when a brand throws in little extras like this. They allow you to have all your workout essentials within reach. Plus, you don’t have to worry about potentially placing multiple orders or paying extra shipping fees to get them.

Overall, our product testers rated the conveniences 4 out of 5 stars. The only reason we docked a point is that we wish the bike came with a wind guard to prevent cold air from blowing in our faces when training in a cold garage. There is one available on the Assault Fitness website, but you have to buy it separately for an additional $39.

The Assault Bike ProX is a part of the Assault Fitness line of exercise machines that operate using the Assault Fitness app. The app was one of our product testers’ favorite features.

Free to download from the App Store and Google Play, the Assault Fitness App provides you with a multitude of instructor-driven workouts. You can do these workouts on your own or compete against other athletes virtually. Many of the workouts also integrate other types of equipment, such as dumbbells and kettlebells, to help you get more well-rounded programming.

While we enjoyed the app, we only gave it 4 out of 5 stars. As of this writing, it’s not available on the most recent version of Android. Athletes with newer Android phones may not be able to use it.

Recent findings suggest that the Assault Bike ProX is Bluetooth-enabled. We don’t necessarily consider Bluetooth connectivity a standout feature, as dozens of cardio machines we’ve tested now come with it. But we’ve also tried inexpensive cardio equipment that doesn’t have this feature, and even Assault Fitness’s classic AssaultBike lacks Bluetooth capabilities. As such, we rated the ProX 5 out of 5 stars here.

When comparing other fan bikes we tested, the Assault Bike ProX generated less noise due to its belt-driven system. The belt-driven system operates more smoothly than chain-drive systems such as those on the Schwinn Airdyne. A noisier system can make it tough to perform workouts at home, especially if you train early in the morning or late at night when others are sleeping.

That said, no fan bike will be completely silent, so you should still expect some noise as air travels through the flywheel. Due to this, we give the noise level of the Assault Bike ProX 4 out of 5 stars.

Sources indicate that the Assault Bike ProX offers some portability, thanks to two small transport wheels at the front. To move it, all you need to do is tilt it onto its wheels to help glide it across the floor. However, although it might be easy for some athletes to move this fan bike, others might struggle to relocate it because it weighs 125 pounds. Based on these findings, we give the portability of the Assault Bike ProX 4 out of 5 stars.

The Assault Bike ProX has a three-year non-wear parts warranty and a seven-year frame warranty. The three-year non-wear parts warranty doesn’t cover normal wear and tear on parts like the seat, pedals, and handle grips. This may seem like a drawback, but in our experience, this is common in warranties on other brands’ fan bikes. But the length of Assault’s warranty is longer compared to Rogue, who only offers a two-year warranty on their Echo Bike, and Titan, who only offers a one-year warranty on their fan bike. We gave the warranty of the Assault Bike ProX 5 out of 5 stars for this reason.

Industry observers note that the Assault Bike ProX is 51.73 inches long, 24.52 inches wide, and 52.51 inches high. Compared to the classic AssaultBike, these dimensions are one to two inches bigger in each category. If you’re between the two, we definitely recommend measuring carefully to ensure you choose the one that will best fit your space.

Sources indicate that the Assault Bike ProX is a fan bike, meaning it builds resistance based on how much air you recruit in the fan wheel as you work. The harder you pedal, the more air resistance is applied, making your workout more challenging.

In addition to air resistance, the ProX uses a belt-driven system, meaning it only operates when you begin to pedal. If you stop pedaling, the machine stops moving. This makes it harder to operate compared to a chair-driven system, like what you’d see with the AssaultBike Classic.

The weight capacity of the Assault Bike ProX is 330 pounds. This is more than the Classic bike, which holds 300 pounds, but less than the Elite, which holds up to 350 pounds.

The Assault Bike ProX can accommodate most body sizes with 11 different height settings and six front-to-back settings. These adjustment levels are relatively standard based on what we’ve seen on other fan bikes. However, some competitors like the Rogue Echo Bike only have five front-to-back seat settings.

Because the Assault Bike ProX does not require an electrical outlet, you can transport it wherever you want to go —outdoors or indoors. The monitor, however, does require AA batteries to operate.

At first glance, it seems the Assault Bike ProX and Rogue Echo Bike have many similarities. When you analyze them more closely, you’ll find that there are several key differences between the two.

Below are the dimensions of both fan bikes:.

According to recent reports, even though the Rogue Echo Bike is bulkier in material and dimensions, it has the same 330-pound weight capacity as the AssaultBike ProX. Both of these fan bikes are also powered by movement, so no electrical outlet is needed. Further, weighing in at 123 and 125 pounds, respectively, the Rogue Echo Bike and the Assault Bike ProX are equally portable, especially given they both have wheels.

Industry observers note that finally, both products use belt-driven mechanics, providing a smooth and quiet riding experience. But the Assault Bike ProX gives more metrics on the monitor, such as watts and RPM. This feature alone could make or break your decision, depending on how important tracking is to your training.

Industry observers note that the Assault Bike ProX comes in with a strong 4.6 out of 5-star rating on the Assault Fitness website. Many users claim that it is super easy to set up, requires low maintenance, and is a favorite piece of equipment in their home gyms. Customers also praise its sturdiness and its ability to handle a tough workout.

Recent findings suggest that one user mentioned that the left peg became loose during their workout. Another buyer mentioned that the Assault Bike ProX was very noisy and didn’t think it was as stable as other reviews might suggest — note, however, that complaints like this are in the minority.

In a recent development, after extensive research and testing of the Assault Bike ProX, we can say that this air bike is worth it. Made with a heavy-duty steel frame finished in a black powder coat, it can take on the toughest workouts. It’s ideal for anyone looking for a full-body, high-intensity interval training machine for improving both endurance and strength.

The smoother and quieter experience you get with the Assault Bike ProX is thanks to the belt-driven system integrated into the design. Although this system might require more effort to operate, this bike can still be a great purchase for everyone from CrossFitters to health and fitness enthusiasts.

In a recent development, the Assault Bike provides a great workout, combining air resistance and a belt-driven system for a tough cardio and muscular endurance workout. You can use both the foot pedals and the arm handles to get a full-body workout. Or you can just use the arm handles to work out your upper body exclusively.

It has been revealed that the Assault Bike Pro X is a belt-driven system. The fan bike only works when you operate the pedals and/or handlebars. The belt-driven system also offers a smoother and quieter workout.

The AssaultBike alone may not aid fat loss if you’re eating too many calories. However,  it can provide a strong enough stimulus for an intense enough workout to help you burn more calories and hit multiple health and fitness goals.

Because the AssaultBike Pro X requires a full-body effort and utilizes a belt-driven system, you could potentially build a small amount of muscle by using it consistently. However, resistance training with implements like dumbbells or barbells (and following a diet that supports muscle growth) will be your best bet if you want to pack on as much muscle as possible.

#149623. I Thought I Was Getting Slower Because of Age. Then an Incidental Scan Revealed the Real Problem—and Likely Saved My Life.

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2796 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Runnersworld ↗ Open Full Page

I Thought I Was Getting Slower Because of Age. Then an Incidental Scan Revealed the Real Problem—and Likely Saved My Life.

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2796 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that last year, a lung scan—ordered even though I’d ground out my last butt decades earlier—incidentally picked up a bulge in my aorta.
  • It has been revealed that I was baffled.
  • Sources indicate that further tests revealed the diameter of my aorta to be twice the normal size.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Smoking may have saved my life.

It has been revealed that last year, a lung scan—ordered even though I’d ground out my last butt decades earlier—incidentally picked up a bulge in my aorta. Because I smoked heavily when I was young, my doctor sent me for a screening after the age eligibility had been lowered, just in case. While the scan didn’t find any signs of cancer, it detected something else. An aneurysm: a weak spot in the body’s main artery that causes it to balloon.

It has been revealed that I was baffled. I was in my mid-fifties and healthy. I had no family history of cardiovascular problems. I was a longtime runner. I ate my veggies and hadn’t had a drink in 27 years. My resting heart rate was borderline smug.

Sources indicate that further tests revealed the diameter of my aorta to be twice the normal size. Putting me at risk of an aortic dissection or rupture, both life-threatening emergencies that demand immediate treatment.

In a recent development, damn. How long had I been walking—and running—around with this fault line trembling in my chest?

Industry observers note that while waiting for an appointment with a cardiologist, I was seized with anxiety. I stopped exercising. I practiced randomly unlocking the emergency feature on my phone and swiftly making a mental note of my location.

In a recent development, an echocardiogram later revealed that the bulge had also pulled apart the leaflets of my aortic valve, preventing them from sealing tightly. With every heartbeat, some of the blood my heart pumped out leaked backward, forcing it to work harder to circulate the same blood twice.

“Given that you’re only in your fifties and live an active lifestyle,” the cardiologist said, “I’d suggest you consult with a cardiac surgeon.”.

The last sentence I thought I’d ever hear. Until I was met with, “Let’s schedule you for open-heart surgery.”.

Looking back, I wondered if there had been signs. I had tried to run at least one marathon or ultra a year, along with some shorter distances. In recent years, no matter how hard I trained, I could never improve my times, my marathons creeping up from low four hours to a whisper below five. I increasingly had to run/walk the final miles. I tried a vegan diet to improve my energy and switched to forefoot running for more spring in my stride. Nothing budged. Maybe I was just getting older.

Gradually, and then seemingly all at once, running became a grind. I started cutting workouts short. The hills felt steeper. The part I looked forward to most was stopping. The joy I had always found in movement was supplanted by fatigue and frustration and more frequent visits to my physical therapist. After plodding across the finish line at the 2025 Falmouth Road Race, I hit the pause button and wondered if I’d ever press play again.

Running has been part of my identity for most of my adult life. After years of flailing, it demonstrated me I was capable. It soothed the anxieties of sobriety and helped me believe I was more than the drunken jerk many people knew when I was in my teens and twenties. It was a sandbox for role-playing difficult conversations, reckoning with my trespasses, and cultivating humility. It was where the idea for my first book took shape and stories took root. It was a way to find people like me, if only through those knowing waves as we passed. Running was more than a healthy habit. It was a partner, my better half.

After all these years, had I fallen out of love? And if I had, who would I be without it?

In a recent development, open-heart surgery involves slicing through the chest, sawing the sternum in two, parting the halves with a retractor, and stopping the heart. The task of keeping you alive is outsourced to a machine. Even though doctors have been successfully performing this procedure for decades, when it’s you going up on that table, it feels like science fiction.

Sources indicate that as the date of my surgery crept closer, fear and anxiety filled me like a helium balloon. The idea of intubation kept me up at night. What if I wake gagging and rip the tube out?

The mortality rate was one in a hundred.

I calmed myself the way I would before a significant race: meditation, yoga, and Peggy Huddleston’s pre-surgery relaxation techniques. I studied “the course” and sought out people who’d been through it, looking for any kind of mental edge. And though I was not a religious person, I asked friends and family for prayers, having read that they’d been shown to influence outcomes.

According to recent reports, early one morning in February, I was wheeled into an operating bay at Massachusetts General Hospital, knocked unconscious and chemically paralyzed. Over the next five hours, my surgeon removed my diseased aortic root and ascending aorta, replaced them with a synthetic graft and carbon valve, and hooked my coronary arteries back up to the upcoming plumbing.

When they took me off bypass, my heart forgot how to beat. Instead of pumping, it quivered, seized by electrical chaos. Ventricular fibrillation. The doctors had to shock my heart back into rhythm. Four times. Inside the cardiac OR, the team was ready. Anywhere else, it would have been goodnight, Irene.

Industry observers note that I knew none of this when I groggily opened my eyes in the ICU that evening. I felt trampled. I could see the breathing tube that had haunted me for weeks protruding from my mouth, my hands bound to the bedrail to keep me from reaching for it, but I felt no urge, couldn’t feel it. The second time I woke up—the first just brief enough to realize where I was—a voice noted, “Squeeze my hand.” My eyelids too heavy to lift, I managed, then drifted back into blackness. When I stirred again, the tube was gone. Relief. But drainage lines snaked from my chest into canisters, while wires and catheters tethered me to a forest of blinking monitors.

Later, in the step-down cardiac ward, I needed a walker to cover even the shortest distance, the drainage boxes hanging on the sides like hard saddlebags. I was carrying 15 extra pounds of fluid, my fingers fat as cocktail wieners. I shuffled down the hall in grippy socks, a tech beside me and a chair trailing behind should I need to sit.

I spent a week at Mass General, three months of recovery ahead of me. In the early weeks, the focus was on walking. Three minutes at a time. Twice a day. Getting to the end of the block took effort. My wife (stone-cold angel!) set up chairs on the landing so I could stop and catch my breath going upstairs in our house outside of Boston. Instead of crushing miles, I was crushing naps.

Sources indicate that at six weeks, I met with my surgeon for a follow-up. She was pleased with my progress and lifted some restrictions and cleared me for cardiac rehab. She showed me a picture of my valve leaflets riddled with holes. Told me the aneurysm had likely been there for a decade, the aortic wall “paper thin.” I felt dizzy as if peering over the edge of a tall building. You hear about runners collapsing at the end of marathons, about shovelers going down after a snowstorm. Had it only been a matter of time?

As she described the repair—a Bentall procedure, one of the more complex operations in cardiac surgery—a seductive thought wormed its way into my brain. Sure, aging may have started to slow me down, but a leaky, punctured valve must have been robbing my body of strength and energy, too. Now that a set of brand-new carbon leaflets was opening and closing tightly, blood safely moving in the right direction, could I get my running back on track? Maybe emerge stronger and faster, start breaking PRs again. Could I fall back in love?

It has been revealed that I stared at my surgeon, the woman who had held my heart in her hands. Had she seen that old spark still flickering in there?

Cardiac rehab is part safety net, part exercise boot camp. A mini gym with EKG leads and blood-pressure cuffs. When I walked in, an elderly woman in jeans pedaled a recumbent bike while a silver-haired man in a rugby shirt and mask worked an arm cycle. Nearby, an old man plucked one of the resistance ropes that hung from hooks like a swarm of eels. Not everyone had undergone surgery. Some were recovering from heart attacks or stent procedures, others from dangerous arrhythmias or heart failure. I didn’t see anyone else my age.

A physical therapist named Andi asked about my surgery and fitness history, then my goals.

“The seven-mile Falmouth Road Race in four months,” I said. Returning a year later, with a sternum fused by wire, felt like a symbolic milestone. For good measure, I added, “and a marathon next spring.”.

Industry observers note that I leaned back, waiting for her eyes to light up with amazement. I bet she didn’t hear that very often. She kept scribbling. Probably too stunned, I figured.

She handed me a laminated workout card. “No treadmill?” I frowned. “Soon. Let’s see how you do with these exercises.”.

I climbed onto a stationary bike and quietly turned the resistance a few notches above the prescribed setting. I watched my heart rate climb on the monitor above the nurse’s station: 100, 110, 120. Sweat prickled my forehead. That old feeling. For almost two months, my body had belonged to surgeons, nurses, and restrictions. Now, little by little, it would be returned to its rightful owner.

It has been revealed that andi kept her promise. A few weeks later, she prescribed one minute of running. Sixty seconds at a 14-minute pace, followed by two minutes of walking. Five intervals. Three-quarters of a mile. The longest I’d run in eight months. It felt every bit as satisfying as finishing a marathon.

According to recent reports, as I built from one-minute intervals to two, then three, I stopped thinking so much about future PRs and training prepares. I was running again. The minutes stretched. The walks grew shorter. The weeks passed. By the third month, I was running two miles continuously and sweating so much that the EKG leads kept popping off my chest. Andi would laugh and hand me a fresh set.

Industry observers note that when I arrived, I’d seen those sticky leads as signs that I was still a patient. Now they wouldn’t stay on, blanking out my little section on the wall monitor.

On August 16, 2026, I stood among the heaving throngs on Water Street in Woods Hole, the staging area for the Falmouth Road Race on Cape Cod. I stroked my chest. Still tender six months later. Amid shouts and laughter, selfies and the sharp medicinal smell of Bengay mixed with sunscreen, my mind hummed with questions: Was I still the runner I used to be? Did we have a future together? Had my slump been caused by my heart—or “my heart?”.

Every few minutes, the crowd surged forward, then stopped, then surged again—an electrical current passing through thousands of bodies as waves of runners were slowly released onto the course.

Sources indicate that at last we crossed the starting line. As I set off, an old familiar voice rose to taunt me: This doesn’t count as your big comeback if you take walk breaks, and Dave McGillivray ran the entire Boston Marathon six months after heart surgery.

But then the race gave me something else to listen to. The pounding of rubber soles like golf applause. Spectators shaking cowbells and waving signs. The theme song from “Rocky” pouring from unseen speakers at Nobska Light. The cheers rose around us, and somewhere beyond them the waters of Vineyard Sound flashed in the sun, the island a squiggle on the horizon. Then an emptiness settled over the salty air.

Sources indicate that I found myself thinking about who I had become. Or maybe who I’d spent my adult life trying to become. The abstinent runner. The marathoner chasing his father’s PR. The ultrarunner. The trail runner, leaping logs and picking my way across rocks with my trusty dog trotting beside me. Every few years, another version of myself to reel in.

Sources indicate that maybe, for the first time, I needed to stop fishing for some future version of myself. Maybe that was the gift of starting over: the chance to be a beginner again. Who I was 20 years ago. The overweight lug, freshly sober, shuffling down a dirt road in Vermont in the predawn blackness, listening to cicadas and coyotes, watching for flattened frogs and gravel stones the size of baby shoes. The accretion of feeling, competence, and the desire to be a better person. I didn’t know what a PR was. Or a starting corral. My finish line was the sunrise over the Green Mountains. Something I could never reach, only watch in awe. Back when distant light was all I needed.

Recent findings suggest that every few miles of the race, I walked for a minute. No earbuds. A friend ran beside me, an easy presence, and we chatted, and sometimes we didn’t. The race was everything I’d hoped it would be, which is to say: nothing. No expectations. No aspirations. Pace didn’t matter. I only checked my watch to make sure my heart rate didn’t climb above 180. Falmouth reminded me of a few things: that we are remarkably resilient, that the ocean never fails to awe, and, according to one spectator’s sign, that you should never “trust a fart after mile 6.”.

According to recent reports, when I crossed the finish line, I raised my arms perfunctorily and smiled for the photographers, lifting my shirt to flash my scar like I was at Mardi Gras. But on the drive home, the emptiness lingered. No epiphany. No transformation. No cinematic moment of rebirth.

I had run seven miles. And somehow, that was all.

Recent findings suggest that that old blah feeling persisted. It took me longer to get out the door, my pace stuck in the basement. So I put a half marathon on the books.

A rare fall nor’easter blew into town one Friday and was still raging on Sunday: rain and wind blowing sideways, tree branches nearly horizontal, deck furniture scattered. I was behind in my training and needed to get a long run in that weekend. I hemmed and hawed for a couple of hours, hoping it would let up. It didn’t.

Finally, I got dressed. My Garmin had died the week before, so I set off blind. No pace, distance, or heart-rate information. By the time I reached the bike path along the Charles, my clothes were plastered to my skin. Broken branches and leaves littered the pavement. It looked like the aftermath of a house party. Rain hammered the river. With a playlist in my ears, I felt as if I were running through an adventure movie.

Cars sent waves of water rolling over the guardrails. Enormous puddles swamped the path. At first I tried to avoid them. Then I realized there was no point, and it became fun. I splashed through them like a kid.

It has been revealed that I was the only one out there. Despite the wild weather, everything felt quiet, abandoned. And somehow that spurred me on. A small tree had fallen across a wooden footbridge. I had to wrestle it out of the way. Storylines bubbled up. I was racing to the next town after a catastrophic event, seeking help; lives depended on me. I had to keep going.

Finally, I saw another runner, both of us looking like we’d been fished out of a lake. We waved—not perfunctorily, but with a knowing look. Was he running for help, too?

The slap of my feet on wet asphalt took over the soundtrack, along with the gusts of my own breathing and the faint ticking of my mechanical valve in my throat. I had no idea how far I’d gone or how much farther I had to go.

In a recent development, for once, I didn’t need to know. I felt inside and outside everything at the same time, the rain somehow lighting the way.

Caleb Daniloff is a Boston-area writer and author of Running Ransom Road: Confronting The Past One Marathon at a Time and co-author of November Project: The Book: Inside the Free Grassroots Fitness Movement That’s Taking Over The World.

Industry News: Start the Day Strong With This 30-Minute Workout You Can Do Right at Home

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (979 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that an at-home workout that requires zero equipment might sound easy—but this one will change your mind!
  • Sources indicate that dane Miklaus, C.S.C.S., founder of WORK Training Studio in Idaho, took on the puzzle of creating this tough, no-equipment workout and pieced together a creative routine to get your muscles firing on all fronts.
  • In a recent development, “I chose to focus on areas where traditional endurance athletes may have weaknesses due to underutilization,” Miklaus tells Runner’s World.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that an at-home workout that requires zero equipment might sound easy—but this one will change your mind! The fun, challenging exercises (all bodyweight!) target every major muscle of the body, which means you make the most of just 30 minutes of work. Squeeze it in before you head out for the day or whenever you need a movement break today; it’s easy to fit in at any time.

Sources indicate that dane Miklaus, C.S.C.S., founder of WORK Training Studio in Idaho, took on the puzzle of creating this tough, no-equipment workout and pieced together a creative routine to get your muscles firing on all fronts. Consider it your go-to during a busy holiday schedule.

In a recent development, “I chose to focus on areas where traditional endurance athletes may have weaknesses due to underutilization,” Miklaus tells Runner’s World. Because running and most of our daily movements occur in the sagittal plane of motion—that’s forward and backward—we tend to neglect muscles used in lateral (or side-to-side) and rotational movements, causing weakness in these areas. While that not only leads to suboptimal performance, it can also increase your risk of injury, he explains.

“By implementing a lower-body routine that incorporates lateral and rotational movements, as well as upper-body and core training, runners can increase their overall athletic standards and the functional capacity of their bodies,” Miklaus notes.

In addition to making you move in different planes of motion, this workout also alternates lower-body and upper-body or core exercises. That way, one muscle group gets rest as the other works, Miklaus explains, without you having to take much actual rest time.

The lower-body moves also get more difficult as you work through the seven-exercise circuit, while the upper-body ones become less intense. “This is intended to provide a balanced challenge and allow each athlete space to scale the difficulty [of the workout] to their own fitness level,” Miklaus explains.

How to do the workout: Do each exercise in order for 45 seconds. Rest for 15 seconds while also transitioning into the next move. Repeat for four total sets.

You don’t need any equipment for this workout, but an exercise mat is optional. Miklaus demonstrates each exercise in the video above so you can learn proper form.

In a recent development, why it works: Target the muscles that support the hips—including the gluteus medius and minimus (the smaller backside muscles) and the piriformis (deep butt muscle)—as well as the hamstrings, adductors (inner thighs), and gluteus maximus (biggest muscle of the butt). “A more stable hip is a stronger hip, and because runners rely on their hips for every stride, exercises like these are a must,” Miklaus notes.

Sources indicate that why it works: While you’ll hit your chest and shoulders, push-ups are also great for strengthening the deep core muscles and shoulder stabilizers, Miklaus indicates. The shoulder tap also adds an anti-rotation element to turn up the core-stability challenge.

Why it works: “When all you have for equipment is in your own bodyweight, adding a speed or power component is a great way to increase muscular recruitment,” Miklaus claims. “So, by dropping into the squat and absorbing that force, then rebounding back out of it quickly, we turn on more of our leg muscles than if we performed a basic bodyweight squat.” The twist at the top means more fire in the rotational hip and core muscles, too.

Why it works: While runners get some biceps activation on the run during the arm swing, they often neglect their triceps, Miklaus says. This move changes that, plus it still taps into core strength.

Industry observers note that why it works: Build hip strength and stability with this exercise that creates a “triple extension” a.k.a. when the hip, knee, and ankle joints all get in on the action.

In a recent development, plus, “just like with the drop squat, this single-leg hop variation will recruit almost every fiber in an athlete’s glutes, quads, and calves, to make them more forceful and dynamic,” Miklaus says. “What runner couldn’t stand to be a bit more explosive?”.

Why it works: “When performing bodyweight exercises, it’s very difficult to stimulate the back muscles,” Miklaus notes. But this move activates the latissimus dorsi (major muscle of the back), teres major, and posterior deltoid (both on the back of the shoulder). “This is important for helping to provide postural balance for athletes who only incorporate pushing movements into their upper-body routines,” he adds. Finally, the plank hold with knee drive means your abs and obliques get worked, too.

Sources indicate that why it works: The skater exercise forces you to slow down momentum, stabilize, and then explode again, Miklaus explains. “When moving laterally, and into a hinged position, we are able to recruit more of the deep hip muscles than is possible when only moving in the sagittal plane,” he indicates. In addition to strengthening muscles at the hip, it also improves ankle stability.

Mallory Creveling is an ACE-certified personal trainer and RRCA-certified run coach, who also holds certifications in kettlebell training, sports performance, and more. She has more than 15 years of experience covering fitness, health, and nutrition for a wide range of publications, and nearly 10 years of experience as a trainer and fitness instructor. Mallory stays on top of her continuing education in fitness, as well as the latest science in wellness. She has worked with some of the best experts in their medical fields, and regularly interviews researchers, trainers, athletes, and more to find the best advice for readers looking to improve their performance and well-being. As a freelance writer, Mallory's work appeared in Women's Health, Self, Men's Journal, Reader's Digest, and more. She has also held staff editorial positions at Family Circle and Shape magazines, as well as DailyBurn.com. A former New Yorker/Brooklynite, she's now based in Easton, Pennsylvania.
